text.S1: Chapter 1 - Famous Last Words
text.T1: Caandaano Cakutaanguna – Majwi Adumide amamanino

text.S1: All children grow up. All except one. Wendy learned this when she was playing in the garden one day at the age of two. She brought her mother a flower, and Mrs. Darling hugged her and said, “Oh, why can’t you stay like this forever and ever?” Before that day, Wendy didn’t realize she wouldn’t stay the same. Wendy had two younger brothers, John and Michael. They were growing, too.
text.T1: Boonse bana balakomena. Boonse ikuzwisya omwe. Wendy wakaiiya eeci naakali kusobana mumuunda ibuzuba bomwe naakali amyaka yakuzyalwa yobilo. Wakaletela banyina iluba, mpoona bamuka Darling bakamukumbata akwaamba kuti, “Oh, ino ninzi ncotakonzyi kubedelela mbweenaoobu kukabe kutamani?” kabutana sika ibuzuba oobuya, Wendy tanakayeeya kuti tacikonzyi kukkala mbweena buya. Wendy wakalijisi basyoonto bakwe basankwa bobilo, John aa Micheal. Abalo bakali kukomena.

text.S1: Mrs. Darling stayed home with the children while Mr. Darling went to work in stocks. His stocks didn’t always work for him, however, and so the family had to scrimp and save. They still had a nanny, of course, because all the other families in the neighborhood had one, and Mr. Darling cared very much about keeping up with the neighbors. But the Darlings were poor, and so their nanny was actually just a giant dog named Nana.
text.T1: Bamuka Darling bakacaala kung’anda abana iciindi ba Darling nibakaunka kukubeleka muziliba. Iziliba zyakwe tezyakalikumubelekela kabotu, pele, imukwasyi wakamufutula. Bakalijisi imubelesi, nkokuti, nkaambo kakuti yoonse mikwasyi iikkala munsimunsi yakalijisi mubelesi, alimwi ba Darling bakali bakali kubikila maano kulangalanga bamikwasyi iili munsimunsi lyabo, pele mukwasyi waba Darling wakali pengede, nkokuti imubelesi wakali biyo mubwa mupati wakali kwiitwa kuti Nana.

text.S1: Nana was an interesting nanny, to say the least. She didn’t believe in all this newfangled talk about germs. Sometimes she would lovingly lick the children right after she licked her own foot. Mr. Darling was ashamed of Nana, and sometimes he was cold to her as a result. He shouldn’t have been. She was actually quite a treasure. If the children wandered or dilly dallied on their way to school, she would bump them with her big head to get them back on track. She never once forgot John’s soccer uniform, and she usually carried an umbrella in her mouth, instead of a bone, in case of rain. And it did rain quite often in England.
text.T1: Nana wakali mubelesi ukondelezya, kwaamba biyo cancobeni. Takasyoma mumakani akatalika kwambaulwa aa tuzunda. Izindi zimwi wakali kumyankuta bana caluyando bwamanina kulimyankuta kukulu. Ba Darling bakali kufwa nsoni kaambo ka Nana, mpoona zimwi ziindi bakali kucita mbuli kuti tabamubwene. Tebakaelede. Wakali kuyandika nankaambo kakuti kufumbwa bana kuti bamukamuka akuunka kucikolo, wakali kubauma amutwe wakwe mupati kutegwa babikile maano kukweenda kuunka kucikolo. Kunyina nakalubide iyunifoomu ya John ya mu bbola, kabwezede acikwabililo camvula kumulomo wakwe, muciindi cakubweza ifuwa, kuti ndiza inga yawa imvula. Mpoona zindi yakali kuwa imvula ku England.

text.S1: All in all, the Darlings were a normal, happy English family. Until, that is, the arrival of a boy named Peter Pan. Mrs. Darling had never heard of Peter Pan until one day when she was tidy- ing up her children’s minds. Most good mothers do this after their children are asleep—as if minds are drawers and children’s memories are underwear and socks that need to be neatly folded and put away. Oh, how Mrs. Darling would wrinkle her forehead sometimes at the sweet things she found in her children’s minds, wondering where on earth they had picked them up. These things, she would lay out and lovingly smooth on the bed for the children to slip on first thing in the morning. Other times, however, she found mean or ugly thoughts in her children’s sleepy heads. She would shake these out and quickly hide, like something pushed under the bed. Children’s minds are a curious place. If someone could draw a map, it would be full of zigzag lines and squiggles. Eventually, however, all the lines and squiggles would lead to Neverland.
text.T1: Imukwasyi waba Darling ulilomene, alimwi mukwasyi uukkomana wabamakuwa. Ikusikila kuboola kwa, mwana musankwa witwa zina lya Peter Pan. Bamuka Darling tabana mvwide izina lya Peter Pan kusikila buzuba nobakali kubamba mizeezo ya bana. Bamazyali boonse balacita oobu kufumbwa bana baunka mukoona – mbuli kuti ibongo ninkomo alimwi imizeezo ya bana ntwakusama twakunsi ama sokesi aelede kupimpwa akubikwa kabotu.Oh, Bamuka Darling mbobakonzya kumemenyana kumutwe zimwi ziindi kuzintu zibotu nzyobakajana mumizeezo yabana babo,kukakilwa kuyeeya nkobakabajana na nkuli. Izintu eezi, bakalikuyala kabotukabotu abulo aakuti bana baone cakutanguna mafumofumo. Izindi zimwi. Bakali kujana imizeezo mibyabi mumitwe yabana babo.inga baizungaanya mitwe yabana babo mpoona bayuba, mbuli kuti kuli ncobatonkela munsi aabulo.Imizeezo yabana lyoonse njakuyandisisya kuziba zintu. Ikuti muntu umwi wasola kweenga maapu yacilao cimwi, inga yazula biyo myeengo iinyongene iinyina ankoigama. Camamanino, yoonse myeengo iiyongene inga yagama ku Neverland.

text.S1: What is Neverland? you ask. It is the magical island in the middle of every child’s mind. It is a place children go to mainly in their imaginations, unless of course they have an invitation and a very special guide. Every child’s Neverland is slightly different. Some are in color and others are in black and white. Some have ragged coral reefs with tiny smashed - up boats, lonely caves, and tiny huts on the beach. Others have hunchbacked little old ladies, turtles laying eggs, or gnomes who like to sew. Others still have scary first days at school, trying not to laugh at church, pop quizzes on grammar that you haven’t studied for, money from the tooth fairy, and chocolate pudding. There are no rules to what one’s Neverland should be. John’s Neverland had a lagoon with flamingos flying over it, while Michael, who tried hard to be like his older brother, had a flamingo with lagoons flying over it. Wendy, mean- while, had a pet wolf and a boat.
text.T1: Ino Neverland caamba nzi? Mula buzya. Ncilao cijanika biyo mumitwe yabana akati kamizeezo yabo, cita biyo kuti baitwa alimwi akutolwa kabotuabotu. Neverland ya mwana uuli oonse iliimpene. Imwii njamabalamabala mpoona yacaala ilasiya aakutuba. Imwii ijisi mabwe aayasa aakumbali kumulonga antoomwe atubeela-beela tunji twakazwa kubwato bwakanyonyoka, itwanda twamusokwe twamabwe, alimwi atwaanda tujanika kumbali aamulonga. Imwii ijisi tucembele tuli aantunda naa kaduuli, tunondo tubikila maji, atubantu tufwafwi katusuma zisani. Bamwi bajisi mazuba akutanguna kucikolo aayoosya, kusola kutaseka mucikombelo, imali ikuzwaku kumeno akupanga. Kunyina milao ijanika mu Neverland yamwana. Neverland ya John yakali jisi cilao cizingulikidwe aamenda azintu zimwi zyuluka atala. Wendy, wakalijisi itudooli twatuyuni abwato itwakusobanya.

text.S1: The island doesn’t appear on any map, because it never stands still. If you can find it, Neverland is a very fun place to visit during the day when it’s sunny. But in the two minutes before children go to bed, it becomes scary and full of shadows. That is why night - lights were invented.
text.T1: Icilao cizingulukidwe aameenda tacijaniki amaapu noiba yomwe, nkaambo tacikonzi kwimikila kakunyina kuzungaana. Kuti naa mwakonzya ikuijana Neverland ncilao cikkomanisya kuswaya ciindi camasikati nokucili izuba. Pesi mukaindi kasyoonto ibana kabatanaunka mukoona, cileta kuyoowa akweeta izinzimwemwe. Ncecakapa kuti kubikwe malaiti aayaka masiku.

text.S1: Mrs. Darling didn’t know anything about Neverland. Or rather, she did, from her own childhood. But she had long since forgotten, and so was confused when she bumped into the island in her travels through her children’s minds. There were other things that confused her, too. For starters, there was the name Peter, which came up again and again, in bolder letters than any other word in all of her children’s minds—especially Wendy’s. “Who is this Peter?” she asked her daughter. “Is he a friend of yours?” “Well,” Wendy admitted, “not always.” “You know I don’t like you talking to strangers,” Mrs. Darling said. “But he isn’t a stranger, Mother. Don’t you remember him?”
text.T1: Bamuka Darling tebakazi cintu nociba comwe caamba ali Neverland. Naa ndiza wakali jisi nakacili mwana. Pele wakaluba izyakubwana, icaamba kuti bakanyongana nobakasika kuciao cizingulukidwe aameenda mumizeezo yabo. Kwakali zintu zimwi zyaka banyonganya abalo. Cakutaanguna, kwakali izina lyaamba kuti Peter, lyakalikuboola ciindi aciindi, mumabala mapati kwiinda mabala mumizeezo yabana yoonse – ikapati kui Wendy. “Nguni ooyu Peter?” bakabuzya mwana wabo musimbi. “Sena mwenzinyoko?” “Inzya,” Wendy wakazumina, “kutali lyoonse.” “Ulizi kuti nseyandi kuti koambaula abantu mbotazi,” Bamuka Darling bakavwiia. “Pesi talimuntu uutazibidwe, baama. Tamumuyeeyinaa?”

text.S1: “Why, I’ve never heard of him in my life!” Mrs. Darling insisted, but as soon as she said this, she knew it was not quite true. She could not remember meeting Peter, or ever knowing him—no, she was too old for that. But in the back of her mind she recalled a story about a boy who kept children company so that they would not be scared. She was sure that she had believed in him when she was Wendy’s age. “Well, anyway, even if I did remember him, by now he would be grown up, just like me,” she said and tucked Wendy in for the night. “I’m worried about this Peter person,” Mrs. Darling told her husband later that evening. “Don’t be,” he said. “It’s probably just some nonsense put into their heads by that no - good nanny. It will all blow over, wait and see.” These are what are sometimes referred to as “famous last words.”
text.T1: “Ino kayi, nsena mumvide mubuumi bwangu!” Bamuka Darling bakasinikizya, pesi mbwakmanina kwamba boobu, wakaziba kuti taakali masimpe pe. Takalikuyeeya kuswaanganya Peter, na kumuziba – peepe, wakakomenesya kumakani aaya. Pele mumoyo wakwe wakyeeya makani aa mwana musankwa wakali kulanga bana kutegwa kabatayoowi. Wakali syomede kuti wakali kumusyoma naakali aciimo ca Wendy. “Inzya, pesi, nokuba kuti ndamuyeeya, kusikila ciindi ecino wakakomena, mbweena mbuli ndime,” wakavwiia akulalikizya Wendy mubulo imasiku. “Ndiliyoowede akaambo ka muntu wiitwa kuti Peter,” bakaamba bamuka Darling bakaambila balumi babo imangolezya. “Utasoli,” wakavwiia. Ndiza mbuyanga bwakubika mitwe kuli uuya – mubelesyi.ciya ku donkoka kolindila ubone,”Eezi nzyotwita kuti “majwi azzibidwe aamamanino”.

text.S1: Chapter 2 - Now, Peter, Now!
text.T1: Caandaano cabili – Lino, Peter, Lino

text.S1: Children often find even the strangest events rather commonplace. For example, they might casually mention that when they were playing in the woods last Wednesday, they met a ghost and played tag with him on roller skates. It was in just this way that Wendy revealed something quite upsetting to her mother one morning. Mrs. Darling was tidying up the nursery where all of the young Darling children slept and discovered some leaves on the floor. She asked Wendy about them, but Wendy merely replied, “Oh, Peter must have left those leaves.” “What do you mean?” Mrs. Darling asked nervously. “He really is quite messy,” said Wendy, who was a very tidy child. With a sigh, she explained that Peter often came to the nursery at night and sat at the foot of her bed, playing the flute
text.T1: Ibana izindi zinji balajana zintu zigambia zicitika kujanika muzilao zimpeneimpene. Cakutondezya, inga basola kwamba kuti bakali kusobana musokwe ibuzuba bwatatu imvwiki yainda, bakaswanganya ceelo akutalika kusobana acalo. Munzila eeyi buyo Wendy naakasola kwaamba cintu cakanyemya banyina buzuba bomwe mafumofumo. Bamuka Darling bakali ku bamba acilao aakali koona bana boonse ba mukwasyi wa ba Darling akujana matuvu aansi. “Ino waamba nzi” Bamuka Darling bakabuzya cakuyoowa. “Ngwa ddooti ooyu,” wakaamba Wendy, nkaambo walo wakali mulondo. Wakayoya akupandulula kuti Peter wakali kulaboolaboola kucikolo ca bana imasiku akukkaa kumaulu aabulo, kasobanya muntolilo. .

text.S1: “Sweetheart,” Mrs. Darling assured her, “the front door is locked at night. No one can get in.” “He comes in through the window,” Wendy insisted. “He can’t possibly. We are three stories up! Why didn’t you tell me this be- fore?” her mother cried. “I got hungry and forgot,” said Wendy, who was now feeling rather hungry again. While Wendy went to look for a snack, Mrs. Darling stayed behind, still frowning about the leaves. The thing that scared her most was that she was fairly certain they were from a tree that did not even grow in England. She searched the room for other clues, but found none. “You are making a fuss out of nothing at all,” Mr. Darling insisted when she told him. “Now come to bed.”
text.T1: “Omuyandwa wangu” Bamuka Darling bakamwambila, “imulyango wakumbele inga ulajalwa imasiku lyoonse. Kunyina uukonzya kunjila”.”Inga unjilila aa mpulungwido,” Wendy wakavwiila. “Tacikonzyi pee. Tukkala mujulu bwaanda bwatatu! Ino ninzi ncotakandambila?” bakalila banyina. Ndakamvwa inzala mpoona ndakaluba,” wakavwiila Wendy, iwakatalika kumvwa inzala aalimwi. Wendy naakali kuyooyandaula twakulya, bamuka Darling bakacaala, kabamemenyene akaambo ka matuvu. Icintu cakabakonga kapati ncakuti bakalisyomede ikuti akazwa kucisamu catakali kujanika ku England. Bakalangaula mung`anda pesi tabakajana ibwiinguzi. “Ulatongooka kakunyina akaambo, Ba Darling bakazumanana nobakabambila ku balumi kuti “kamuboola mung`anda kwasiya”.

text.S1: I suppose you are right,” Mrs. Darling said. Only he wasn’t. The very next night, she tucked the children in, went downstairs to sit by the warm fire and sew, and fell asleep. Almost immediately she started to dream. She dreamed that Neverland had drifted too close to the beach, and that a strange boy had jumped into the water and was swimming toward her children. Wendy, John, and Michael were on the shore, happily waving him in. This might have only been a silly dream were it not for the fact that, upstairs, the window of the children’s bedroom had blown open and a boy really had flown in and dropped onto the floor. With him was a little light, no bigger than a fist, that darted around the room like a mosquito. Mrs. Darling woke up with a start. She knew at once that the swimming boy was Peter Pan. She ran upstairs, threw open the door to the children’s bedroom, and—sure enough—there he was.
text.T1: “Ndasyoma uliluleme”, Bamuka Darling bakamba. Pele tanakakonzya. Imasiku ngamunya aalya, wakalalikizya ibana, akuseluka kuyookkala kuyotela mulilo, ikusuma akoona. Mpoona mpoona. Mbwakaonena wakatalika ikulota. Wakalota kuti Neverland yakaswenena mumbali aa mulonga, mpoona akuti imwana musankwa uutazibidwe kabotu waksotokela mumeenda mpoona waktalika kusamba kutozya kwakabede ibana. Wendy, John, aa Micheal bakali kumbali aa mulonga, bakanyamuna maanza icakumukkomanina. Ndiza cakali biyo ciloto cabuyanga nkaambo kakuti impulungwido yamung`anda mwakali koona ibana yakapwaika mpoona imwana musankwa wakauluka akuwida aansi. Wakalijisi amumuni uukwana kwaanza, wakamunika mung`anda mbuli kansenya. Bamuka Darling bakabuka cakufwambana. Bakalizi ikuti imwana musankwa iwakali kusamba wakali Peter Pan. Wakalundukila mung`anda yamujulu, akujula cijazyo kwakali koona ibana mpoona - camasimpe inzya – wakaliko

text.S1: He was wearing clothes made of leaves—the same strange kind that he had left behind the last time. But the strangest thing about him was that—although he must have been very old now, at least as old as she—he still seemed to have all of his baby teeth. When Peter saw Mrs. Darling, he bared those pearly little teeth at her and growled. Mrs. Darling screamed, and in a split second Nana was there. She growled, too, and lunged at Peter. He dodged her and jumped out the window. Mrs. Darling screamed again. After all, she didn’t want the boy dead! She looked down but saw no broken body. Looking up, she saw what looked like a shooting star speeding away. When she turned, she saw that Nana had something in her mouth. It was Peter’s shadow. Nana had nipped it with her teeth right before Peter jumped, and the shadow had snapped off.
text.T1: Wakasamide zisani zisumidwe amatuvhu – izikozyanya aa nzyakasiya mazuba aakainda munsi. Icakali kugambya ali nguwe ncakuti – nokuba kuti wakali cembeede, kwendelanya ambwakabeede – wakali kulibonya kuti ucijisi imeno aakubuvwanda. Peter naakabona bamuka Darling, wakavumbula itwino twakwe tusyoonto akuvuluma. Bamuka Darling bakakwiila, mukaindi kasyoonto Nana wakasika. Wakavuluma awalo, akusotokela Peter. Wakamuleya akusotokela ampulungwido. Bamuka Darling bakakwiila alimwi. Nkaambo kakuti tebakalikuyanda ikuti imwana musankwa afwe! Bakalanga aansi pele kwakanyina mafuwa aatyokede. Nobakalanga mujulu, bakabona cikozyanya aanyenyezi iilunduka. Nobakaceba, bakabona Nana kajisi cintu mu kanwa. Cakali cinzimwemwe ca Peter. Nana wakacitenda ameno aakwe Peter katana sotoka, acinzimwemwe cakasweeka.

text.S1: Nana wanted to hang the shadow out the window so Peter could come back and get it without bothering the children. But Mrs. Darling thought that it would look like laundry drying. Mr. Darling would be upset if the neighbors saw that. Instead, she decided to stuff the shadow into the bottom of a drawer, hidden away like one of her children’s unpleasant thoughts. “That horrid dog,” Mr. Darling said when she told him the next day what had happened. “She can’t go around snapping off people’s shadows left and right. Why, we’ll be sued!” Poor Nana. And poor Mr. Darling, too. He knew he was being awful and un- fair, but he couldn’t help it. He was frustrated and jealous—about other people doing better in the stock market, and about the children loving Nana so very much—possibly more than him. It didn’t help matters that Nana had brushed up against him yesterday, getting white hair all over his coat. “Go to the doghouse where you belong!” he yelled at her.
text.T1: Nana wakalikuyanda kusyanikizya cinzimwemwe aa mpulungwido kutegwa Peter ndiza inga wajoka akucibweza kakunyina kupenzya bana. Pesi bamuka Darling bakayeeya kuti inga caboneka mbuli kusanzya kakunyina meenda. Bamuka Darling balakonzya kunyema kuti naa mbobabambene limwi babona. Bakayeeya kubika cinzimwemwe mu cibikilo, kusiswa mbuli mizeezo mibi yabana. ‘Uuya mubwa mubyabi” ,bamuka Darling bakamba nobakabambila bu zuba bwakacilila cakacitikide. “Takonzyi kuyabuzinguluka akubweza zinzimwemwe zya bantu lumwenhi alimwi akululyo. Ino kai, tuya kubetekwa!” Mucaangu Nana. Alimwi bacaangu ba Darling, abalo. Bakalizi kuti bakali kuubizya alimwi akuta-loma, pesi bakibulide mbobakali kukonzya zyakucita.bakali nyemede alimwi amunyono – kaambo kakuti bamwi bantu babeleka kabotu mumakwebo aabo, alimwi akaambo ka bana kuyandisisya Nana kapati – kwiinda nguwe. Teshakagwasya nokuba kuti Nana taakamubikila maano ibuzuba bwakainda, ikubweza boya butuba kujansi lyakwe yoonse. “Koya kung’anda ya mubwa nkokkala nkkoelede kujanika! Wakamubwentela

text.S1: “George,” Mrs. Darling whispered, “remember what I told you about that boy. What if he comes back and Nana’s not here to guard the children?” But Mr. Darling would not listen. He was determined to show everyone who was the master of the house. And so out Nana went. That night, as Mrs. Darling was putting the children to bed and lighting their night - lights, they heard Nana downstairs in the yard, barking. “She is just protesting being chained up,” John said. Wendy was wiser, however. “No, that is how Nana barks when she smells danger,” she said. Mrs. Darling shuddered. Outside, she saw a million stars, some of which seemed to her to be hovering around the house, as if trying to get in. Oh, how she wished that she and Mr. Darling did not have to go to a dinner party tonight! “Don’t worry, Mama,” Michael said. “Nothing can hurt us when our night - lights are lit, isn’t that right?”
text.T1: George,” Bamuka Darling bakavwiya, “koyeya ncendakakwaambila amwana musankwa uuya. Ino kuti wajoka mpoona Nana katako wakulanga bana?” Pele ba Darling tebakali kukonzya kuswiilila. Bakalikukonzya kutondezya bantu boonse iwakali mupati mung`anda. Mpoona Nana wakaunka. Imasiku aalya, bamuka Darling nobakali kulazika bana akuyasya mumuni – wamasiku, bakamvwa Nana aanze, ulakuwa. “wakali kubwenta nkaambo wakali angidwe,” John wakavwiila. Wendy uliamano, nokuba boobo. “Peepe, mbwavuluma Nana kuti wabona ciyoosya,” wakavwiila. Bamuka Darling bakakankkamana. Aanze, bakabona inyenyeezi zinji, zimwi nzibakabona mbuli kuti zizinguluka ing`anda, mbui kuti ziyanda kunjila mung`anda. Oh, bakalombozya kuti bataunki kupokwe masiku aano! “Mutapengi, baama,” Michea wakasomezya. “Kunyina cinga catucisa kuti imumuni – kaumunikide, tee mbombubo?”

text.S1: This was something Mrs. Darling had told the children in the past, so she couldn’t very well take it back now. “That’s right,” she said soothingly. “Night - lights are the eyes a mother leaves behind at night to watch over her babies.”
text.T1: Eeci ncobakali kwaambila bana bamuka Darling, mpoona tebakali kukonzya kucinca calino. “Mbombubo, wakasyomezya kabotukabotu. Imumuni wamasiku nga meso aabanyina ngobasiya kubalangila ibana imasiku,”

text.S1: Besides, she told herself, she and Mr. Darling would be so close, only a few houses away. What could possibly happen? A few minutes later, Mr. and Mrs. Darling were outside, strolling arm in arm to their dinner party. But they were being observed from above. It was the stars, spying. The old stars were glassy - eyed and bored, but the little ones were curious and full of wonder and winks. They didn’t particularly care for Peter, who liked to sneak up behind them and try to blow them out, but they were generally fond of fun—and Peter was all about fun, so they decided to help him tonight. The instant Mr. and Mrs. Darling were safely inside the neighbor’s house, a commotion broke out in the heavens. A chorus of the smallest stars in the Milky Way cried out, “Now, Peter! Now!”
text.T1: Pele, bakalyaambila, balo aba Darling balaswenana munsi, kwainda biyo maanda masyoonto akati. Nciznzi cikonzya kucitika? Nikwakainda kaindi kasyoonto, bamuka Darling abalumi babo bakai aanze,kabayaabweenda kaba jatene kumaanza kabayabuya ku pokwe lya masiku. Pele bakali kulangwa ikuzwa kujulu. Zyakali inyenyezi, izyakali kubalanga. Inyenyezi zyakacembaala zyakali kuboneka – akulangsya, pele zisyoonto zyakali kuyandisisya kumunika akulabalaba. Tezyakali kubikila maano kuli Peter, wakai kuyanda kucilila munsi lyabo akusola kubabbolosya, pele bakali kuyanda kusobana – alimwi Peter wakai kuyanda kusobana, cakapa kuti bayande kumugwasya imasiku aaya. Ba Darling abamuka Darling mbobakanjilila mung`anda yabenzinyina, kwakaba manyongwe kujulu. Inyenyezi zisyoonto syoonto zyakali kusabila, kuti “Lino, Peter! Lino!”

text.S1: Chapter 3 - Acorn Kisses and Jealous Friends
text.T1: Caandaano catatu – Acorn Kisses aa beenzinyina bali aa munyono

text.S1: The night - lights were still burning when Mr. and Mrs. Darling left the house. But even a night -light gets tired sometimes. It is an awful lot of work, as you might imagine, trying to stay bright and shiny all the time. Wendy’s light went out first. It yawned and, yawns being contagious, the other two lights promptly yawned as well. Then, before any of the lights could close their mouths, all three went out from the resulting breeze. The children’s room, however, was still not dark. A strange blinking glow came from within a water jug. Inside was a fairy, no bigger than your hand. Her name was Tinker Bell, and she was in the jug looking for Peter’s shadow. Peter appeared next. “Tink?” he called softly. “Is my shadow in that jug?” “No,” Tink replied, emerging.
text.T1: Imasiku – imumuni wakacili kuyaka ba Darling abakaintu nobakazwa mung’anda. Pele amumuni wa masiku ulakatala kuyaka zimwi ziindi. Cilalemya kapati, kusola kuyaka kuti kutube akumweka ciindi coonse. Imumuni wa Wendy wakasanguna kuzima. Wakaba aa myaayi, mbuli mbomuzi myaayi ilayambukila, imimuni yacaala yobilo ayalo yakaba aa myaayi mpoona-mpoona. Icakaciila, imimuni yacaala kaitana zima, yoonse yacaala yotatwe yakazima akaambo ka muo. Imwakali koona bana, mwalo temwakaningasiya. Iciggambya cakaboola kuzwa mucikapu kacilabalaba. Mukati mwakali kantu, kasyoonto kwiinda janza. Izina kakalinkanga Tinker Bell, mpoona kakali mu cikapu kakalangaula cinzimwemwe ca Peter. Cakatobela Peter wakabonekela. “Tink?” wakaita kabotukabtu. “sena cinzimwemwe cangu mocili mucikapu?” “Peepe,” Tink wakavwiila, naakali kuboola.

text.S1: When Tinker Bell spoke, it sounded like bells. It was a special fairy language that only Peter and his boys could understand. Tink told Peter that she had just spotted his shadow in the chest of drawers. Peter threw open the drawers, piling the clothes in a heap on the floor, and found his shadow. Grabbing it, he tried to slip it back on like a pair of pants, but it would not fit. He tried to put it on like a hat, but it jumped off his head. His shadow, it seemed, did not want him back! Peter sat on the floor and started to cry. His cries woke Wendy, and she sat up in bed.
text.T1: Nakaambaula Tinker Bell, cakalikuvwika mbuli ma bello. Wakali mulaka uuggambya wakali kuvmwa biyo ibana basankwa. Tink wakaambila Peter kuti wakabona cinzimwemwe cakwe mucijazyo cakkabati. Peter wakajula cijazyo cakkabati, mpoona akubika zisani aansi, akujana cinzimwemwe cakwe. Nakacibweza, wakasola kucijosya mbuli kabbudula, pele tecakamwelela. Wakasola alimwi kucisama mbuli nzyeete, pele cakasotoka kuzwa kumutwe. Cinzimwemwe cakwe, cakaboneka mbuli kuti tecakali kumuyanda limbi! Peter wakakkala aansi akutalika kulila. Kulila kwakwe kwakabusya Wendy, mpoona wakabuka akukkala aabulo.

text.S1: “Excuse me,” she asked politely. “Who are you?” “I am Peter Pan,” he said. “Who are you?” “My name is Wendy Darling. I live here.” “I live second to the right,” said Peter, “and then straight on until morning.” “That’s a funny address,” Wendy said. “ “I don’t see what’s so funny about it,” Peter huffed, embarrassed. “Well, what do people write on the envelope when they send you letters?” Wendy asked. “No one sends me letters,” Peter said in a low voice. Now he was not only embarrassed, but sad, too, about his lack of letters. “When your mother gets letters?” Wendy tried weakly. “Oh, I don’t have a mother,” Peter said in a normal voice. The funny address and the lack of letters had bothered him briefly, but mothers, he felt, were over-rated. For Wendy, however, a funny address, no letters, and no mother seemed in- credibly sad.
text.T1: “Amundijatile,” wakalomba kabotukabotu. “Ndinywe bani?” wakavwila. “Nduwe ni?” “Mebo ndime Wendy Darling. Ndikkala waano.” “Ndikkala nga’nda yabili ku lulyo,” wakavwila Peter, “mpoona kuya kumbee kusikila mafumofumo.” “ooko nkokkala kulasesya,” Wendy wakavwiila. “Kunyina nceebona cisesya aawa,” Peter wakayoya ca kuggunwa. “Ino, cinzi bantu ncobalemba atala aaluggwalo nobatuma luggwalo?” Wendy wakabuzya. “Kunyina uunditumina maggwalo,” Peter wakaamba aajwi lya aansi. Takaggunwa buyo, pele wakali tyompedwe, akaambo kakubula maggwalo. “Banyoko nobatambula maggwalo?” Wendly wakasola cakubula nguzu. “Oh, nsejisi bamama, Peter wakapandulula kabotukabotu. Ikukkala kucilao kusesya akutatambula maggwalo kwakamupenzy mumizeezo asyoonto, pesi bamanyina, wakamvwa mbuli kuti cakaindilila. Wendy walo, ikuba aacilao cisesya, ikutatambula maggwalo, akubula banyina cakausisya kapati.

text.S1: “Oh, Peter, no wonder you were crying!” she said. She got out of bed and ran to hug him. “I wasn’t crying about not having a mother,” he huffed. “I was crying be- cause I can’t get my shadow back on. Do you have any glue?” Wendy smiled. How exactly like a boy. “You can’t glue it back on, silly. It must be sewn on. I will do it for you.” Feeling very important, Wendy got her sewing kit. Within minutes, the shad- ow was back where it belonged, even if it was a bit wrinkly. Wendy wondered briefly whether she should have ironed it first. “Yippee!” Peter cried, twirling in front of the mirror. “Look at me and my handsome shadow!” “A thank - you might be nice,” Wendy suggested. “For what?” Peter asked. This made Wendy so mad that she got back into bed and covered her face with the blankets until Peter apologized.
text.T1: “Oh, Peter, anu ncolikulilila!’ wakaamba. Wakabuka kuzwa aabulo akuundukila kuyoomu kumbata. “Tendakalikulila kaambo kakubula bamaama,” wakayoya. “Ndakali kulila nkaambo kakukakilwa kujosya cinzimwemwe. Ulijisi bunzuke bunamatika?” Wendy wakseka. Ibuti mbuli musankwa. “Tokonzi kucinamatika alimwi. Ceelede kusumwa biya. Ndila kubambila kabotu.” Ikulimvwa kulemekwa Wendy wakabweza zyakusumizya. Ikaindi kasyoonto, icinzimwemwe cakajoka mpoceeleede kuba, nokuba kuti cakali nyongene asyoonto. Wendy wakakatazigwa kuti naa wakaelede kucicisa kutegwa cololoke. “Yippee!” Peter wakalila, akuzinguluka kumbele aa mboni. “Kondilanga acinzimwemwe cangu cibotu!” “Ikulumba – inga kwaggwasya,” Wendy wakapa muzeezo. “Ino kai?” Peter wakabuzya. Eeci cakapa Wendy kunyema cakuti wakajokela mubulo akulivumba kumeso angubo kusikila Peter naakalomba kulekelelwa.

text.S1: “I’ll forgive you if you give me a kiss,” Wendy said, turning her cheek to him. She was of the age when she was starting to think about kisses. Peter hesitated, confused. Finally, he dropped an acorn button into her hand. Realizing that Peter was not quite that age yet, and not wanting to embarrass him, Wendy politely thanked him and said that she would wear his kiss on a string around her neck. “How old are you?” she asked. “I don’t know,” Peter said. “I ran away on the very day I was born, after I heard my parents talking about what I would be when I grew up.” “Why?” Wendy asked. “I didn’t want to grow up,” Peter said simply. “Now I live with the lost boys and the fairies.” “Fairies?” Wendy breathed, wide - eyed. Immediately she began to ask Peter everything she could think to ask about fairies.
text.T1: “Ndilakulekelela ikuti undimyonte,” Wendy wakmwaambila, akumujata masaya akumulanga. Wakatalika kuyeeya kumyonta ciindi naakakomena. Peter wakawayawaya, akunyongana. Mamanino wakalosya wakubeza mumaanza. Wakayeeya ikuti Peter tanakomena, akutayanda kumusampuzy, Wendy wakamulumba akwaamba kuti ulasama kumyonta kuzinguluka insingo yakwe. “Ulamyaka yongae?” wakabuzya. “Tandizi pe,” Peter wakvwiila. “Ndakatija buzuba mbondakazyalwa, nondakamvwa ibzyali kabamba mbonditikabe ndakukomena.” “Ino kai?” Wendy wakabuzya. “Tendakali kuyanda ikukomena,” Peter wakavwiila. “Lino ndikkala abasankwa basweekede amizimo.” “Mizimo?” Wendy wakabuzya, ameso – aajulidwe. Mpoona mpoona wakataika kubuzya Peter zyoonse nzyaakali kuyeeya akaambo ka mizimo.

text.S1: “You see,” Peter explained, “when the very first baby laughed for the very first time, its laugh broke into a million pieces. Each piece then became a fairy.” This talk of fairies suddenly reminded Peter of Tinker Bell, who was being awfully quiet. He rose to look for her. Wendy jumped up, excited. “Do you mean to say there is an actual fairy in this room?” They both listened for her, but all Wendy could hear was the tinkle of bells. “Oh, that’s Tink. That’s fairy language.” Peter frowned. “And it seems to be coming from inside that chest of drawers.” Suddenly Peter laughed. He realized he had locked Tinker Bell in the drawer. She must have flown in when he reached for his shadow. Oh, how she screamed when he let her out. “Tink,” he said, watching her fly around the room in a fury, “such language!” “What’s she saying?” Wendy asked, watching the angry blur. “I do wish she would stand still so I could see her! Will she be my fairy?”
text.T1: “Wabona,” Peter wakapandulula, “naakaseka mwana wakutaanguna ciindi cakutanguna, inseko zyakapwaika mutubeela-beela mutuulunzuma. Kufumbwa kabeela kakaba muzimo.” Aaya makani aa mizimo akayeyezya Peter akaambo ka Tinker Bell, iwakaumwine kakunyina akwaambaula. Wakanyamuka akumuyandaula. Wendy wakasotoka cakukkomana. “Undabila kuti muli muzimo oomuno?” Boonse bakamuswiilila, pele Wendy wakali kumvwa biyo kulila kwa milangu. “Oh, ngu Tink. Mulaka wa mizimo.” Peter wakamemenyana. “Alimwi cakaboneka mbuli kuti yakali kuzwida kkabati lijalulwa.” Mpoona mpoona Peter wakseka. Wakayeeya kuti wakajalila Tinka mukkabati lijalulwa. Welede kuti wakasotokelamo nakali kuyanda kujata cinzimwewmwe. Oh, mbwakakwiila nobakamuzwisya aanze. “Tink,” wakaamba, naakali kumulanga kauluka mung`anda, “mulaka ooyu!” “Waamba nzi?” Wendy wakabuzya, kalanga cakunyema. “Nicalikukonzyeeka kaimikila aantomwe kutegwa ndamubona! Sena inga waba muzimo wangu?”

text.S1: “Tink,” Peter said. “Stand still for a second, would you? Wendy wants to see you, and for you to be her fairy.” Tinker Bell clinked something angry in reply. “She says you are a huge ugly girl, and she can’t be your fairy because she is my fairy.” “Well,” Wendy huffed. “She is not very polite.” Peter had to agree. Since Tinker Bell wasn’t cooperating, Wendy turned her attention back to Peter. She had so many more questions for him. He told her all about the lost boys, who had fallen out of their strollers when they were babies and had never been claimed. “I’m their captain,” he said. “What fun!” Wendy replied. “But are there no girls on the island?” “Oh, no,” Peter replied. “Girls are too smart to fall out of their strollers.” “What a nice thing to say,” Wendy replied, blushing.
text.T1: “Tink” Peter wakaamba. “Koimikila kwakaindi kasyonto, yawee? Wendy uyanda kukubona. Akuti ukabe muzimo wakwe.” Tinker Bell wakaamba cimwi kanyemede mukumuvwiila. “Waamba kuti uli cisimbi cineneede cibi, alimwi tokonzi kuba muzimo wakwe nkaambo uli muzimo wangu.” “Pele”, Wendy wakanyema. “Talomene pee.” Peter wakazumizya. Akaambo kakuti Tinker Bell taakali kubelekela aamwi, Wendy wakabikila maano kuli Peter. Wakali jisi mibuzyo minji yakumubuzya. Wakamwaambila zyoonse zya makani aa bana basankwa bakasweeka, ibakawa kuzwa muma pulemu aabo nobakali bana bavwanda mpoona kwiina wakaboola kubabweza. “Ndime mupati wabo,” wakamba. “Eeci casesya!” Wendy wakavwiila. “Pele kunyina basimbi ansumbu?” “Oh, peepe,” Peter wakvwiila. Ibasimbi balicenjede tabakonzi kuwa kuza mumapulemu aabo.” “Icintu kubota cakwaamba,” Wendy wakavwiila, icakuusa.

text.S1: Suddenly Wendy screamed. It felt as if someone had pulled her hair! “That must be Tink,” Peter explained. “She certainly is being naughty today!” Tinker Bell told Peter that she would continue to misbehave so long as Peter kept being nice to Wendy. Just like Mr. Darling, it seemed that the little fairy suffered from one enormous case of jealousy.
text.T1: Mpoona mpoona Wendy wakakwiila. Cakaboneka mbuli kuti kuli wakamukwela masusu! “Ooyu welede kuba Tink,” Peter wakapandulula. “Sunu watalika kuba kayanga!” Tinker Bell wakaambila Peter kuti ulatolelela kunyonganya zintu kuti Peter atolelele kuba kabotu kuli Wendy. Mbuli ba Darling, cakaboneka mbuli kuti muzimo musyoonto wakamvwa bufwi.

text.S1: Chapter 4 - The Birds Leave the Nest
text.T1: Caandaano cazyone – Ituyuni Twazwa mu Cinteente

text.S1: “Peter,” Wendy said, “why did you come to the nursery?” “To hear the story your mother was telling,” Peter replied. Wendy was a bit disappointed to learn that he had not come for her, but she asked, “Which story was it?” “It was the story about the lady who lost her glass slipper. But I had to leave, and I missed the ending.” “That’s ‘Cinderella,’” Wendy said. “I can tell you how it ends. The prince finds her, and they live happily ever after.” Peter turned to the window. “Wait, where are you going?” Wendy asked. “Back to Neverland to tell the other boys!” Peter replied.
text.T1: “Peter,” Wendy wakaamba, “wabolelanzi kung`anda ya bana balesi?” “Ndaboola kumvwa kaambo kakalikwaamba banyoko,” Peter wakavwiila. Wendy wakatyompwa naakajana kuti taakaboolela nguwe, pele wakabuzya, “ino nkaambo kali buti?” “Nkaambo ka mukaintu wakasowa mapatapata amagilazi. Pele ndakazozwa cakapa kuti nditamvwi kaambo mbokakamana.””Ooyo ngu Cinderella,” Wendy wakavwiila. “Inga ndakwaambila mbokakamana. Imwana musankwa wa mwami wakazoomujana, mpoona bakakkala cakukkomana mazuba oonse.” Peter wakalanga ku mpulungwido. “kolindila, uunka kuli?” Wendy wakabuzya. “Ndijokela ku Neverland mukwaambila bana basankwa bamwi!” Peter wakavwiila.

text.S1: “Don’t go,” Wendy begged. “I know lots of other stories, even better than that one.” “Well, then, come on!” he said, dragging her. “We’ll fly back together. You can tell the stories to the lost boys.” “Let go of me!” Wendy cried. She was very flattered to be asked, of course, but she couldn’t leave her poor mother. Besides, she couldn’t fly. “I’ll teach you,” Peter said. Wendy had always wanted to learn how to fly. “Think how much the lost boys will love you,” Peter continued. “You could be a sort of mother to them. You could even tuck them in. None of them has ever been tucked in before.” This was too much for Wendy to resist. She did have very strong maternal feelings. “What about John and Michael?” she asked. “If I leave them, they will be lost boys in a way as well.”
text.T1: “Utaunki,” Wendy wakakombelezya. “Ndilizi twaambo tumwi twandeneandeene, kwiinda aa kaako kaambo.” “Pele, ndamvwa!” wakaingula, kayaakulikwela. “Tuyakuuluka aantoomwe. Inga wambila basankwa baswekeede ikaambo aako.” “kondileka mebo!” Wendy wakakwiila. Wakacimwa ikumubuzya, pele taakali kukonzya kusiya banyina. Alimwi taakali kukonzya kuuluka. “Ndiyakukwiisya, Peter wakaamba. Wendy wakali kuyanda lyoonse ikwiiya kuuluka. “Koyeeya bana basankwa bakasweeka mbobatikuyande,” Peter wakatolelela. “Uyakuba muzyali kuli mbabo. Inga wabavumba akubavumba baunka mukoona. Kunyina naba omwe wakabavumbide.” Eeci cakamuyumina Wendy kuti akake. Wakali jisi inguzu zya muzyali. “Ino John aa Micheal?” Wakabuzya. “Kuti ndabasiya, bayakuba bana basankwa baswekede abalo.”.

text.S1: “They can come. I’ll teach them to fly, too.” At this, the boys jumped out of bed. They had been listening quietly the en- tire time, not letting on that they were really awake. But at the thought of flying, they could no longer stay still. Suddenly Peter spun around. “Shhh,” he said. His eyes narrowed. “Listen. Do you hear that?” Wendy didn’t hear anything. “Exactly,” Peter said. Nana, sensing his presence, had been barking since Peter had entered the nursery. Now she was oddly quiet. “There can be only one explanation,” John said. “She’s broken her chain and is running up here. I want to learn how to fly, and Nana’s going to ruin every- thing!” “Pretend to be sleeping,” Peter instructed. “Tink and I will hide.”
text.T1: “Inga baboola. Ndiya kubaisya kuuluka, abalo.” Nobakamvwa boobo, ibasankwa bakasotoka kuzwa abulo. Bakali kuswiilila kabotukabotu ciindi coonse, kakunyina kulitondezya kuti bakali kulanga. Pele nibakayeeya kuuluka, bakakakilwa ikulilemeka. Mpoonampoona Peter wakazinguluka. “Shhh, wakaamba. Imeso aakwe akaceya. “Kamuswiilila. Mwamvwa eeco?” Wendy takamvwa cili coonse. “Mbombubo,” Peter wakaamba. Nana, wakaziba kuti wasika, wakali kukuwa kuzwa Peter mpakanjilila mung`anda ya bana balesi. Lino wakaumuna. “kuli biyo bupanduluzi bomwe,” John wakamba. “Wadunsula ntambo mpoona ulundukila kokuno. Ndiyanda kwiiya kuuluka, mpoona Nana ulanyonganya zintu – zyoonse!” “Kolicengezya koon,” Peter wakamwambila. “Tink andime tulayuba.”

text.S1: And so it was that Liza, the family cook, saw the children resting peacefully when she entered with the very excited Nana. Liza had finally had enough of Nana’s barking and thought the best way to ease the dog’s mind would be to bring her upstairs and show her that the children were fine. “I told you so!” she whispered to Nana. “They are all safe and sound. Silly dog!” Nana was still suspicious, but Liza would have no more of it. She dragged Nana downstairs and chained her up again. What else could Nana do? She strained and strained at her chain until it fi- nally broke. Then she ran over to where Mr. and Mrs. Darling were dining and burst into the house, barking for help. Even Mr. Darling realized at once that some thing must be seriously wrong at home. Thanking their hosts, he and Mrs. Darling rushed out. But it had been ten minutes since Nana had been in the nursery, and Peter Pan could do a lot in ten minutes.
text.T1: Cakacitika ncakuti Liza, uujikila mukwashi, wakabona bana balalyokezya naakanjila antoomwe aa Nana kakkomene. Liza wakakatala kuswiilila Nana naakali kukuwa akuyeeya kuti inzila mbotu yakulesya Nana ikukuwa nkumuleta mung`anda yamujulu akumutondezya kuti ibana bali biyo kabotu. : Ndali kwambilide!” wakavwiiya kuli Nana’ “Boonse bali biyo kabotu. Okafubafuba kabwa!” wakamuyeeyela Nana, pele Liza taakali kukonzya kuswiilila alimwi. Wakakwelela Nana kuunka kung`anda yaansi akumwaangilila alimwi. Cinzi cimbi nana ncakonzya kucita? Wakasola canguzu kuti aliangulule kusikila limwi nketani yakadunsuka. Mpoona waklundukila kokuya kwaka[i ba Darling abakaintu babo nkobakali kulida akunjila akusabila mpoona akukuwa kuyanda kugwasigwa. Ba Darling mpoona mpoona bakaziba kuti kuli cakalubila mung`anda. Mukulumba balang`anda balo abamuka Darling bakazwa aanze cakufwambaana. Pele kwakainda biyo maminiti aali kkumi kuzwa Nana naakanjila mu nga`nda ya bana balesi, mpoona Peter Pan wakali kukopnzya kubamba zintu zinji mumaminiti aali kkumi.

text.S1: “You simply think wonderful thoughts,” Peter explained, “and they lift you up in the air.” The children tried and tried, thinking the happiest thoughts they could, but still they could not rise from their beds. Of course, Peter was not telling them the whole truth. No one can fly unless some fairy dust has been blown on them. Tinker Bell was still being uncooperative, but Peter had some dust on his hands from holding her earlier. He blew a bit on each of the children and— wouldn’t you know it—they flew! Oh, how they laughed as they sailed clumsily around their room.
text.T1: “Uyeeya biyo zintu zibotubotu,” “Peter wakasola kupandulula, “akukunyamuna mujulu.” Ibana bakasola kwakaindi kalamfu, kabayeeya mizeezo mibotu yalo, pele tebakali kukonzya kuuluka kuzwa abulo. Inzya, Peter taakali kubaambila masimpe. Kunyina uukonzya kuuluka kakunyina kumufululidila lusuko. Tiker Bell waklikukakakaka kubelekela aantoomwe, pele Peter wakali jisi lusuko lusyoonto kumaanza aakwe kuzwakukujana maanza. Wakafulida lusuko kubana boonse mpoona – tamukonzi kuziba – bakauluka! Oh, mbobakasekaseka nobakali kuuluka mung`anda.

text.S1: “Watch out!” Michael cried as he narrowly missed crashing into his brother by the bathroom. “Let’s go outside,” John said. “I’m going to fly for one million miles!” Michael said. Wendy frowned. It suddenly all seemed a bit too real, and risky, now that her brothers were involved. But the sly Peter knew how to make her come along. “Did I tell you about the mermaids?” he said. “Mermaids?” Wendy breathed. Mermaids were even more exciting than fairies. “And pirates,” Peter added. “Let’s go at once,” said John.
text.T1: “Kamulanga!” Micheal wakalila naakali aafwafwi akuliumputa mumpati wakwe munsimunsi aa ku cisambilo. “Atweende aanze,” John wakaamba. Ndiyakuuluka kwiindilila makkilomita manjianji!” Micheal wakaamba. Wendy wakamemenyana. Cakaboneeka mbuli kuti ncancobeni, alimwi cipantenda, linonkaambo kakuti ba mukwabo bakalisangene. Pele Peter wakalizi bwakumubweza kuti atobele. “Sena kuli nendakamwaambilide akaambo ka tosi?” wakaamba. “Itosi!?” Wendy wakayoya. Inswi zikonzya mukaintu zilakondelezya kwiinda mizimo. “Alimwi azigwebenga,” Peter wakabikila. “Atweende linolino,” wakaamba John.

text.S1: Mr. and Mrs. Darling were almost home, but they were not close enough. From the middle of the street, they gasped as they looked up at the bedroom window. Beyond the curtain, the room was ablaze with light. Inside they could see three little shadows whirling around and around—not on the floor but, incredibly, in the air! No, not three figures but four. The stars, still watching from up above, called out a warning. “Peter! The grown - ups are coming back!” There was no time to lose. Peter threw open the window. “Come on!” he cried, soaring into the night. John, Michael, and Wendy followed. Still on the street, Mr. and Mrs. Darling and Nana watched in horror as their three little birds left the nest and were gone.
text.T1: Ba Darling abakaintu babo bakali aafwafwi akusika kung`anda, pesi teebakali munsimunsi. Kuzwa akati kanzila, bakamaninwa muya nobakalanga ampulungwido ya mobaona. Kumbele aa cisitilizyo ceebeka, munga`nda mwakatuba amumuni. Mukati bakabona zinzimwemwe zyotatwe kazizinguluka mung`anda – kutali aansi pele, mujulu, muluo! Peepe, kutali zinzimweemwe zyotatwe, zyakali zyone. Inyenyeezi, zyakali kulanga kuzwa mujulu, kaziita akucenjezya. “Peter! Ibapati - baboola!” Kwakanyina kusowa ciindi . Peter wakajula mpulungwido bukwazi. “Kamufwambaana!” wakalila, kalanga mbokwakali kusiya masiku. John, Micheal, aa Wendy bakatobela. Kabacili munzila ba Darling abakaintu babo aa Nana bakaebela cakugamwa ituyuni totatwe notwakali kuzwa muciteente mpoona twaunka.

text.S1: Chapter 5 - The Long Flight
text.T1: Caandaano casano - Ikuuluka kuunka kule

text.S1: Second to the right, and then straight on until morning. Wendy remembered what Peter had said, but it seemed that even birds car- rying street maps and consulting them at windy corners couldn’t have found Neverland with those directions! And so Michael and Wendy and John had no choice but to follow Peter, and to trust him completely. He led them around in circles, flying past church spires and clock towers and any other tall object that struck his fancy. John and Michael didn’t mind. They were having too much fun flying over the ocean, racing each other be- tween waves. Wendy, however, was worried. It seemed to her that they had been flying for days now. Was the island called Neverland because they would never land? It certainly seemed a possibility!
text.T1: Kutobela kululyo, mpoona kuunka kakunyina kuleya kusikila kubucedo. Wendy wakayeeya Peter mbwakaambide, pele cakaboneka kuti atuyuni tubwezede zipepa zyakubasololela akuzibuzya muluo bakakakilwa kujana Neverland azitondezyo eezyo! Mpoona Micheal aa Wendy aa John bakanyina cakusala pele kutobela Peter, akusyoma biyo nguwe. Wakabatola kayabubazingulusya, kabauluka kwiinda atubulo twakabikwa atala aa cikombelo aa nkoloko ya ningazi alimwi acintu kufumbwa cilamfu cakali kunyomenezya. John aa Micheal teebakali kubikila maana. Bakali kkomene kuuluka atala aa milonga mipati, kabatandana akati ka mayuwe. Wendy, walo wakali yoowede. Wakabona mbuli kuti wakauluka kwa mazuba manji lino. Sena nsumbu yakali kwiitwa Neverland nkaambo kakuti kunyina nobaya kukkala aansi binikuli buyo mujulu naa? Mbocakaboneka!

text.S1: She was relieved, at least, that Peter was feeding them, although his way of doing so was rather strange. He would chase birds that had food in their mouths and steal it. The birds would then steal it back. And so it went like this for a while, until someone managed to gobble the food down. Worst of all, the children were getting incredibly sleepy. Occasionally, one of them would fall asleep while flying and drop like a heavy stone toward the cruel sea below. It always turned out all right. Either the other children would shout, “Wake up!” or Peter would swoop down at the last minute to save the falling child, but they each came awfully close to the water a few times. One of these days, Wendy thought, Peter might let them fall just for the fun of it, because it would be an interesting sight to see. “Don’t make him mad,” Wendy whispered to John. “What would we do if he left us?” “We would go back,” John said.
text.T1: Wakakkomana, nkaambo kakuti Peter wakli kubasanina, nakuba kuti inzila njaakali kubelesya yakali kukankkamanisya. Wakali kutanda tuyuni twakajisi zykulya mukanwa akuzibba. Ituyuni mpoona twkali kuzozibba alimwi. Mpoona cakatolelela mbubwena oobo kwa kaindi kalamfu, kusikila umwi naakakwanisya ku zilya zyoonse mukubinda. Icakabija maningi ncakuti, ibana bakafwa ing`onzi. Iziindi zimwii kwakali kuba kuti omwe mwana ulauluka mpoona zyamubweza ing`onzi wamana wawa walokela mumeenda mbuli bbww lilema. Cakali kucitika lyoonse masiku. Mpoona ibana bamwi bakali kukwiila, “Kobuka!” naa Peter wakali kuseluka cakufwambaana camana ciindi kutegwa agwasye mwana, pele boonse bakali kujanika kuti basika munsimunsi aa meeenda ziindi zisyoonto. Bumwi buzuba, Wendy wakayeeya, Peter uyakubaleka bakawe kabona mbuli kuti nkusobana, nkaambo ciyakuba cintu cikkomanisya ikweebela. “Mutamunyemyi,” Wendy wakapetekezya kuli John. Tuyakucita buti kuti akatusiye?” “Tuya kujokela,” John wakaamba.

text.S1: “We don’t know the way.” “Well, then, we would go on,” said John. “We don’t know that way, either. In fact, we don’t even know how to stop fly- ing.” John thought about this. Wendy was right. Peter had never shown them how to stop. “Well,” he said, “worse comes to worst, we could always just keep going. The world is round, after all. Eventually, we would get back to our bedroom window, don’t you think?” Peter was nowhere to be found. It wasn’t uncommon for him to leave them occasionally. Easily bored and distracted, he would fly up high to talk to the stars, or down low to talk with a mermaid. He always came back, but sometimes he seemed barely to remember them, as if he had already moved on to his next adventure.
text.T1: “Tatuzi kwakugama.” “Nkokuti, lino, tuyakutolelelela, wakaamba John. “Tatuizi inzila eeyo, ayalo. Akuziba tatucizi mbotunga twaleka kuuluka”. John wakayeeya ali ceeci. Wendy wakaliluzi. Peter taakabaiside bwakuleka kuuluka. “Lino” wakaamba, “icibi casika kububi bwiindilila, tulakonzya lyoonse kutolelela. Inyika ilizingulukide, mboibede. Kumamanino, tuyojokela ku mpulungwido ya nkotoona, muyeeya buti?” Peter wakabula aankwazulilwa. Teecakali cintu cicitika lyoonse kuti abasiye ziindi zimwi. Kuti wafwa butolo , wakali kuuluka mujulu kule kuyoambaula aa nyenyeezi, naa tali boobo wakali kuboola aansi kuzokanana aa tosi. Lyoonse wakali kujoka, pele zimwi ziindi wakali kuboneka kutayeeya nociba comwe, mbuli kuti waunka kale mukuuluka alimwi.

text.S1: “I’m Wendy,” Wendy had reminded him once when he had flown back and looked at her blankly. “I know that,” Peter had said, but she could tell he was lying. Eventually, the children learned how to fall asleep without falling. Peter, how- ever, found this boring, so he would cry out and wake them up anyway—just to see them jump. At last they reached Neverland—less due to Peter’s guidance, it seemed to Wendy, than through sheer luck, or perhaps because the island had been look- ing for them. “There it is,” Peter said. He gestured in the direction the sun was shining, like a hundred golden ar- rows pointing to the island. “Look, there’s the coral reef and the tiny hut and the cave!” cried John. “And my lagoon with the flying flamingos!”
text.T1: “Ndime Wendy,” Wendy wakamuyeeyezya naakajoka akumulangisisya mbuli kuti kunyina ncazi. “Ndilizi oobo,” Peter wakaliambide, pesi wakali kukonzya kuziba kuti wakali kubeja. Kumamanino, ibana bakaiya ikoona kakunyina kuwa. Peter, pele, wakajana ceeci kumupaq butolo, cakali kupa kuti akwiile akubabusya boonse – kutegwa abone kuti basotoka. Kumamanino bakazosika ku Neverland – kwiinda asyoonto kukusololelwa aa Peter, cakaboneka kuli Wendy, buli kuti ncoolwe, kuti ndiza insumbu yakali kubalangaula. “Njiiya okuya,” Peter wakaamba. Wakalanga kwakali kuzwida izuba kalimweka, mbuli masumo aa ngolide kaatondeka ku nsumbu. “Kamulanga, moomuya mumbali aamulonga akaanda kasyoonto aa ciyubilo!” wakalila John. “Mpoona cizyiba cangu aa ziyuni ziuluka!”

text.S1: “And there’s the hunchbacked little old lady and the turtles laying their eggs and the sewing gnomes!” Michael added. “And my flamingo with the flying lagoons!” “Hello, Wolfie,” Wendy called down to her pet wolf. “Hello, boat!” The children also saw and recognized the scary first days at school, trying not to laugh at church, the pop quizzes they hadn’t studied for, the tooth fairy money, and the delicious chocolate pudding. It was all so familiar! Peter was a little annoyed with the children for knowing so much about the island. He wanted to be the one who knew everything. Shortly, however, the sun went down and the children got scared. Then Peter felt better because they needed him again. Down below, black shadows grew and strange noises could be heard. Out in the open sky, there were no night - lights or Nanas to keep a child safe. The children were on their own. Huddling close to Peter, they flew so low now that their toes occasionally brushed the ocean. Something strange hung in the air. All of them could sense it.
text.T1: “Mpoona nkaakaya kacembele kajisi ntunda kusule acula uubikila mai akacembele kasuma zisani!” “Micheal wakaamba. “Alimwi aa ziyuni zyangu aziziba zyuuluka!” “Kamwamba Wolfie,” Wendy wakaita kanyama kakwe nkaanga wolf. “Kamwamba, ibwato!” ibana abalo bakabona imazuba aayoosya aakucikolo, kusola kutaseka mu cikombelo, imali aajisi meno, acipoleji. Zyoonse zyakali zibidwe! Peter wakalinyemede nkaambo ibana bakalizi zintu zinji akaambo ka nsumbu. Wakali kuyanda kuti abe nguwe uuzi zintu zyoonse. Kaindi kasyoonto, izuba lyakabbila mpoona ibana bakayoowa. Mpoona Peter wakakkomana nkaambo bakali kumuyanda alimwi. Munsi, izinzimwemwe zisiya zyakakomena azisabila ziyoosya zyakali kumvwika. Mujulu lijulidwe, kwakanyina mumuni wa – masiku alimwi aa Nana wakulanga bana. Ibana bakali balike. nobakaswenena kuli Peter, bakaulukila munsimunsi cakuti maulu akaguma meenda. Cimwi cintu ciyoosya cakali kuuluka mumuwo. Boonse bakacimvwa.

text.S1: “They don’t want us to land,” Peter said. “Who are they?” Wendy whispered, shuddering. Peter wouldn’t say. Instead he said, “This island is full of pirates, and their captain, Hook, is the biggest pirate of all.” The boys had been excited about the pirates, but at the reality of them Michael began to cry, and even John gulped. “Of course, Hook’s not quite as big as he used to be,” Peter added, “thanks to me. During our last battle, I chopped off his right hand with my sword. Now he has an iron claw instead of fingers. If you meet him, you leave him to me, got it?” “Yes.” “Don’t say yes. Say Ay, ay, sir. Every boy who serves under me has to say that.” “Ay, ay, sir,” John replied.
text.T1: “Tabayandi kuti tusike aansi,” “Peter wakaamba. “Ino mbaani abo?” Wendy wakapetekezya. Peter wakabula mbwaamba. Wakaamba kuti, “Ino nsumbu izwide bantu banyongene, aubasololela, Hook, ngomupati wabanyongene boonse.” Ibana basankwa bakali kkomene akaambo ka kunyonganya, pele cili masimpe Micheal wakatalika kulila, mpoona aa John wakatalika kusotooka.“ “Inzya, Hook tali mupati mbuli mbwakabede,” Peter wakaamba, “ndalilumba. Ciindi ca nkondo yamamanino, ndaka mutyola kwaanza aa ceba lyangu. Lino ujisi mala aa nsimbi kwinda kuba aa tunwe twa ncobeni. Kuti wamuswanganya, nkumulekela ndime, wamvwa?” “Inzya.” “Utaambi kuti inzya. Kwaamba kuti Ay, ay, badaala. Kufumbwa mwana musankwa uubelekela ndime weelede kwaamba kuti “Ay, ay badaala,” John wakavwiila.

text.S1: It occurred to John then that Tinker Bell’s light might make it easier for the pirates to see them. “Tell her to go away at once, Peter,” the children cried, but he refused. “She gets scared and lonely, too,” he said. They compromised. John would carry Tink in his hat, which he would hold in his hand. This worked for a while until John got tired and Wendy took over. “Don’t think that this changes anything between us,” the still - jealous Tink clinked, if only for Peter’s benefit. Suddenly the quiet black sky was split in two by a loud boom. The noise echoed through the dark mountains.
text.T1: Cakacitika kuli John mpoona mumuni wa Tinker Bell inga wacuubyaubya kuti banyonganya zintu ba bababone, “Kamumwaambila aunke linolino, Peter,” ibana bakalila, pele wakakaka. “Ulayoowa akuusa awalo,” wakaingula. Eeci cakabeleka kwa kaindi kasyoonto kusikila John wakatala mpoona Wendy wacibweza. “Mutaboni mbuli kuti eeci cilacinca zintu akati kesu,” uulabufwi – Tink wakanyema, nokwali biyo kutambula kwa Peter. Mpoonampoona ijulu lisiya lyakadulwa muzibeela zyobile acoongo cipati. Icoongo cakazomvwika mbuli kuti cizwida mumalundu aasiya mbii!

text.S1: “It’s their cannon!” John cried. “The pirates have fired it at us! Is anyone shot?” “I’m not,” Michael said. But wait—where were Peter and Wendy? The wind from the cannon fire had carried Peter far out to sea, and Wendy (and Tink) blew high up into the black sky. Tink wasn’t all bad, but fairies are so small that they only have room for one feeling at a time. When she was around Wendy, the jealousy Tink felt could barely fit. Seeing a chance to rid herself of Wendy, Tink gestured for the girl to follow her. What else could Wendy do, all alone in the sky? She flew trustingly after the fairy to meet her fate.
text.T1: “Nintobolo zyabo zya mavwiili!” John wakalila. “Izigwebenga zyatuyasa! Sena kuli ngobayasa?” “Mebo peepe,” Micheal wakaamba. Pele nkulindila – ino Peter aa Wendy bainkide kuli? Imuwo uuzwa ku ntobolo zya mavwili wamutola Peter kuyoomusisya kumulonga, aa Wendy (aa Tink) kubatola mujulu imusiya mbii. Tink taakali mubi pee, pele mizimo misyoonto cakuti ijisi biyo libazu lomwe aciindi comwe. Naakali aa Wendy, ubufwi bwakajisi Tink tebwakali kuyandika. Naakabona kaindi kakuzwa kuli Wendy, Tink wakalanga kumusimbi kumutondezya kuti amutobele. Ncinzi cimwi ncakonzya kucita Wendy, alike mujulu? Wakauluka cakusyoma kuyooswangana amamanino aakwe.

text.S1: Chapter 6 - Island Come True
text.T1: Caandaano cacisambomwa - Insumbu ya Masimpe

text.S1: As though it were a living, breathing thing, Neverland seemed to sense that Peter was almost home. Like a puppy, it strained and wiggled to meet him at the door. Whenever Peter went away, the island slowed. The fairies slept late. The wild animals nursed their babies. The pirates and the lost boys and the Indians stopped fighting wars and just called one another names instead. With his return, however, the whole place started to rumble as if a train were coming. The lost boys set out to find Peter, the pirates started looking for the lost boys, the Indians began looking for the pirates, and the wild animals started looking for the Indians. All of them went around and around the island, but at the same speed, so they never met.
text.T1: Mbuli kuti yakali kuputauka, akuyoya, Neverland yakali kuboneka mbuli kuti ilazyiba kuti Peter ulaafwafwi akusika kung`anda. Mbuli kabwa, yakali kukkmana akulisyaanikizya kuya mukumuswaanganya kumulyango. Kufumbwa Peter aunka, insumbu yakali kuimikila. Imizimo yakamuka kuya mukoona. Izyinyama zya musokwe zyaka lilangila twana. Izigwebenga abana basankwa bakaswekede aba mweenye bakaleka ikulwana nkondo pele bakali kwiitana biyo mazyina. Naakajoka, pele, icilao coonse cakataika kuvuluma mbuli kuti citima cili munzila. Ibana basankwa bakasweekede bakanyamuka kuyooyandaula Peter, izigwebenga zyakatalika kulangaula bana basankwa bakasweekede, ba mweenye bakatalika kulangaula zigwebenga, mpoonya zinyama zyamusokwe zyakataika kulangaula ba mwenye. Boonse bakatalika kuzinguluka nsumbu, pele bakali kweendela aaciindi coomwe icakapa kuti bataswaangani.

text.S1: Let us take a moment to examine each group as it passes. The first to come our way are the lost boys. The number of lost boys varies. If someone grows up, which is against the rules, he is kicked out. Right now, there are six. They wear bearskins and carry daggers, and they creep through the bushes like sol- diers in single file. Leading the group is Tootles. Tootles has bad luck. The biggest adventures always seem to happen whenever he steps around the corner for a snack. When he returns, he inevitably finds the boys putting on bandages after a bril- liant and bloody fight. He could be bitter about it, but Tootles is the sweetest and humblest lost boy. Next comes Nibs, the best dressed of the lost boys, followed by Slightly, who can carve whistles out of wood and dances to his own tunes. Slightly is also the most arrogant lost boy; he sticks up his nose at everyone so much that sometimes you can see right up inside.
text.T1: Atusole kulangalanga kabunga komwekomwe mbuli mbo kainda. Ikakusaanguna nka bana basankwa bakasweekede. Imweelwe wabana basankwa bakasweekede ulimpeneimpene. Kuti omwe wakomena, icitayandiki akati kesu, welede kumutanda. Aano mpotwambawida, bali cisambomwe. Basama mikupo ya zinyama mpoona bakali kweenda aa maceba, akuyaabusobelela musokwe mbuli kuti mbaa sikalumamba mumulongo omwe. Iweembela kabunga ngu Tootles. Tootles unyina coolwe. Ikweendenda mumasena kupati linjanji kucitika kuti naa waunka kulangaula kakulya anselelo aalya. Aajoka lyoonse, ujana basankwa balyaanga mabbandaji bamana kulwana nkondo mpati. Inga wanyema akaambo kaako, pele Tootles mwana musankwa uulomene alimwi uulilemeka. Mpoona kwatobela Nibs, imusankwa uusama kabotu, mpoona kwacilila Slightly, uukonzya kubeza milosi kuzwa ku zisamu akuzyana kunyimbo zyakwe. Slightly musankwa uulimvwa, inga unyamuna mpemo yakwe kumuntu kufumbwa ngwaaswanganya icakuti inga wabona ankwali mujulu mukati.

text.S1: Curly is the fourth boy. He is always getting into trouble, and he has grown accustomed to taking the blame even for things he didn’t do. Last are the twins. We will not describe them because no one can ever tell them apart, anyway. Instead, let’s move on to the pirates, close behind, on the boys’ trail. They are a scary-looking bunch. Leading their ragged group is the handsome Italian pirate Cecco, who carved his name in blood on the back of the warden of the prison from which he had escaped. Behind him is the giant, tattooed Bill Jukes, who once took six bullets before dropping the bag of gold pieces he’d been stealing. Next are Cookson and Gentleman Starkey. Starkey is the most polite of the pirates; he always apologizes before stabbing anyone with his sword. Then came the Irish pirate, Smee, and Noodler, followed by a few more ruffians.
text.T1: Curly ngo musankwa wa zyone. Kufumbwa ciindi walo ulanjila mumapenzi, mpoona ino wakzyibila cakuti wakatalika kuzumina aa zintu zyoonse nzyataciti. Bakulekelezya mbana bamaanga. Tatukonzyi kubapandulula nkaambo kakuti kunyina uukonzya kubaandaanya, nokuba omwe. Nkokuti atuggame kuziggwebenga, munsimunsi, kuyaabucilila basankwa mobayaabwiinda. Baboneka mbuli cikama ciyoosya. Uusololela kabunga aaka ku Cecco omwe waziggebenga wakazwa ku Italy, iwakalemba izyina lyakwe mubulowa kunze ya sikulanganya basintolongo nkwaakatija. Kunze kwakwe kuli mubbabbani, wakalembwa nsimbo Bill Jukes, wakaumwa ntobolo katana losya cisaka ca ngolide nzyakali kubba. Ibacilila ngu Cokson Gentleman Starkey. Starkey muntu uulomene wa ziggwebenga; lyoonse ulalomba kulekelelwa kufumbwa nayanda kuyasa muntu aa ceba. Mpoona kwaboola ci gwebenga ca ku Island, Smee, aa Noodler, mpoona kwatobela bapenzya bantu.

text.S1: Somewhere in the middle of this dark and dangerous group is James Hook, the most feared pirate of them all. His hair is styled in long, shiny black curls, framing a sternly handsome face. His eyes are deep and black and dead— unless he is plunging his hook into someone, in which case his eyes sparkle a bright and happy red. Hook is a different breed of pirate from the rest of his crew. Except at the sight of his own blood, he is courageous. He is a master storyteller. He speaks beautifully and softly—even when he is swearing—and is never more sinister than when he is being polite. After the pirates come the Indians. Creeping quietly like shadows, they carry tomahawks and knives. Among them is Tiger Lily, the beautiful Indian princess, whom none dare approach for fear that she will raise her hatchet to them. Behind the Indians creep the beasts—lions, tigers, bears, and other animals. The beasts are so hungry that their tongues are hanging out. Finally, there comes a giant crocodile. He is hungry, too, but not for just any meat. No, he has a craving for something—or, rather, someone—very specific. The boys stop first. They are getting tired.
text.T1: Kumwi kucilaoakati mbunga eeyi iisiya akuyoosya kuli James Hook, ngobakali kuyoowesya akati ka Ziggwebenga zyoonse. Imasusu aakwee malamfu aamweka kabotu, amubamba kuti abote kumeso. Imeso aakwe aasiya alimwi aafwide – cita katabiki ndobyo ku muntu kufumbwa, mu nzila imeso aakwe naayaka akumweka akusalala akukkomana. Indobyo cintu ciimpene ca zigwebenga kuzwa kubeenzinyina. Cita biyo kuti wabona bulowa bwakwe, ulaacamba. Ulicizyi kwaana twaano. Uambaula kabotukabotu alimwi abutetete – aciindi na konkezya – alimwi kunyina nbija kwiinda ciindi nalomene. Nozyakamana ziggwebenga kwakaboola ba mweenye. Kabayaabusobelela mbuli zinzimwemwe kabajisi itweembe azipeni. Akati kabo kwakali Tiger Lily, imwana musimbi mubotu wamwami waku India, ngobayoowa boonse kuti ndiza inga wanyamuna kambezyo akubacisa, kunze kwaba mweenye kwakanjila zinyama – basyuumbwa, basiluwe, masekese, cibeeya azinyama zimwi ziyoosya. Zinyama zilaanzala cakuti imilaka yoonse ilalengelela. Kumamanino, kwakaboola ciwena mupati loko. Ulaanzala, awalo, pele kutali yakufumbwa nyama. Peepe,wakalijisi nyama njakalikuyandisisya kulya, naa kuti ngwakai kuyanda – ngwakajisi mumoyo. Ibasankwa bakaimila cakutaanguna. Bakali kateede.

text.S1: “I wish Peter would get home already and tell us how ‘Cinderella’ ends,” Slight- ly said, out of breath. Tootles was about to respond when the boys heard the pirates walking and singing in the distance. The lost boys had stopped, but the pirates were still coming! Peter had trained the boys well, and they knew exactly what to do. In a flash they each ran to a nearby tree. Instead of climbing up, however, the boys went down. The trees were hollow, each with a hole in it exactly as big as one of the boys, and all leading to the same underground cave. Hook had heard about these tree-doors, and thought it silly that each boy had his own tree. For his purposes, however, it suited him just fine: Seven trees should be easier to find than one!
text.T1: “Ndaikuombozya kuti Peter inga wasika kufwambaana kung`anda kuzootwaambila kaambo ka ‘Cinderella’ mbokakamana., “Slightly wakaamba akuyooya. Tootles wakali kuyanda kuvwiila ibasankwa nobakamvwa ziggebenga kazyeenda akwiimba aalale. Ibana basankwa bakasweekede baimikila, pele ziggwebenga zyakacili kuzaabweenda! Peter wakali baisyide kabotu basankwa, mpoona bakalizyi kabotukabotu cakucita. Mukaindi kasyoonto aumwi wakalundukila kucisamu. Muciindi cakutanta mujulu, pele, ibasankwa bakali kuselukila aansi. Kufumbwa cisamu cakai bboonkene, acimwi cakai jisi iciddonkwi iceelene kukomena mbuli basankwa, zyoonse zyakali kutolezya mumpako na muciyubilo. Hook wakalimvwide kaambo ka zisamu zijisi – milyango, akuyeeya kuti bwakali buyanga kuti aumwi musankwa kajisi cisamu cakwe. mumizeezo yakwe, pele, cakalimweelede kabotu: Cilaububa kujana zisamu ciloba kwiinda kujana comwe!

text.S1: The pirates soon arrived in the clearing where the lost boys had just been. While the others fanned out to continue their search, Hook and Smee stayed behind. “I think I spotted that Nibs boy, Captain,” Smee said. “Shall I run after him? I could tickle him with my sword.” “No,” Hook said. “I want them all, especially their captain, Peter Pan. He cut off my arm and threw it to a passing crocodile.” His waved his iron claw in the air. “One of these days, I’m going to shake his hand with this!” “Is that why you fear crocodiles?” Smee asked. “Not all crocodiles,” Hook replied. “Just that one. It thought my arm was so tasty that it has followed me ever since, licking its lips, just waiting to eat the rest of me. The only reason it has not caught me yet is that it swallowed a clock, which ticks inside it. I always hear the beast coming and run away!” “One day, that clock’s battery will die,” Smee pointed out. “The ticking will stop.”
text.T1: Mukaindi kasyoonto ziggwebenga zyakasika ikwakali bana basankwa. Bamwi nobabkkomene kuyaabuyandaula, Hook aa Smee bakacaala. “Ndabona mbuli kuti ndabona uulya Nibs, Nobasololeli,” Smee wakaamba. “sena inga ndamulundukila? Inga ndamutekunya aa ceba lyangu.” “Peepe,” Hook wakaamba. “Ndabayanda boonse, ikapati musololeli wabo, Peter Pan. Wakandikosola kwaanza akukusowela kuli ciwena waakali kwiinda.” Wakanyamuna mala aakwe mujulu. “Ibuzuba bomwe ndiyaku jatana mumaanza anguwe!” “Ncoyowela ba ciwena?” Smee wakabuzya. “Kutali boonse baciwena,” Hook wakavwiila. “Pele biyo uulya. Wakai kubona mbuli kuti kwaanza kwangu kula nona icakuti ulanditobela kufumbwa nkondainka, akulimyaankuta milomo, kulindila biyo kundilya mubili oonse. Ikaambo nkatana ndijata nkaambo kakuti wakamena nkoloko ibeleka muli mukati mwida lyakwe. Kufumbwa ndamvwa cinyama eeci cilaboola ndila tija!” Buzuba bomwe, inkoloko iyakufwa, Smee wakatondeka.” “Iyakuleka kubeleka.”

text.S1: “Ay,” Hook agreed darkly, sitting down on a mushroom. It was a strangely warm mushroom, Hook thought. Standing up, he pulled at the mushroom and discovered that its top easily came off. The headless mush- room then started to smoke. Why, it wasn’t a mushroom at all; it was a chim- ney! Down the chimney, Hook heard voices. It was the lost boys; he had found their cave! Looking around now, he could also see holes in seven of the nearby trees. The entrances! “I heard them say that Peter is away,” Smee whispered. Hook smiled and nodded. He carefully replaced the mushroom top. He had a plan.
text.T1: “Ay,” Hook wakazumina, naakakede aboowa. Bwakali boowa bukasaala, Hook wakayeeya. Naakanyamuka wakkwela boowa, akujana kuti icaatala cakazwa. Iboowa butajisi mutwe mpoona bwaktalika kufweba. Ino tebwakali boowa, wakali mupaipi! Munsi wa mupaipi Hook wakamvwa imajwi. Akali aa basankwa bakaswekede; wakajana mpako naa ciyubilo cabo! Naakai kulangalanga, wakabona azipulo muzisamu ziliciloba munsimunsi. Imilyango! “Ndabamvwa kabaamba kuti Peter tako,” Smee wakapetelezya. Hook wakasekaseka akuzuminizya kubelesya mutwe. Mpoona wakajosya mutwe waboowa kabotukabotu. Wakali jisi muzeezo.

text.S1: “Let’s return to the ship,” Hook said. “We will bake a cake for them and leave it on Marooners’ Rock in the mermaid lagoon. The boys are sure to find it and gobble it up, and it will make them sick so that we can more easily capture them.” Oh, how Hook and Smee laughed as they walked back to the boat. Soon, however, another sound replaced their laughter. It was the sound of ticking! Hook stopped short, shuddering. “Run!” yelled Smee, but Hook was already gone.
text.T1: “Katujokela ku bwato,” Hook wakaamba. “Tulabajikila kkekke akuisiya ali Marooner`s Rock icaamba kuti cizyiba kujanika ima tosi. Ibasankwa bai masimpe ikuijana akuilya mpoona mpoona, bakumana kuilya iyakubapa kuciswa icitikape kuti tukabajate kakunyina aakupenga.” Oh, mbwakaseka Hook aa Smee nobakali kujokela kubwato. Linolino, icoongo cimwi cakabalubya kuseka nkobakajisi. Cakali coongo ca nkoloko! Hook wakaimikila asyoonto, akuliolola. “Kamutija!” wakaompolola Smee, pele Hook wakaliunkide kaindi.

text.S1: Chapter 7 - The Wendy Bird
text.T1: Caandaano Ciloba – Wendy Ciyuni

text.S1: Unaware that the pirates had found their hiding place, the boys waited for a while and then emerged from their underground cave. Suddenly Nibs saw something in the sky. “Look at that white bird,” he said. “It sounds as if it is saying, Poor Wendy! It must be a Wendy bird.” It wasn’t actually a bird that Nibs saw at all, but poor Wendy herself, flying up above. Now the boys heard another sound. It was the voice of Tinker Bell, shrill and jealous. She was no longer pretending to be nice to Wendy, but was pinching her and trying to make her fall. “Peter wants you to shoot this white bird,” Tink called down to the boys.
text.T1: Ikutazyiba kuti ziggwebenga zyakajana nkobakai kuyubila, ibana basankwa bakalindila aasyoonto mpoona bakazwa mu mpako yabo. Kaindi kasyoonto Nibs wakabona cimwi mujulu. “Kamulanga ciya ciyuni cituba,” wakaamba. Cimvwika mbuli kuti caamba kuti, Wendy uupengede! Ceelede kuti nciyuni ca Wendy.” Teecakali ciyuni ncaakabona Nibs, pele mweendoma Wendy, ngowakali kuuluka mujulu. Lino basankwa bakamvwa kusabila kumwi. Lyakali jwi lya Tinker Bell, ikusabila amunyono. Limwi wakaleka kulicengezya kuba kabotu kuli Wendy, pele wakali kumusyamba akumukwela kusola kuti awe aansi. ”Peter uyanda kuti uddubule kayuni aaka katuba,” Tink wakaita basankwa.

text.S1: “Quick,” the boys cried. “Bows and arrows!” Tootles excitedly fitted an arrow to his bow. “Get out of the way, Tink,” he shouted. He fired, and Wendy fluttered to the ground with an arrow in her breast. “I shot the Wendy bird!” Tootles bragged. “Peter will be so proud of me!” “Silly donkey,” Tinker Bell clinked, laughing at her trick before going to hide. She knew she would be in trouble for urging poor Tootles to shoot Wendy. Slightly frowned as he looked at Wendy. “That is no bird,” he said. “I think it is a lady.” “A lady?” Tootles replied nervously. “Peter was bringing a lady to take care of us, and you’ve gone and killed her!” Curly said.
text.T1: “Kamufwambaana,” bakalila basankwa. “Buta amivwi!” Tootles kakkomene wakabika muvwi ku buta. “Kozwa munzila, Tink,” wakabwenta. Wakayasa, mpoona Wendy wakawa aansi amivwi mucamba. “Ndamuyasa Wendy ciyuni!” Tootles wakaimvwa. “Peter uulandilumbaizya!” “Buyanga ombongolo,” Tinker Bell wakasabila, akusekelela katana unka mukuyuba. Wakalizyi kuti ulaba mumapenzi akaambo kakusungilizya Tootles kuti addubule Wendy. Wakamemenyana naakaanga Wendy. “Tacili ciyuni,” wakaamba. “Ndisyoma kuti mukaintu.” “Imukaintu?” Tootles wakavwiila cakuyoowa. “Peter wali kutuletela mukaintu wakuzotubamba, mpoona ebo wamujaya!” Curly wakaamba

text.S1: Tootles took a deep, sad breath. “I did it. I shot the Wendy-lady,” he said quietly, and turned to leave the group. Just then the boys heard a crowing sound up above. It was Peter’s signal. He was back! They gathered around Wendy so that Peter would not see her. He dropped to the ground in front of them, but no one said a word. “Why so quiet, boys?” Peter asked. But still none of the boys spoke. “Never mind,” Peter said. “I have news. I’ve brought you back a mother! You may even have seen her already. I think she was flying this way.” Tootles cleared his throat. “Boys,” he said bravely, “step aside.” The boys obeyed, revealing Wendy’s body. Peter bent, took the arrow from Wendy’s heart, and turned to face his band of boys. “Whose arrow is this?” he asked sternly. “Mine, Peter,” Tootles replied.
text.T1: Tootles wakayoya, cakuusa. “Ndacikonzya. Ndamuddubula Wendy-mukaintu.” Wakaamba cakumuna, mpoona wakazinguluka kuti abasiye boonse. Mpoonampoona basankwa bakamvwa kulila mbuli mukombwe mujulu. Kwakali kutondezya Peter. Wakajoka! Bakamuzinguluka Wendy kutegwa Peter atamuboni. Wakawa aansi kumbele lyabo, pele kunyina wakaamba ijwi noliba lyomwe. “Ino mwaumuna buti, nobasankwa?” Peter wakabuzya. Pele kunyina nokuba omwe wabo wakavwiila. “Mutapengi,” Peter wakaamba. “Ndijisi makani. Ndamuletela ba nyoko! Ndiza kuli nkkomwakababwene. Ndiza bali kuulukila kulubazu ooku.” “Tootles wakakwenga amukosi. “Nobasankwa, “ wakaamba canguzu, “kotantamuka.” Ibasankwa bakamvwida, akutondezya mubili wa Wendy. Peter wakaongomana, akugusya muvwi kuzwa kumoyo wa Wendy, mpoona wazinguuka kulanzya kwakali basankwa. “Muvwi wabani ooyu?” wakabuzya cakufwambaana. “Nguwangu, Peter,” Tootles wakavwiila.

text.S1: Angrily, Peter raised the arrow, prepared to hit Tootles with it. But he couldn’t do it. At just that moment, Nibs saw Wendy move. “The Wendy-lady!” he cried. “She moved her arm!” Peter bent over Wendy again and saw the acorn he had given to her when she’d asked for a kiss. It was on a string around her neck. The arrow had hit the acorn and saved her life! “Hurry up and get better,” he said, “so I can introduce you to the boys and the mermaids.” From her hiding spot up above, Tink sighed loudly. “Listen to Tink crying because the Wendy-lady is alive,” Curly said. The boys told Peter about her crime.
text.T1: Kanyemede, Peter wakanyamuna muvwi, akuibambila kuyasa Tootles anguwe. Pele cakamukakila kucita boobu. Aciindi mpoona aawa, Nibs wakabona Wendy wazungaana. “Wendy mukaintu!” wakalila. “Wakazungaanya kwaanza!” Peter wakaongomana atala aa Wendy alimwi akubona kakubeza kamumukosi nkkakamupede naakalombede kumumyonta. Kakali angilidwe kuntambo yakazingulukide mumukosi wakwe. Imuvwi wakayasa kakubeza kakali munsingo akumufutula! “Kofwambaana kupona,” wakaamba, “kutegwa ndikakupandulule ku basankwa alimwi aa ku ma tosi.” Kuzwa ku cilao nkwakayubide mujulu, Tink wakayoya canguzu. “Kamumvwa kulila kuzwa kuli Tink nkaambo kakuti Wendy-mukaintu muumbulu,” Curly wakaamba. Ibasankwa bakambila Peter akaambo kakacitika.

text.S1: “We are not friends anymore, Tink,” Peter cried. “Go away and never come back!” Frantically, Tinker Bell flew onto Peter’s shoulder and begged his forgive- ness, but he brushed her off. Lying on the ground, Wendy stirred slightly. She was waking up. “I’ll be alright,” she said wearily. “You don’t have to banish her.”
text.T1: “Icilongwe camana kuzwa sunu, Tink,” Peter wakaila. “Kozwa aawa alimwi utakajoki limwi!” Kayoowede, Tinker Bell wakaulukila ansingo ya Peter akulomba kulekelelwa, pele taakabikila maano. Kalede aansi, Wendy wakazungaana aasyoonto. Wakabuka akukkala. “Ndilaba kabotu,” wakaamba cakupenga. “Tamwelede kumutanda.”

text.S1: Well, all right,” Peter told Tinker Bell. “You can come back, but not for a whole week.” You would think Tinker Bell would be grateful to Wendy for defending her, but Wendy’s generosity only made Tink want to pinch her even more. Wendy, in the meantime, was so tired and sore from her hard fall that she rolled onto her side and fell asleep. “I have an idea,” Peter said. “Let’s build Wendy a house.” The boys were thrilled; they loved to build. They were incredibly quick carpenters, too, scurrying around for firewood, branches, and twigs, and look- ing for soft cushiony flowers to use for her bedding. Just then John and Michael dropped from the sky. They had been flying in their sleep, but they woke up as soon as they hit the ground. “Mama?” Michael cried, rubbing his eyes. “Nana?”
text.T1: “Ndamvwa, acibeboobo,” Peter wakaambila Tinker Bell. “Inga wajoka alimwi, pele kutali kwa mvwiki yoonse.” Inga wabona mbuli kuti Tinker Bell ulapa kulumba kuli Wendy akaambo kakumwiiminina, pele kuloma kwa Wendy kwakapa biyo kuti Tink ayande kumucisa alimwi. Wendy, muciindi eeci, wakalikateede akupenga ikuzwa kukuwa nkwaakawa akoona. “Ndaamuzeezo,” Peter wakaamba. “Atuyakile Wendy ing`anda.” Ibasankwa bakakkomana, bakali kuyanda ikuyaka. Alimwi bakicizyi ikubeza, akwalo, ikutebba nkuni, itusamu, akulangaula maluba akubika aakuti kaona. Mpoonampoona John aa Micheal bakawa kuzwa mujulu. Bakali kuuluka kung`onzi, pele bakabuka nobakalyuumputa aansi. “Mama?” Micheal wakalila, akulipikisa mumeso. “Nana?”

text.S1: “Where are we?” John asked. “Are we dreaming?” Finally, the boys spotted Peter. “Oh, hello,” Peter said distractedly. He had forgotten all about them. Using his feet as a ruler, he bent to measure Wendy to see how big her new house should be. “Come on,” he told her brothers. “We are building a house for Wendy, and you have to help.” “I don’t see why Wendy should get her own house,” John said. “She’s only a girl.” “She’s going to be our mother,” Curly said. “Now, you heard Peter. Get to work!” Wendy moved and groaned a bit in her sleep. “Slightly,” Peter cried. “Go get a doctor.”
text.T1: “Tuli kuli?” John wakabuzya. “Sena tulalota?” Kumamanino, ibasankwa bakabona Peter. “Oh, kamwaamba,” Peter wakaamba cakunyonganya. Wakalibalubide boonse.
