Ikubeesya zitutambuli cakupimina, wakaongomana kuti aa pime Wendy kubona nga`nda yakumuyakila mboyeelede kukomena. “Kamubikila maano,” wakaambila bamukwabo. “Tuyaka nga`nda ya Wendy, ayebo welede ku gwasya.” “Nsezyi kaambo Wendy ncotutakonzyi kumuyakila nga`nda,” John wakavwiila. “Ooyu musimbi biyo” “Uyooba muzyali wesu,” Curly wakaamba. “Lino, mwamumvwa Peter. Kamutalika kubeleka!” Wendy wakaputauka akulyoolola aasyoonto kung`onzi. “Slightly,” Peter wakalila. “Koya ukalete basilisi.”

text.S1: Slightly said, “Ay, ay,” and left at once, before remembering that there were no doctors on the island. Still, he knew better than to disobey Peter, so he re- turned wearing John’s hat and looking very serious. Although the other boys knew that Slightly was just pretending, Peter did not. To him, make-believe was the same thing as true. And so, convinced that Slightly was in fact a doctor, he said, “Help this lady. She is very ill.” “I will give her some medicine,” said Slightly, bending over the sleeping Wendy and pretending to do just that. “And, there—she is cured!” “What a relief,” Peter said. While Wendy slept, the boys built her house around her. They knew she would love it because as she slept, she sang: “I wish I had a pretty house, the smallest ever seen, with bright and shiny reddish walls, and a roof of mossy green.” As they worked, the boys sang back: “We’ve built your walls and mossy roof, and made a lovely door. So tell us now, Wendy mother, do you want something more?”
text.T1: “Slightly wakaamba kuti, “Ay, ay,” akuunka mpoonampoona, katanayeeya kuti kwakanyina ba silisi kunsumbu. Pesi, wakalizyi kabotu kwiinda kukakila Peter, mpoona wakjoka kasamide izyeete ya John akuboneka uubikide maano kuli ncacita. Nokuba kuti ibasankwa bamwi bakalizyi kuti Slightly wakali kulicengezya biyo, Peter takazyi. Walo, ikusyomezya muntu cakali kwaamba masimpe. Mpoona, kasyomede kuti Slightly wakli musilisi, wakaamba kuti, “Kamuggwasya mukaintu ooyu. Uli cisidwe.” “Ndilamupa imusamu,’’ mbwakaamba Slightly, nakaongomana atala aa Wendy akulicengeezya kucita boobo. “Mpona, ngoyu-wapona!” “Imukuli wamana,” Peter wakaamba. Naakali koona Peter, ibasankwa bakayaka nga`nda imuzingulukide, isyoonto njatana bwene, ya bwaanda busalala akumweka, aciluli ciboneka mbuli bwizu.” Nobakali kubeleka, ibasankwa bakali kwiimba nyimbo. “Twakuyakila nga`nda aa ciluli, akubika mulyango. Lino kotwaambila, bamaama ba Wendy, muciyanda azimwi zintu na?”

text.S1: Still sleeping, Wendy sang: “Well, since you ask, I’d surely grin, for windows all about, with daffodils peeping in, and babies peeping out.” And so the boys built windows and pulled flowers for Wendy, but they weren’t quite sure what to do about the babies. “Let’s just pretend that part,” they said. When they were finished, the house was beautiful, and Wendy was com- pletely contained inside. They were about to go inside to surprise her when they realized they had forgotten to put a knocker on the door. “Silly donkeys!” Tinker Bell cried from above. Tootles gave the sole of his shoe to hang on the door, which did the trick. Now there was nothing left to do but knock. “Everyone stand up straight,” Peter warned, “and be on your best behavior.” He knocked politely, and all of the boys waited. When Wendy opened the door, blinking sleepily, the boys whipped off their hats and bowed.
text.T1: Kacioona, Wendy wakaimba: “Inzya, nkaambo kakuti wabuzya, ndilabotelwa, ampulungwido amaluba, abana kabasondela.” “Mpoona ibasankwa bakayaka mpulungwido akukwela maluba aakupa Wendy, pele tebakali kuzyiba cakucita akaambo ka bana. “Katulicengezya biyo,” bakaamba. Nobakamana inga`nda yakali mbotu, mpoona Wendy wakali mukati. Bakali kuyanda kunjila mukati, kuyoo mugambya mpoona bakayeeya kuti bakalilubide kubika kakukonkkomwezya amulyango. “Imbongolo ifubafuba!” Tinker Bell wakalila kuzwa mujulu. Tootles wakabweza ntambo yamabbusu aakwe akwangilila kucijazyo, iyakapanga ciggambya. Lino kwakabula cimbi cakucita pele kukonkomona. “Nyoonse kakaimikila,” Peter wakabacenjezya, “mpoona mulilemeke.” Wakakonkkomona cabulemu, mpoona boonse basankwa bakalindila. Wendy naakajula mulyango, kalabalaba ang`onzi, ibasankwa bakasamununa nzyeete zyabo akukotama.

text.S1: Where am I?” she said, confused and surprised. The boys practically tumbled over one another to explain. “We built you this house,” Slightly said. “Do you like it?” asked Nibs. ”It’s lovely,” she said, looking around. “How did you know it’s exactly what I wanted?” “Just clever, I guess,” said Slightly. He saw no need to tell her what she had been singing in her sleep. “Can we be your children?” the twins asked. “Well,” Wendy said, “that’s awfully nice of you, but I am only a child myself. I have no real experience.” “That’s okay,” Peter said, although he actually knew less about mothers than any of them. “We just need a nice motherly person. You’ll do.” Wendy agreed to try, and invited all the boys into her new house. As they gathered around, she did her first motherly thing and told them the end of “Cinderella.” When she was finished, she followed the boys to their cave and tucked them in for the evening before returning to her own home.
text.T1: “Ndili kuli?” wakaamba kanyongene akuggambwa. Ibasankwa bakaingana kuyanda kupandulula. “Twakamuyakila nga`nda,” Slightly wakaamba. “Mulaiyanda?” wakabuzya Nibs. “Nimbotu,” wakavwiila, akulangalanga mumbali lyakwe. “Mwakazyiba buti kuti njeekali kuyanda?” “Nkucenjela biyo, ndasyoma,” wakavwiila Slightly. Taakabona kaambo kakumwambila kuti wakali kwiimba kungo`nzi. “Sena inga twaba bana benu?” bana bamaanga bakabuzya. “Inzya,” Wendy wakavwiila, “ncibotu kwaamba boobo pele ndicili mwana musyoonto. Kunyina aa ncezyi” “Cii biyo kabotu,” Peter wakvwiila, nokuba kuti wakzyi biyo zintu zisyoonto alwakuba muzyali kwiinda bacaala boonse. “Tuyanda biyo kuba abamaama babotu moyo. Uyo cikonzya.” Wendy wakazumina kusola, akwiita basankwa boonse munga`nda yanyoane. Nobakaswaangaanaa, wakacita cintu cimwi cabu zyali akubaambila kaambo mbokakamana ka “Cinderella.” Naakamana, wakatobela basankwa ku mpako akunjizya kuti baone katanajokela kunga`nda yakwe.

text.S1: Chapter 8 - Something Worse Then the Night
text.T1: Caandaano Lusele – Cintu Cibyaabi Mpoona Imasiku

text.S1: The next morning, the Darling children were measured for their trees. Hook, if you recall, thought it silly to have one tree for each lost boy, but it actually made a great deal of sense. Each different-size boy had a door that fit him as perfectly as a tailored suit. This way, they could all enter the cave at once, without having to wait in line. More importantly, no other body except each lost boy’s exact body could fit in that particular tree. This was especially helpful in case of sneak pirate attacks! After a few days’ practice, the Darling children became very quick and graceful about using their trees. To enter the cave, they sucked their breath in, and down they went at exactly the right speed. To rise, they sucked in and blew out and so wiggled up.
text.T1: Imafumofumo aakacilila, ibana baba Darling bakapimwa kuzisamu. Hook, kuti naa ulayeeya, wakai kuyeeya kuti mbuyanga kuti aumwi musankwa wakasekede waba aacisamu cakwe, pele caka pa maano. Kufumbwa mubili wakali jisi insaizi ya mulyango iimweelede mbuli nsuuti yakasumwa. Munzila eei, boonse bakalikunjila mu mpako mpoonampoona, kakunyina kulindila mumulongo. Icakali kuyandika, kunyina imubili nouba omwe uunga wainda aa mulyango kunze kwa basankwa bakaseekede. Eeci cakali kuggwasya kukasya ziggwebenga! Kwainda mazuba masyoonto aakusola, ibana baba Darling bakatalika kufwambaana akulumbaizya akaambo kakubelesya zisamu zyabo. Akunjila mumpako, bakali kunjizya muya akuyoya, mpoona banjila cakufwambaana. Ikunyamuka, bakali kunjizya akuzwisya muo mpoona bafwambaana kuzwa.

text.S1: They also grew to love their new underground home. It was simple and sweet, a bit like camping. Even Wendy stayed there now. It was lonely in her own house, and this felt so much more like a real family. The cave was one large, cozy room with a floor made of dirt. The boys used mushrooms as chairs and a sawed-off tree trunk as a table. There was one big bed, on which all the boys (except Michael) slept, packed in like sardines in a tin. Because space was so tight, there was a strict rule against turning around until one boy gave the signal, and then everyone had to turn at once. Michael could have slept in the bed, too—there was always room in Neverland for one more—but he was the littlest and Wendy liked to pretend that he was her baby, so she hung him in a basket next to her bed. Her pet wolf, who followed her everywhere, slept on the floor, guarding them both.
text.T1: Bakatalika kuyanda maanda aabo aamumpako. Cakali cuubauba akulweela, aasyonto mbuli nkambi. Alimwi aa Wendy wakali kukkala kokuya lino. Wakali kulendelelwa munga`nda yakwe, mpoona eeci cakali kulibonya mbuli kuti ngowakali mukwashi wakwe. Impako yakalinga`nda iipati, aansi akali syingululidwe aa dooti. Ibasankwa bakali kubelesya boowa mbuli zyuuno acisamu ciggonkedwe mbuli tebule. Kwakali bulo bupati bomwe, mpobakali koona basankwa (kuzwisyabiyo Micheal), mpobakali kulundana mbuli tuswi twamu ka ggabba. Nkaambo kakuti busena bwakaliceyede, kwakali mulao wakuti kunyina kusanduka, kusikila omwe musankwa wapa cizyibyo kuti lino nciindi ca ku sanduka. Mpoona boonse aciindi comwe basanduka. Micheal wakali kukonzya koona abulo, kwakali busena ku Neverland bukkwana omwe-pele weelede kuti kali musyoonto mubili mpoona Wendy wakali kuyanda kulicengezya kuti wakali kavwanda, pele waka mulengelezya mu muntanga munsimunsi aa bulo. Ikanyama kakusobanya, ikakali kumutobela kufumbwa nkwaunka, kakali koona aansi, kakabakwabilila boonse.

text.S1: Tinker Bell also lived in the cave, in a tiny space carved into the wall, no larg- er than a bird cage. Over the entrance to her room hung a curtain that she could pull shut when she wanted privacy. Small as it was, Tink’s room was the fanciest part of the whole cave, filled with the finest fabrics, soft tiny bed- spreads, and delicately carved antique furniture. “Your house may be bigger,” Tinker Bell informed Wendy, “but mine is better.” Still, Wendy had bigger concerns than whether Tink’s house was better. The boys kept her so busy, cooking and cleaning and sewing, that weeks would sometimes go by before she left the cave and saw daylight. It makes one long for the old single life, she thought wistfully, as a real grown-up might. As for her parents, she missed them and worried about them, but there was something about Neverland that made time and those worries blur. Somehow, she was confident that the bedroom window—and her parents’ arms—would always remain open for her to fly back into.
text.T1: Tinker Bell awalo wakali kukkala mumpako, mukasena kasyoonto kaddonkokede mubwaanda, kasyoonto kwiinda kaanda ka kayuni. Kumulyango wakunjilila mwaakali koona kwakali kulengelela mulembo ngwaakali kukonzya kulosya akulisisa na wayanda kuba alike. Nokubakuti kakali kasyoonto, ikaanda ka Tink kakali kabotu kwiindilila mu mpako yoonse, kakazwide milembo mibotu, amilembo yakuyala abulo miteteete, azyuuno zyakabezwa kabotu. “Inga`nda yenu inga yaba mpati,” Tinker Bell wakazyibya Wendy, “pesi yangu nimbotu kwiinda.” Pele, Wendy wakali kubikila maano izintu zimwi kwiinda kuyeeya kuti inga`nda ya Tink yakali mbotu. Ibasankwa bakamu pa kutalyookezya, kujika kukula akusuma, icakuti imvweeki zyakali kuunka katana zwa mumpako akubona mumuni. Cipa kuti omwe akale mazuba manji, wakayeeyesya, mbuli mupati mbwakonzya kuyeeya. Ibazyali bakwe wakabayeeya akulibilika, pele kwakali cintu comwe ku Neverland icakalikupa iciindi akulibilika kutalibonya. Pele wakalisyomede ikuti impulungwido ya nkwaakali koona –amaanza aa bazyali bakwe-ayakucaala bukwazi kutegwa waajana ciindi cakujokelako.

text.S1: What did disturb Wendy, however, was the fact that John was starting to for- get their parents—and Michael had already forgotten them entirely. He actually thought she was his real mother! To fix this, Wendy set up a little school, with their old life as the subject in- stead of spelling or math. The other boys wanted to go to school, too, so she let them sit in. Of course, they always failed the quizzes, especially the ones with hard questions like “What color are Mother’s eyes?” “How did we spend last Christmas?” and “Describe Father’s laugh.”
text.T1: Icakanyonganya Wendy ncakuti, John wakatalika kuluba bazyali bakwe-mpoona Micheal walo wakali balubide kaindi. Waklikuyeeya kuti mbabakali banyina bancobeni! Ikubamba ceeci, Wendy wakayaka cikolo cosyoonto, abuumi bwabo bwakaindi muciiyo ca cikuwa naa inamba. Ibasankwa bamwi bakali kuyanda kuunka kucikolo, icakuti wakabazumizya kunjila. Lyoonse bakali ku feela, ikapati imibuzyo miyumu mbuli “ Meso aabanyoko ali buti?” “ino Christmas yakali buti?” aa “Kopandulula inseko zya bauso.”

text.S1: Peter never came to school or took a quiz. He said it was because he de- spised mothers and holidays and even, sometimes, laughs—but really it was that he couldn’t read or write. While the other boys were in school, Peter would go off alone. Whether he went on real or imaginary adventures, Wendy could never tell unless she or one of the other boys had also gone—and, with Peter, sometimes not even then. But Wendy had many of her own adventures. Which such tale would you now like to hear? The night attack by the Indians on the underground cave, when a few of them got stuck in the hollow trees like fat Santas in chimneys? Or perhaps the time Peter saved Tiger Lily’s life in the mermaid lagoon, and so made her a lifelong friend? Maybe I should tell you, instead, about the cake the pirates baked and kept leaving around to make the boys sick, but which Wendy kept finding and snatching from the hands of her children until it got stale and they didn’t want it anymore and Hook eventually tripped over the hard stale lump in the dark, stubbing his toe.
text.T1: Peter taakaboolede kucikolo naa kuvwiila mibuzyo. Wakaamba kuti nkaambo taakali kuyanda bamanyina naa kulyookezya, zimwi ziindi, ikuseka – pele ca ncobeninkaambo taakali kukonzya kubala akulemba – ibasankwa bamwi nobakali kucikolo, Peter wakunka alike. Naa wakali kuunka biyo mumizeezo, Wendy taakali kukonzya kuzyiba cita kuti walo naa basankwa bamwi baunka – zimwi ziindi aa Peter. Pele, Wendy wakali kweenda masena. Ino inga mwayanda kumvwa nzi? Ikulwana kwa masiku kwa ba Mweenye mumpako zya mubwina, ibanji nobakajatwa muzilindi zyazisamu mbuli Fat Santas mumupaipi? Naa ndiza iciindi Peter naakafutusya siluwe, buumi bwa Lily mu nsumbu lya tosi, mpoona akumubamba mweenzinyina kukabe kutamani? Ndiza inga ndamwaambila, Ikkekke lyakapangwa aziggebenga akulibika kutegwa ibasanka baciswe, pele ngu Wendy wakali kusola kuyandaula akuzibweza kuzwa mumaanza aabana kusikila zyabola, mpoona teebakaziyanda limwi, Hook camamanino wakawa nkaambo kwakabula mumuni, akuliyasa kukanwe.

text.S1: I could tell you about the birds that were Peter’s friends, especially the Never bird who lived in the tree above the lagoon, and how her nest fell in the water once, but she kept sitting on it anyway, to protect her eggs, and Peter gave orders that no one was to disturb her. A shorter lagoon adventure, and almost as exciting, was Tinker Bell’s at- tempt—with the help of some other fairies—to float a sleeping Wendy back to the mainland on a leaf, until Wendy woke up and swam back to Neverland, foiling Tink again. Perhaps the best way to choose is simply to toss a coin. And so the lagoon has won. If you are lucky, when you close your eyes at night you will sometimes see a lovely lagoon where the mermaids live and sing their beautiful songs.
text.T1: Inga ndakwaambila kaambo ka tuyuni twakali tweenzinyina aa Peter, ikapati tuyuni twa ku Never twakali kukkala mu mucisamu atala aa cizyiba, aa mbokakawa kateente kuwida mumeenda, pele wakatolelela kukkala ali nkako, kutegwa aa kwabilile mai, mpoona Peter wakapa malailile kuti kunyina weelede kumu nyonganya. Ikwendeenda kuzinguluka cizyiba, kwakali kukkomanisya, kwakali kusola kwa Tinker Bell-akuggwasiggwa kuzwa ku mizimo misyoonto-kubika Wendy naakali koona atala aa meenda kumutola ku manyika atuvu, kusikila wendy wabuka akusamba kujokela ku Neverland, ikutyompya Tink alimwi. Ndiza inzila mbotu yakusala nkusobanya mali.icaamba kuti icizyiba cazunda ikwakali kukkala tosi kaliimba nyimbo zibotu.

text.S1: When you are awake, the nearest you can get to this lagoon is the beach, at sunset, in the surf. The children spent long summer days at the lagoon, swimming or lazily floating. Much to Wendy’s disappointment, the mermaids turned out to be as unfriendly as Tinker Bell. When they weren’t splashing her with their tails, they ignored her entirely. The mermaids didn’t like the boys, either—except, of course, Peter. Peter spent hours talking to the mermaids or sitting on their tails when they got particularly cheeky. The lagoon was most beautiful at night, when the moon came up and the mermaids began to sing their strange, wailing songs to lure sailors onto the rocks. But it was not a safe place for humans then. Wendy knew this, and made sure that she always gathered her children and left before dark. On this day, however, as they were all dozing on Marooners’ Rock after lunch, something strange and frightening happened. It wasn’t night yet—at least Wendy didn’t think it was—but the lagoon seemed to shift around them. Little shivers ran over the water, and shadows re- placed the sun. It was not night that had come. It was something worse.
text.T1: Notanaona, ikufwaafwi nkkokonzya kuunka ku cizyiba, nolibbila zuba. Ibana bakatola mazuba manji kucizyiba, kabayabusamba naa kulengelela atala aa menda. Wendy wakatyompwa, nkaambo itosi lyakabija moyo mbuli Tinker Bell. Nobatakali kumusekelela amucila, teebakamubikila maano. Imatosi taakali kuyanda basankwa, kuzwisya ko Peter. Peter wakabelesya ciindi coonse kwaambaula aa matosi naa kukkala aamicila yabo nobaba aankanzi. Icizyiba cakali kuboneka kabotu imasiku, imwezi no wakali kumweka mpoona imatosi atalika kwiimba, inyimbo zya yo zinyongene kutegwa aiite basikweenzya bwato. Pele tecakali cilao cibotu ca bantu ciya ciindi. Wendy wakalizyi eeci, akubona kuti waleta bana boose aantoomwe akuunka kakutana siya. Ibuzuba oobu, nobakali kuumfula ku Marooner`s Rock nocakainda ciindi cacakulya ca aakati, cimwi cakali kuyoosya cakacitika. Teekwakaninga siya – Wendy wakalizyi kuti takunasiya – pele cizyiba cakali kuboneka mbuli kuti cilabazinguluka. Imeenda akazungaana, mpoona icinzimweemwe cakabweza cilao ca zuba, taakali masiku aakaboola, cakali cintu cimbi cibyaabi.

text.S1: Chapter 9 - The Mermaid Lagoon
text.T1: Caandaano fwuke – icizyiba Ca Tosi

text.S1: Wendy probably should have woken the children at once, but she was a young mother and it had not yet been half an hour since they had eaten. Even when she heard the sound of muffled oars she did not wake them, although she was so scared that her heart seemed to leap into her throat. Instead, she stood guard over them while they digested. Peter, however—who was snoozing on the rock as well—could smell danger even in his sleep. At the sound of the oars, he jumped to his feet, as alert as a dog, and quickly woke the boys. “Pirates,” he whispered. Just that one, awful word. The others huddled close around him. “Dive!” he cried. “Now!” There was a flash of legs, and all of the boys were in the water. They hid as best they could while the pirate dinghy pulled up to the rock they had just been sitting on. In the boat were Smee and Starkey, and their captive, the Indian princess Tiger Lily.
text.T1: Ndiza Wendy wakelede kubusya bana mpoona mpoona, pele wakali banyina basyoonto mpoona teekakaninga lampa kaindi kuzwa mpobakalida cakulya. Aa naakamvwa kusabila kwa bwato taakababusya, nokuba kuti wakaliyoowede cakuti imoyo wakwe waka dduntauka. Wakaimikila akubalanga langa nobakali kulya. Peter, iwakali amabwe – wakamvwa kuti kuli ciyoosya akungo`nzi. Naakamvwa kusabila kwa bwato, wakasotoka akwiimikila, akulibambila mbuli mubwa, mpoona icakufwambaana, wakabusya basankwa. “Iziggwebenga,” wakapetekezya. Ijwi biyo lyomwe, libyabi. Ibacaala bakaswenena munsi munsi akumuzinguluka. “Kosotoka!” wakalila. “Lino!” kwakazoboneka maulu, mpoona boonse ibasankwa bakawida mumeenda. Bakayuba kweendelana ambobakali kukonzya iciggwebenga dinghy cakakwela ibbwe lipati mpobakakkede. Mubwato mwakali Smee aa Starkey, aa mbobakajatide, imwana musimbi wa mwami Tiger Lily.

text.S1: The pirates had caught her trying to sneak aboard their ship with a knife, and had tied her hands and ankles. They were going to leave Tiger Lily on the rock to drown when the tide came up and covered it. She did not beg. A true princess, she sat up straight and stared proudly ahead. In her dark, watery hiding spot, Wendy cried. She had never witnessed such cruelty—or bravery. Peter had seen plenty of both, and was not particularly moved. What he did hate, however, was unfairness, and this was two against one. It would have been easy for him to wait until the pirates were gone to rescue Tiger Lily, but Peter never chose the easy way out. “Ahoy there, you rascals,” he cried out in his best imitation of Captain Hook’s voice. “Captain?” the two pirates called back, squinting into the darkness. “He must be swimming out to us,” Starkey said. “We are putting Tiger Lily onto the rock,” Smee called.
text.T1: Iziggwebenga zyakamujana naakali kusola kutijila mu bwato aa cipeni, mpoona bakali mwaangide ku maanza akumaulu. Bakali kuyanda kusiya Tiger Lily abbwe lipati kutegwa anywide mumeenda kwaboola muwo uulaanguzu. Taaka kombelela. Imwana wamwami wamasimpe, wakabuka akukkala akulanga kumbele cakulimvwa. Mucilao musiya muli meenda, mwaakayubide, Wendy wakalila. Tanabwene ikubija moyo kwamusyoobo ooyu-naa busicamba. Peter wakabona zyoonse, cakapa kuti atazungaani. Ncaakazondede, pele, kusalulula, eeci cakali cakukasya. Nocakaubauba kuti naakalindila kuti ziggwebenga ziunke kuyoo futula Tiger Lily, pele Peter taakali kukonzya kusala inzila iubauba. “Ahoy ookuya, nywebo basilunya,” wakalila mbuli mbwakali kukonzya kutobelezya ijwi lya Captain Hook. “Captain?” iziggwebenga zyobilo zyakaita, akulabalaba imusiya. “Weelede kusamba kuboola kuli ndiswe,” Starkey wakaamba. “tulabika Tiger Lily abbwe, “ Smee wakaita.

text.S1: “Set her free immediately,” was the surprising answer, “or I’ll plunge my hook into you both.” The command made no sense to the pirates, but they were afraid to disobey their captain. They cut Tiger Lily’s cords, and with one last look she slid into the water like a graceful eel. “Boat ahoy!” Hook yelled suddenly. Only this time it was the real Hook, who was apparently also in the water and swimming toward the boat. Wendy and Peter watched from the dark water as Hook used his metal claw to grip the side of the boat and pull himself aboard. From the light of the pi- rates’ lantern, Wendy could see his roughly handsome face. She desperately wanted to swim away, but Peter signaled for her to stay put. Once on board, Hook sat with his head in his hands, groaning in extreme frustration. “Captain, what’s wrong?” Smee asked. “It’s over,” Hook said, sighing. “The lost boys have found a mother.”
text.T1: “Kamumwaangulula lino lino,” nko kwakali kuvwiila ku ggambya, “naa ndila muyasa nyoonse nyobilo.” Imulao tewakatondezya maano ku ziggwebenga, pele bakali kuyoowa kutyola mulao ku musololeli wabo. Bakaddunsula intambo zyakangililide Tiger Lily, mpoona nobakalanga camamanino wakawida mumeenda kabotu kabotu mbuli nswi iikonzya nzoka. “Ibwato ahoy!” Hook wakakwiila mpoona mpoona. Eeci ciindi wakali ngu Hook wancobeni, iwakali mumeenda alimwi wakali kusamba kuboola kwakali bwato. Wendy aa Peter bakaebela kuzwa kumeenda aasiya Hook naakali kubelesya kabulo kakwe ikujata bwato kumbali akulikwela kuti akkwele mukati. Ikuzwa ku mumuni wa ziggebenga, Wendy wakali kukonzya ku bona kumeso kwakwe kubotu. Wakali kuyanda kusamba kuunka, pele Peter wakamwambila kuti ataunki. Naakatanta, Kook wakakkala akujatilila mutwe wakwe mumaanza, akooloma katyompedwe. “Nobasololeli, ino kai ninzi?” Smee wakabuzya. “Kwamana ,” Hook wakaamba, akuyoya. “Ibana bakasweekede bajana banyina.”

text.S1: Wendy puffed up with pride, floating now a little higher. “O evil day!” Starkey said. “What’s a mother?” asked Smee. Just then, the nest belonging to the Never bird floated by, with the mother bird still sitting on it. “That is a mother, and a good example of one at that,” Hook told Smee. “Her nest fell into the water, but has she deserted her eggs? No.” There was a break in Hook’s voice, as if—for one moment—he was recalling his childhood and his own mother. But he brushed away this weakness and what might have been a small tear with his hook. “Captain, I propose we kidnap the boys’ mother and make her our own,” Smee suggested. “Yes,” Hook said. “We will capture the boys and make them walk the plank! Then we will keep their mother.” Smee and Starkey cheered.
text.T1: Wendy wakalisumpula, naakali kulengelela mujulu. “O buzuba bwa satani!” Starkey wakaamba. “Ino banyina ncinzi?” Wakabuzya Smee. Mpoona mpoona, iciteente ca Never cakalengelela, abanyina kabacikkede mpao. “Mbaanyina abaya, alimwi ncitondezyo,” Hook wakaambila Smee. “Iciteente cawidide mumeenda, sena basiya mai? Peepe.” Kwakali kuumuna ku jwi lya Hook, mbuli kuti-kwa kaindi kasyoonto – wakali kuyeeya kubwana aa ba nyina. Pele wakauluba muzeezo ooyu acakali kukonzya kuba misozi. “Nobasololeli, ndayeeya kuti tubatizye banyina ba basankwaakubapanga kuti babe besu,” Smee wakapa muzeezo. “Inzya,” Hook wakaamba. “Tulabatizya basankwa akubaleka baende aa pulanga! Mpoona tulababweza banyina.” Smee aa Stark bakakkomana

text.S1: “Wait,” Hook said suddenly, remembering Tiger Lily. “Where’s the princess?” “We let her go,” Smee replied. “Why?” Hook demanded. “Why, you told us to,” Smee stammered. “I heard you, too, Captain,” Starkey said. “What kind of trickery is going on here?” thundered Hook. “I gave no such order.” He looked around and shivered. “Dark spirit that haunts the lagoon tonight,” he called out. “Do you hear me?” “I hear you,” Peter replied in Hook’s own voice. Hook was brave, but Smee and Starkey hugged each other, shaking. “Who are you?” Hook called out. “I am James Hook,” replied the voice, “captain of the Jolly Roger.” “No, you aren’t!” Hook screamed angrily. “Yes, I am,” the voice insisted.
text.T1: “Kolindila,” Hook wakaamba mpoona mpoona, akuyeeya Tiger Lily. “Ulikuli mwana wamwami?” “Twamuzumizya kuunka,” Smee wakavwiila. “Ino kai?” Hook wakabuzya. “Ino kai, wakali twaambilide, Smee wakbbabbaika. “Ndalimvwide, andime, Nobasololeli,” Starkey wakaamba. “Ino nkucenga kwabuti ooku kucitika ookuno?” wakabwenta Hook. “Teendakaamba boobo,” Wakalangalanga akubimba. “Omuzimo uusiya uuzinguluka cizyiba sunu masiku,” wakaita. “Sena wandimvwa?” “Ndakumvwa,” Peter wakavwiila mujwi lya Hook. Hook wakali muyumu, pele Smee aa Starkey bakakumbatana, akubimba. “Nduwe ni?” Hook wakaita. “Nndime James Hook,” lyakavwiila ijwi,” “nobasololeli ba Jolly Roger.” “Peepe toli nduwe!” Hook wakakwiila akunyema. “Inzya, ndendime,” ijwi lyakazumanana

text.S1: “If you are Hook,” Hook said, trying to sound friendly, “then who am I?” “You are a codfish,” Peter said promptly. Smee and Starkey were slightly stupid, and proud—a bad combination. “A codfish?” they muttered. “Have we been taking orders all this time from a mere fish?” Hook barely heard them. It was not their lack of faith in him that most bothered him but, suddenly, his lack of faith in himself. He felt his ego slipping away from him. “Don’t desert me,” he whispered, hoarsely. “Hook,” Hook asked cleverly, “do you have another voice?” Peter could never resist a game, so he answered in his own voice, “I do.” “And another name?” “Yes.” “Are you an animal, vegetable, or mineral?” Hook asked. ”Yes, no, and no,” Peter replied. “Are you a man?” Hook tried next.
text.T1: “Kuti naa nduwe Hook,” Hook wakaamba, kusola kwaambaula kabotu kabotu, “mpoona mebo ndime ni?” “Uli nswi,” Peter wakambaula kufwambaana. Smee aa Starkey bakali tufubafuba, akulimvwa – cintu cibyabi. “Inswi?” bakanyema. “Nkokuti twakali kutambula milao kuzwa kunswi?” Hook taakamvwa kabotu. Takuli kutasyoma muli nguwe kwakapa kuti apenge mumizeezo, pele, mpoona mpoona, ikutalisyoma mwini. “Mutandisiyi endike,” wakapetekezya, ajwi lyaangide. “Hook,” Hook wakabuzya cakucenjela, “sena ulijisi ijwi limbi?” Peter takonzyi ikukaka cisobano, mpoona wakavwiila mujwi lyakwe, “Inzya,” “Azyina limbi?” “Inzya.” “Sena uli cinyama, imatuvu, na mukuba?” Hook wakabuzya. “inzya, peepe, alimwi peepe,” Peter wakaingula. “Sena uli musankwa?” Hook wakasola awalo.

text.S1: No,” Peter practically spit. “A boy, then?” “Yes.” “An ordinary boy?” Wendy wanted to play, too. “He is a wonderful boy!” she shouted out, giggling. Hook was stumped. “You can’t guess, you can’t guess,” Peter bragged. “Give up?” In Peter’s pride, the pirates saw their chance. “Yes, we give up,” they cried. “Tell us who you are.” “I’m Peter Pan!” Peter yelled out, laughing. Instantly Hook was himself once more, and Smee and Starkey his faithful crew. “Get him!” Hook roared. “Dead or alive!”
text.T1: “Peepe,” Peter wakaingula. “Imusankwa, mpoona?” “Inzya. “ Imusankwa biyo?” Wendy wakalikuyanda kusobana, awalo. “Musankwa mubotu!” wakaompolola, akusekaseka. “Tokonzyi kuzyiba, tokonzyi kuzyiba,” Peter wakalimvwa. “Wacileka?” Ikulimvwa kwa Peter, kwakapa ziggwebenga ciindi. “Inzya, twacileka,” bakalila. “Kotwambila nduwe ni.” “Ndime Peter Pan!” Peter wakabwenta, akuseka. Mpoona mpoona Hook wakajokela mbwabede alimwi, mpoona Smee aa Starkey ambobabeleka limwi. “Amumubweze!” Hook waka vuluma. “Uufwide naa Uupona!”

text.S1: Quickly Peter whistled for his own crew. The lost boys were resting in various parts of the lagoon. “We’re coming, Peter,” they cried. The fight was short but sharp. Swords flew in the water and air, followed by many wheezes and whoops and wails as the two pirates and the lost boys clashed. Hook and Peter had their own private battle to fight. They met not in the water but on the rock—which they both, coincidentally, climbed at the same time, from opposite sides. It was so dark that they didn’t see each other until they were almost in the middle, nose-to-nose.
text.T1: Mukufwambaana Peter wakasiba muluso kubeenzinyina. Ibasankwa bakasweekede bakali kulyookezya muzilao zyaandeene andeene zya cizyiba. “Twaboola, Peter,” bakalila. Ikulwana kwakali kwa kaindi kasyoonto. Imapanga akuluka mumeenda aa mumuo, kwakatobela akusiba akuliyeeya akulila iziggwebenga nozyakaswaangana akulwana aa basankwa bakasweekede. Hook aa Peter abalo bakalijisi inkondo yabo balike. Bakaswanganina kutali mumeenda pele abbwe-mukutazyiba, boonse mpobakatanta, aciindi comwe, kuzwa mumbali zyaandeene zyobilo. Kwakali kusiya cakuti tebakabonana kusikila nobakali aakati, impemo-ampemo.

text.S1: Peter grabbed a knife from Hook’s belt and was about to finish him off when he noticed that he was higher up on the rock than Hook. This would not have been fighting fair, so Peter offered Hook a hand to hoist himself up. Hook was not a fan of fighting fair. He leaned over and bit Peter in response. It was not the pain of the bite but the pain and surprise of the unfairness that dazed Peter, making him quite helpless. All children are affected like this the first time they realize the world is unfair. People had been unfair to Peter before, but he had always forgotten it, and so he reacted as if it were the first time. Hook clawed Peter twice with his hook, and might have finished him off had he not just then heard a ticking. Instead, Hook slid immediately into the water, swimming madly for his ship.
text.T1: Peter wakabweza cipeni kuzwa kuli Hook mpoona wakali aafwaafwi akumumanizya naakabona kuti wakali mujulu atala aabbwe kwiinda aakali Hook. Teekwakali kulwana kululeme, icakapa kuti Peter ape Hook ikwaanza kutegwa amukwele mujulu. Taakali kuyanda kulwana kabotu. Wakaongomana asyoonto akuluma Peter. Teekwakali kucisa kwakumuluma pele kucisa akuggambwa kwakutaloma nkokwaka ggambya Peter, akumumana nguzu. Boonse bana balapenga iciindi cakutaanguna nobabona kuti inyika tailuleme. Ibantu tebakali kuba kabotu kuli Peter, pele walo taakali kubikila maano, mpoona wakali kucita mbuli kuti cakali ciindi cakusaanguna. Hook waka kwamba Peter ziindi zyobilo, alimwi naakamumanizya kuti natakamvwa kulila kwa nkoloko. Icakacitika, Hook wakanjila mumeenda mpoona mpoona, akusamba mbuli uusondokede kuya kubwato bwakwe.

text.S1: Chapter 10 - The Never Bird
text.T1: Caandano ikkumi – Iciyuni Citwa Never

text.S1: Out on the water, the lost boys had won their fight with Smee and Starkey, but they couldn’t find Peter or Wendy or Hook. Taking the pirates’ dinghy, they sailed home in it, shouting for Peter and Wendy the entire time. But there was no response, except for an occasional mocking from the mermaids. “They must be swimming or flying back,” the boys concluded. Had they stayed in the lagoon, they might have soon heard two voices crying for help. Peter and Wendy—injured and weak—had climbed back onto Marooners’ Rock. As the water rose dangerously around them, they fell uncon- scious one right after the other. A mischievous mermaid pulled Wendy by her toe, trying to get her into the water. Feeling her slip from him, Peter woke up just in time to pull her back.
text.T1: Ikuzwa mumeenda, ibasankwa bakaswekede bakali zundide inkondo antoomwe aa Smee aa Starkey, pele tebakamujana Peter naa Wendy naa Hook. Ikubweza bwato bwa ziggebenga, bakaunka kunga`nda, kabayabompolola kwiita Peter aa Wendy iciindi coonse. Pele kwakanyina kuingulwa, pele biyo kusekwa ku ma tosi. “Bakali kusamba naa kuuluka akujoka,” basankwa bakapandulula. Nobakalikkede mucizyiba, nobakali mvwiide imajwii obilo aalilila kugwasigwa. Peter aa Wendy-bakalicisa akubula nguzu-bakali tantide aali Marooner`s Rock. Imeenda naakali kuzula cakuyoosya , bakafwa ngo`nzi. Itosi linyongene lyakakwela kanwe ka Wendy, kusola kumunjizya mumeenda. Peter wakamvwa nolyakamukwela, mpoona wakabuka kaindi nkoona akumujosya.

text.S1: “Our rock is shrinking,” he told her. “Soon it will be gone.” “Let’s go, then!” Wendy cried. “We can swim or fly away.” “I can do neither,” Peter replied. “I have been injured. You go.” But Wendy was too weak to make it on her own. The children put their hands over their eyes to shut out the sight of the rising water, and prepared to meet their end. Just then something brushed Peter’s leg. It was as light as a feather, and it seemed to be asking, Can I help? What luck! It was the tail of a kite, which Michael had made a few days earlier but then lost to the wind. Peter grabbed it and wrapped it around Wendy. “Now you!” Wendy cried.
text.T1: “Ibbwe lyesu liyaabunyikila,” wakamwaambila. Lino lino lila nyikila lyoonse.” “Atweende, ino!” Wendy wakalila. Inga twauluka naa kusamba.” “Kunyina ncekonzya kucita,” Peter wakavwiila. “Ndalicisa. Kounka ebo.” Pele Wendy wakanyina nguzu zyakweenda alike. Ibana bakabika maanza aabo mumeso kutegwa basinkile meenda akali kuvula, akulibambila mamanino aabo. Mpoona mpoona kui cakaguma kuulu kwa Peter. Cakali cuubauba mbuli pepe, alimwi cakali kuboneka mbui kuti cilabuzya, Sena ndikuggwasye? Icoolwe nceeco! Wakali mucila wa kkaiti njaakabamba mazuba aainda yakasweeka noyakai kuuluka akaambo ka muo wakavula. Peter wakaijata akuizambaila amubili wa Wendy. “ Lino ebo!” Wendy wakalila.

text.S1: “It can’t lift us both,” Peter explained. “Michael and Curly tried.” Wendy clung to Peter, refusing to go without him, but he pushed her from the rock and away she flew. Peter was left all alone in the lagoon. The rock grew smaller and smaller. In the distance, the mermaids called sadly to the moon. Like any boy, Peter was scared to die. But soon his fear changed to excitement. “To die will be an awfully big adventure,” he said. Around him, the lagoon grew quieter and quieter. Peter heard the mermaids saying good night to one another and shutting the doors to their coral caves. He heard the water gurgle greedily as it rose to nibble on the rock. Then he saw something white floating on the water. He thought it was a piece of paper, or perhaps a piece of Michael’s kite. But as he continued to stare at it, he realized that it had a more definite sense of purpose than a mere piece of paper would have. It seemed to be fighting the tide instead of just going with the flow. Peter found himself rooting for the white streak to win.
text.T1: “Inga yatunyamuna swebo toonse,” Peter wakpandulula. “Micheal aa Curly bakasola.” Wendy wakajatilila Peter, ikukaka kuunka kakunyina Peter, pele wakamutonkela kuzwa kubbwe mpoona wakauluka. Peter wakacaala alike mucizyiba. Ibbwe lyakali kuyaabuceya. Ikulaale, imatosi akali kwiita mwezi icakutyompokelwa. Mbuli musankwa oonse, Peter wakayoowa kufwa. Mukaindi kasyoonto ikuyoowa nkwakajisi kwakacinca kwakaba kukondeezya. “Ikufwa Inga kwaba cintu cipati.,” wakapandulula. Mpaakabede, icizyiba cakaumuna. Peter wakamvwa imatosi kaambilana kuti akusiye akujala mulyango wa mu mpako. Wakamvwa meenda kaasabila nakali kuyaabuzula kuti ibbwe lizule. Mpona wakabona cintu comwe cilaibuka atala aameenda. Wakali kuyeeya kuti ndiza ncipepe, naa ndi kkaiti lya Micheal. Pele naakali kulangisisya, cakaboneka mbuli kuti cilwanina kuti citaunki aameenda. Peter wakalijana kayandisisya kuzunda.

text.S1: The piece of paper was actually the Never bird, still sitting on her now- floating nest. She was trying desperately to reach Peter. Although he had teased her in the past, he had also given orders that her nest was not to be disturbed. For this reason, and perhaps because she was above all things a mother, she would disturb her nest herself—to save his life. “Swim to the nest,” she called to him. “I am too tired to row all the way to you.” But Peter didn’t speak bird language, and couldn’t understand her. And, even near death, he could be very impatient. “What are you quacking about?” Peter asked rudely. “I don’t understand a word!” “Why, I never!” the Never bird said, and tried again. “Same to you!” Peter replied. “Whatever you just said!”
text.T1: Ikapepa nkakabwene kakali ciyuni ciitwa Never, kacici kede – aci teente. Cakali kuola canguzu kuti cisike kwakali Peter. Nokuba kuti ikaindi wakali kumuseka, wakapa mulao wakuti iciteente cakwe taciyandiki kunyonganya. Akaambo kaako, naa nkaambo kakuti wakali mupati kuzintu zyoonse banyina, wakali kulinyonganizyila citeente imwini – kutegwa amufutule. “Kosamba kusika ku citeente,” waka mwiita. “Ndakatala ikuboola kusika kuli nduwe.” Pele Peter taakali kwambaula musyobo wa ziyuni alimwi taakali kumvwa.alimwi, amunsi munsi akufwa, wakali kukakilwa kujata moyo. “Ino usabila nazi?” Peter wakabuzya. “Kunyina bbala nokuba lyomwe ndyendimvwa!” “Ino, nsecizyi!” Iciyuni ciitwa Never cakavwiila, akusoa alimwi. “Ayebo,” Peter wakavwiila. Kufumbwa mbubona oobo mboamba!”

text.S1: Remembering that he was only a child, the maternal Never bird took a deep breath and made one last push to row her nest to the rock. Upon reaching it, she flew up, leaving her eggs behind to make some room for Peter. Finally realizing her meaning, Peter waved his thank-you to the Never bird. Looking down, however, he saw there was not enough room in the nest for both him and her two large white eggs. He lifted the eggs up, and the Never bird covered her eyes with her feathers, afraid of what Peter might do. On the rock next to Peter was a waterproof hat, broad and wide, which Starkey had left behind. Peter put the eggs into the hat and set them afloat. With a final happy quack, the Never bird swooped down and settled herself on top of her eggs. Peter got into the Never bird’s old nest, waved good-bye, and pushed off. He in his nest and Wendy with her kite arrived back at the cave at nearly the same time. Oh, how everyone rejoiced! The party went on until Wendy realized how late it was and told everyone it was well past their bedtime. The boys tried to stall, insisting they were injured and in need of slings and bandages, but Wendy would have none of it and sent them to bed.
text.T1: Naakayeeya kuti wakacili mwana, iciyuni ciitwa Never cakayoya cakuyoowa akulitonkka camamanino kuunka kuciteente naakamana wakauuka, akusiya mai munsi alike kuteggwa abambe busena bwa Peter. Kumamanino, naakabona ncaakali kupandulula, Peter wakanyamuna maanza mukumulumba Never bird. Pele naakalanga aansi, wakabona kuti, kunyina busena muciteente, bwabo boonse bobilo a mai. Wakanyamuna mai mujulu, mpoona Never bird waka vumba meso aakwe amababa, akuyoowa kuti naa Peter ulatyani. Abbwe musimunsi aa Peter kwakali nzyeete iitanjizyi meenda, icipati akulampa, Starkey ncakasiya. Peter wakabika mai mu nzyeete akucibika atala aameenda kaciibuka. Mukulekelezya Never bird kakkomene wakasabila, akuseluka mpoona akukkala atala aa mai. Peter wakanjila muciteente cakaindi ca Nmever bird, akutambika maanza, mpoona waunka. Walo muciteente aa Wendy kajisi kkaiti, bakasika aampako aciindi comwe. Oh, boonse mbobakakkomana! Ipokwe lyakatolelela ikusikila Wendy naakabona kuti ciindi camana akubaambila boonse kuti caindilila ciindi cakoona. Ibasankwa bakasola, ikwaamba kuti bakalicisa akuti bakali kuyanda nkwisyo aa ma bbandeji, pele Wendy taakai kuyanda nociba comwe akubatuma mukoona.

text.S1: Chapter 11 - The Happy Family
text.T1: Caandaano ikkumi aa comwe – Imukwasyi uukkomene

text.S1: On the night that would come to be known as “the night of all nights,” the children ate a make-believe dinner. Unfortunately, their hunger was real, and as a result they were noisy and misbehaving. “Be quiet!” Wendy yelled finally, for she was hungry and grumpy, too. “Is your plate empty, Slightly?” Slightly looked down at his imaginary plate. “Not quite, Mommy.” “He didn’t take one bite of his carrots,” Nibs said. John raised his hand. “Since Peter isn’t here, can I sit in his chair?” “Sit in Father’s chair? No,” replied Wendy, who had taken to referring to Peter as Father. “He’s not our real father,” John complained.
text.T1: Imasiku ayooitwa kuti “imasiku aa masiku oonse,” ibana bakalya icakulya ca mangolezya cakusyoma. Pele, inzala njobakajisi yakali yamasimpe, akaambo kaako bakali kusabila akutalilemeka. “Amuumune!” Wendy wakakwiila mamanino, nkaambo wakali aanzala aa kunyema, awalo. “Sena mutiba wako taukwe zyakulya, Slightly?” Slightly wakalanga aamutiba wamumizeezo. “Peepe, Baama.” “Tanalya nokaba kasyoonto ka kkalot,” Nibs wakapanduula. John wakanyamuna kwaanza. “Akaambo kakuti Peter tak ookuno, sena inga ndakkala acuuno cakwe?” “Kukkala acuuno ca bausi? Peepe,” wakavwiila Wendy, ikwakali kwiita Peter kuti Bataata. “Tabali bataata bamasimpe,” John wakatongooka.

text.S1: Tootles wanted in, too. “Can I be the father?” he asked. “No,” Wendy said. “What about the baby?” he asked. “I’m the baby,” Michael said. He was already settled in his comfortable bas- ket. Tootles moped. “Slightly has his elbows on the table,” someone reported. “The twins ate their dessert before their vegetables,” someone else added. “Curly is eating all the butter and honey.” “Nibs is speaking with his mouth full.” Wasn’t this just like normal family life? Later, after the imaginary dishes were washed, Wendy sat by the fire and sewed socks with very real holes in them. As her boys played around her, she felt very content with her familiar little family. Just one thing was missing. Suddenly she heard a step above them.
text.T1: Tootles wakali kuyanda, awalo. “Sena inga ndaba bausyi?” wakabuzya. “Peepe,” Wendy wakavwiila. “Ino kuba mwana?” wakabuzya. “Micheal wakaamba. Wakalikkede kale kabotu kabotu mu cinzuwa. Tootles wakaswena. “Slightly wabikka kamboyo aa tebule,” umwi wakatola makani. “Bana bamaanga bakalya kakulya kakusaanguna, kabatana lya cisyu,” aumwi wakayungizya. Curly ulya bbata abuci.” “Nibs wambaula azyakulya zizwide mukanwa.” Sena oobu teebwakai buumi bukala mukwasyi uululeme? Nokwakainda kainda nobakamana bakasanzya imitiba yamumizeezo, Wendy wakakkala munsu munsi aa muilo akusuma masookesi azidonkwi mumbali’ ibana nobakali kusobana munsi lyakwe, wakamvwa kabotu abuumi bubotu bwa mukwasyi musyoonto. Comwe biyo cintu cakabulila. Mpoona mpona wakamvwa nsindo atala lyabo.

text.S1: “That’s Peter’s step,” Wendy said. “Children, go greet Father at the door.” Peter entered, dropping down through his own personal tree, and the children ran to him happily. He had brought nuts and treats for them and—from the crocodile—the correct time for Wendy. This he obtained by following the crocodile until he chimed the hour. “You spoil us, Peter,” Wendy said. “We want to dance!” the twins cried. “Go ahead,” said Peter, who was in a jolly mood. “You and Mommy, too!” “Come on, Peter,” Wendy said. “Children, go put your nightgowns on first.” While the boys ran to do so, Peter and Wendy had a quiet moment alone. “Life is good, isn’t it?” Peter said, warming his feet by the fire. “You and me, and the little ones?” “It is,” Wendy agreed. “I think Curly has your nose.” “Michael takes after you,” Peter said.
text.T1: “Ooyo weenda waawo ngu Peter,” Wendy wakapandulula. “Nobana, kamuya kumulyango makaanzye bauso.’ Peter wakanjila, akulisowa acisamu cakwe ncaakali kuyandisisya, mpoona bana bakamulundukila kabakkomene. Wakabaletela inyemu aa twakulya tumwi mpoona – kuzwa kuli ciwena – iciindi cibotu ca Wendy. Eezi wakazijana naakali kutobela ciwena kusikila wayungizya zyakwaamba. “Ulatnyonganya, Peter,” Wendy wakaamba. “Tuyanda kuzyana!” bana ba maanga bakalila. “Inzya inga mwazyana,” wakaingula Peter, iwakakkomene. “Andinywe abaama,abalo!” “Kamufwambaana, Peter,” Wendy wakaamba. “yoobana, kutaanguna, kumuya musame zisani zyamasiku.” Ibasankwa nobakali kulunduka kuti bakasame, Peter aa Wendy bakacaala balike akuba aakaindi kabotu balike. “Ibuumi mbubotu, tee kai?” Peter wakaamba kumwi kakasaazya imaulu nakali kuyota mulilo. “Yebo andime, abana?” “Inzya.” Wendy wakazumina. “Ndiyeeya kuti Curly ulijisi impemo yako,” “Micheal ukonzya nduwe,” Peter wakapandulula.

text.S1: But suddenly, Peter looked scared. “Wendy,” he said. “This is all make-believe, right? I’m not really their father?” Wendy looked at him for a few seconds. “It’s make-believe,” she finally said. “Whew!” Peter cried. “I can’t tell you how relieved I am to hear that! It would make me feel so old to be their real father!” “And how do you feel about me?” Wendy asked. Peter just blinked, as if he didn’t quite understand the question. Wendy sighed and went to sit at the other end of the room, with her back to him. At that moment, the boys came out and sang and danced for Peter and Wendy in their nightgowns. When they had finished dancing, the boys got into bed for Wendy’s good-night story—the story that they loved best, and which Peter hated. Usually when she told this story, he put his hands over his ears or left the room. Tonight, however, he stayed to listen. “Once upon a time there was a gentleman,” Wendy began.
text.T1: Mpoona mpoona, Peter wakaboneka kuyoowa. “Wendy, wakaamba. “Eeci ncakusyoma, naa? Mebo nseli bausyi babazyala?” Wendy wakamulanga kwa kaindi kasyoonto. “Ncakusyoma,” wakavwiila kumamanino. “Whew!” Peter wakalila. “Tokonzyi kuzyiba mbondakomana kumvwa boobo! Inga ndalimvwa kucembaala kuti ndaba bausyi baba zyala!” “Ino ulimvwa buti ali ndime?” Wendy wakabuzya. Peter wakabalaba biyo, mbuli kuti taakamvwa mubuzyo. Wendy wakayoya akuyookkala kulubazu lumwi, akulanga kumwi. Aciindi ncoonya ciya, ibana bakaboola kabaimba akuzozyanina Peter aa Wendy kabasamide zyakusama zyamasiku. Nobakamana kuzyana, ibasankwa bakanjila mubulo kuyooswilila ikaano kamasiku kuzwa kuli Wendy – ikaano nkobakali kuyandisisya, kalo Peter nkaakazondede. Ziindi zinji, ikano nokakali kwanwa, Peter wakali kusinka matwi naa kutli boobo wkali kuzwa mung`anda. Imasiku aasunu pele wakacaala mung`anda kutegwa aswiilile kaano. “Mazuba aakaindi kwakali mulombwana,” Wendy wakatalika.

text.S1: “I want a lady,” Curly said. “I want a white rat,” said Nibs. “Shhh,” Wendy said. “Okay, there was a lady as well. Their names were Mr. and Mrs. Darling.” On the other side of the room, Peter flinched. “Hey,” John said, “I know them.” “Me too,” Michael said, but he didn’t sound sure. “Mr. and Mrs. Darling were married and had three—” “White rats?” Nibs cried hopefully. “Children,” Wendy said. “And they had a nurse called Nana. But one day Mr. Darling got mad at Nana and chained her up in the yard, and so all the children flew away to Neverland.” “That is a great story,” said Nibs. “Imagine how sad these parents were after their children left,” Wendy said. “Poor parents,” the boys moaned, but they were just pretending to feel sorry.
text.T1: “Ndiyanda mukaintu,” Curly wakaamba. “Ndiyanda mbeba iituba,” wakaamba Nibs. “Shhh,” Wendy wakaamba. “Mbubo, kwakali mukaintu awalo. Imazyina aabo akali Ba Darling abakaintu babo.” Kulubazu lumwi lwa nga`nda, Peter wakayoowa. “Yawe,” John wakaamba kuti, “Ndili bazyi.” “Andime,” Micheal wakayungizya, pele tanakali kuboneka kusyoma. “Ba Darling abakaintu babo bakali kweteene alimwi bakai jisi abana botatwe-“ “Imbeba zituba?” Nibs wakalila cakupenga. “Yoobana,” Wendy wakaamba. “Mpoona bakali jisi amukaintu musilis wakali kwiitwa kuti Nana. Pele buzuba bomwe Ba Darling bakanyemena Nana akumwaangilila mu lubuwa, mpoona bana boonse bakaulukila ku Neverland.” “Ako nkaano kabotu maningi,” wakaamba Nibs. “Kamuyeeya biyo mbobaklimvwa bazyali ibana boonse nobakauluka akubasiya,” Wendy wakapandulula. “Bacaangu bazyali,” ibasankwa bakalila, pele bakali kulibejezya biyo kufwa luse.

text.S1: “It’s an awfully sad story,” the first twin said cheerfully. “If you knew how strong a mother’s love is, you wouldn’t worry,” Wendy said. And now she came to the part that Peter hated the most. “You see,” Wendy said, “the mother left the window open so her children could fly back one day.” She closed her eyes. “Can’t you see it? Can’t you picture the happy scene when the children finally fly back home?” From Peter’s corner came a hollow groan. “Are you in pain?” Wendy asked. “No, but you are wrong about mothers.” He took a deep breath. “A long time ago, I thought my mother would also keep the window open for me, so I stayed away and played. But when I flew back, the window was locked. She had forgotten all about me, and another little boy was sleeping in my bed.” “Is that true or make-believe?” Wendy asked, alarmed.
text.T1: “Nkaano katyompya aaka,” omwe mwana wamaanga wakaamba kabotu kabotu. “Kuti noolizyi luyando lwa bazyali banyina mboluli luyumu tokonzyi kufwa luse,” Wendy wakaamba. Mpoona wakaboola kulubazu Peter nkwatakali kuyanda. “Wabona.” Wendy wakatondezya, “banyina bakasiya mpulungwido kaijulidwe bukwazi kutegwa ibana baulukile munganda akujoka alimwi bumwi buzuba.” Wakajala meso. “Tamukonzyi kubona oobo? Tamukonzyi kuyeeya mbocitikabote ibana baakuulukila mung`anda alimwi?” kuzwa kuli Peter kwakazwa kulyoolola. “Sena mulicisidwe na?” Wendy wakabuzya. “Peepe, pele ulilubide akaambo ka bamanyina.” Wakayoya. “Ikaindi, ndakai kubona mbuli kuti bamama abalo bayoondisiila mpulungwido kaikkele bukwazi, icakapa kuti ndiunke akusobana. Pele nondakajoka, impulungwido yakalijalidwe. Bakali ndilubide, mpoona aumwi mwana musankwa wakalilede abulo bwangu.” Sena ncamasimpe naa ncakupanga kusyoma?” Wendy wakabuzya cakuyoowa.

text.S1: Peter wasn’t sure, but it scared the children all the same. So that is what mothers are like, they thought. “Wendy, let’s go home right now!” John cried. “Maybe it’s too late and the window’s already locked!” ”Yes,” she said, clutching her brothers. She was so worried about the closed window that she didn’t even think about Peter’s feelings. “Peter, will you ar- range it?” “If you like,” he replied coolly, as if she had asked him to pass the nuts. After all, if she didn’t care, neither would he! Upset at the idea of losing their mother, the lost boys surrounded Wendy threateningly. “We won’t let you go!” they cried. “We’ll keep you prisoner!” “Tootles, help!” Wendy cried. Somehow, even though he was the silliest boy, she knew he was the right person to ask. Tootles stepped between her and the rest of the boys. “You’ll have to go through me first,” he said.
text.T1: Peter taakasyomede, pele eeci cakakonga bana boonse. Nkokuti mbobabede bamanyina, bakayeeya. “Wendy, katuya kung`anda lino lino!” John wakalila. “Ndiza camana ciindi ampulungwido yajalwa kale!” “Inzya,” wakaamba kajatililide banabokwabo. Wakalipengede mumoyo akaambo ka mpulungwido yakajalidwe cakapakuti alube cakalikuyeeya Peter. “Peter, sena inga wacibamba?” “Kuti koyanda,” wakavwiila, mbuli kuti wakamwambila kumutambikizya nyemu. Naa taabikila maano awalo takabikili maano! Ibana basankwa bakanyema akaambo kukuweekela banyina icakapa kuti bamuzinguluke Wendy akumukonga. “Tatukokuzumizya kuunka!” bakalila. Tulakubika muntolongo!” “Tootles, kondigwasya!” Wendy wakalila. Nokubakuti wakali kafubafuba, Wendy wakalizyi kuti ngowakali kuyandika kubuzya. Tootles wakaboola akati kakwe abasankwa. “mwelede kwiinda muli ndime kutaanguna,” wakaamba.

text.S1: Peter spoke up. “We keep no girls here against their will. Since flying makes you so tired, I’ll have the Indians guide you through the woods. Then Tink can take you across the sea.” “Thank you, Peter,” Wendy said. She turned to the lost boys. “Come with us,” she offered. “I am sure my parents would adopt you.” This was meant mainly for Peter, but all of the boys jumped with joy. “Peter, can we go?” they pleaded. “If you like,” he repeated bitterly, and they rushed to pack. He, however, didn’t move. “Go pack, Peter,” Wendy said, her voice low. “I’m not going,” he replied. Then, to show that he didn’t care, he skipped around the room singing. “But we can find your mother,” Wendy begged. “No! I don’t like mothers! She would only tell me I have to grow up and stop having fun.”
text.T1: Peter wakaambaula. “Tatuzumizyi basimbi kukkala kokuno kuti kabatayandi.nkaambo kuuluka kulakukatazya, ndila kupa ba mweenye kukusindikila musokwe. Mpoona Tink ulakulandusya mulonga.” “Ndalumba,Peter,” Wendy wakaamba. Wakaambila basankwa bakasweekede kuti. “koboola kuno,” wakamwiiita. “Ndasyoma bazyali bangu inga bakubweza.” Wakalikwaambila Peter, pele boonse basankwa bakasotoka cakukkomana. “Peter, tuunke?” bakakombelezya. “Naa mulayanda,” wakainduluka kanyemede, mpoona bakalunduka kuyoolibambila. Walo, taakazungaana. “Koyaulibambile, Peter,” Wendy wakaamba. “Nsekoounka,” wakavwiila. Kutondezya kuti unyina ndaba, wakatalika kusotooka akwiimba mung`anda. “Pele tatuna bajana ba nyoko,” Wendy wakakombelezya. “Peepe! Nseyandi bamanyina! Inga bandambila biyo kuti welede kukomena akuleka kusobana.”

text.S1: The other boys watched this exchange nervously. Peter not coming? What would they do? Could they still go? Did they want to? “Now, then,” Peter said, “I’ll have no fuss, no blubbering good-byes. It was a pleasure to meet you, Wendy.” He held out his hand formally. “You’ll take good care of yourself?” she asked. “Yes. Ready, Tinker Bell?” Tinker Bell groaned from her cave. She resented having to help Wendy, but at least the girl would finally be gone. “Then off you go.” At just that moment, however, there was a clashing sound above. The pirates had attacked the Indians. The trip home was off, at least for now.
text.T1: Ibasankwa bakalikulangilila nkobakali kuzwangana. Peter takooboola? Ino balatyani? Sen balaunka? Sena bakali kuyanda? “Pele, lino,” wakaamba Peter, “Nsekabikii maano, nsekayobeki zyakulayana. Cali cintu cibotu kuswaangana, Wendy.” Wakatambika kwaanza kwakwe. “Ucaale kabotu?” wakabuzya. “Inzya. Walibambila, Tinker Bell?” Tinker Bell wakalyoolola kuzwa mumpako. Taakali kuyanda kugwasya Wendy, pesi mbubo musimbi ulaunka. “Nkokuti koya” mpoona mpoona kwakali kusabila kupati kuzwa mujulu. Izigwebenga zyakauma ba mweenye. Ilweendo lwakafwa, calino.

text.S1: Chapter 12 - Extremely Happy Hook
text.T1: Caandaano Ikumi aazyobilo – Ikukkomana kwa Hook

text.S1: The pirate attack was a complete surprise. Hook had broken all of the rules the pirates and the Indians normally followed when they fought. He attacked in neither the time nor the place that was allowed. When it was over, almost all of the Indians were injured. Only Tiger Lily managed to escape unharmed. Finished with the Indians, the pirates still could not rest. It was, after all, not the Indians they had come for. The Indians were just bees to be smoked out so they could get to the honey. The pirates wanted the lost boys and Wendy and, most of all, Peter Pan. Peter was an awfully small boy to inspire such a big hatred in Hook, even if he had thrown Hook’s hand to the crocodile. But there was something about him that enraged Hook. It was more than Peter’s courage, or his cuteness. It was his cockiness, his absolute confidence in himself. This is something many children have, but most grown-ups have lost it entirely. Perhaps Hook had lost some of his, too, and wanted it back.
text.T1: Inkondo ya ziggwebenga yakaggambya. Kook wakatyola milao yakali kutobela ziggwebenga aa bamweenye njobakai kutobela akulwana. Taakatobela ciindi naa cilao. Noyakamana nkondo, bamweenye banji bakaliliciside kale. Tiger aa Lily mbobatakalicisa. Iziggwebenga nozyakamana kulwana abamweenye teezyakalyokezya nkaambo tabali ba mweenye mbozyakali kutobela. Ba mweenye bakali nzuki nzyobbakali kuyoka kutegwa bagusye buci. Iziggwebenga zyakali kuyanda basankwa bakaswekede aa Wendy alimwi, kapati Peter Pan. Peter wakali kasankwa kasyoonto kakali kuyumyayumya ibubi muli Hook, nokuba kuti wakasowede kwaanza kwa Hook kuli ba ciwena. Pele kwakali cintu comwe ali nguwe cakapa kuti Hook akalale. Eeci cakali bunkutwe bwa Peter, naa kubota. Cakali kuliyumyayumya, akulisyoma. Eeci ncobajisi ibana banji, pele bapati boonse bakacisowa. Ndiza Hook wakasowa kale zyoonse eezi, lino, wakali kuziyanda alimwi.

text.S1: The question wa

How could the pirates get down the hollow trees, which were perfectly sized to allow each individual lost boy down but no one else? Below, the boys were still trying to figure out who had won the battle. “If it was the Indians,” they reasoned, “they will beat their tom-tom drums. It is al- ways their sign of victory.” Perched at the edge of the hollow trees up above, the pirates heard this. Smee happened to be sitting on a tom-tom, which Hook ordered him to beat immediately. After a moment of confusion, Smee understood and smiled. BANG! BANG! BANG! went the tom-tom drum. “The tom-tom!” The pirates heard Peter cry. “The Indians have won! Let’s go up and celebrate with them!”
text.T1: Imubuzyo ngwakuti: iziggwebenga inga zyasika butiku zisamu, izyakali kweelela biyo aumwi musankwa wakaswekede kakunyina aumbi? Mukati ibasankwa bakali kusola kuyeeya iwakazunda nkondo. “Naa mba mweenye,” bakaliyeeya, “bakalizya ingoma zyabo. Lyoonse cakali kutondezya kuzunda kwabo” iziggwebenga zyakamvwa zyoonse. Smee wakakede aa ngo`ma, mpoona Hook wakamwambila kuti ailizye mpoona mpoona. nokwakamana kunyongana, Smee wakamvwa akumwetamweta. BANG! BANG! BANG! Mboyakali kulila ngo`ma. ”Ingo`ma!” iziggwebenga zyakamvwa Peter walila. “Ba mweenye bazunda! Katuya tukakkomane aambabo!”

text.S1: The lost boys cheered, and Hook ordered his men to take their positions and get ready for the boys to come up through their trees. The first to emerge was Curly. The pirates threw him around like a ball— from Cecco to Smee, then Starkey, then Bill Jukes, then Noodler. One by one, all of the boys were plucked from their trees and tossed around in this manner. It was, to say the least, a different kind of flying than they were used to. The pirates then gagged the boys and tied them up. With Wendy, the pirates behaved differently. After all, she was a lady—or, rather, a little girl—and even pirates have some manners. When she emerged, Hook offered her his arm and bowed so elegantly that she blushed. When they tied her up, they used the softest rope they had, apologizing and making sure that they weren’t hurting her.
text.T1: Basankwa bakaswekede bakakkomana,mpoona Hook wakaamba kuti balibambile nkaambo basankwa balaboola bainda muzisamu. Wakasanguna ngu Curly. Iziggwebenga zyakamusowa aansi mbuli bbola-kuzwa kuli Cecco mpoona kuli Smee, mpoona Starkey, mpoona Bill Jukes, mpoona Noodler. Omwe omwe, bonse basankwa bakaangulwa kuzwa kuzisamu akuba zingulusya. Mpoona ziggwebenga zyaka baangiila boonse. kuli Wendy ziggwebenga zyakacinca nkaambo wakali mukaintu walo-aziggwebenga zilamaano. Naakabonekea, Hook wakamutambika kwaanza akumulemeka cakuti wakafwa nsoni. Nobakali kumwaangilila bakabelesya ntambo nteteete,akulomba kulekelelwa, akubona kuti teebakamucisa.

text.S1: When it came time to tie up Slightly, however, the pirates found that it took far more rope than it had for the other boys or Wendy. It turned out that Slight- ly had been sneaking so many snacks lately that he had grown greatly. In fact, there had come a day when he no longer fit in his tree. How had he gotten into and out of the cave? Each night while the other boys slept, he had secretly started to widen the hole in his tree. “Why are you so much bigger than the other boys?” Hook demanded. “Why, you’re practically as big as a grown-up.” While the pirates found extra rope with which to tie him up, Hook had a brilliant idea. He knew how he was going to get Peter, who was still down in the cave.
text.T1: Nozyakali kwaangilila Slightly zyakajana kuti zyaka belesya ntambo zinji kwiinda basankwa aa Wendy. Cakaboneka kuti Slighty wakali kubwezabweza twakulyalya cakuti wakazooneneya kapati akuleka kweelea muzisamu. “Ino wakali kunjila akuzwa buti mumpako? Nobakali koona basankwa, wakali kukomezya kapulo mucisamu. “Ino ncoli mupati kwiinda basankwa?” Hook wakabuzya. “Ino, ulinenede mbuli bapati.” Iziggwebenga nozyakali kulangaula ntambo iimbi yakumwangilila, Hook wakajana muzeezo mubotu. Wakalizyi mbwakali kuyoobweza Peter, wakacili mumpako.

text.S1: He signaled for the other pirates to take the lost boys and Wendy to the ship and leave him alone to his plans. Tip Toeing over to Slightly’s tree, Hook saw that it was now wide enough to let him through. He listened for any sound from down below, but all was quiet. Was Peter asleep? Was he waiting at the bottom of the tree with his dagger in his hand? The only way to find out was to try. Hook took a deep breath, stepped into the tree, and let himself fall. When he hit the ground, he crouched for a second, waiting for his eyes to adjust to the dark of the underground cave. Finally, things began to take shape. In the corner, he saw the great bed and, on it, Peter sleeping. For once, Peter wasn’t pretending. He was unaware of what was happening up above. He believed the Indians had won the battle, and that the lost boys had gone up to celebrate with them.
text.T1: Wakaambila beenzinyina kujata basankwa mpoona Wendy kubwato akumusiya alike amizeezo iimbi. Naakali kusobelela kuya kucisamu ca Slightly, Hook wakabona kuti cisamu cakomena cakuti inga wainda. Wakasola kuswiilila kuti naa kumvwika coongo pele kwakali umwine. Sena Peter wakali koona naa kulindila munsi munsi aacisamu amapanga kumaanza? Icakali nkusola kuyandika nkulangaula kaambo. Wakalyoolola, akunjila mucisamu. Naakalyuumputa ansi, wakaongomana kwa kaindi kasyoonto, naakalikulindila kuti meso azyibile mumusinze mumpako. Kumamanino, izintu zyakatalika kuba kabotu. Wakabona bulo kubwaanda, aakalede, Peter. Calino, Peter taakali kulicegeezya. Taakazyi cakali kucitika mujulu. Wakasyoma kuti ba mweenye bakazunda nkondo, mpoona basankwa bakasweekede bakaliunkide kuyoosekelela aambabo.

text.S1: He was happy for the Indians, but the lost boys were going to leave him, and Peter didn’t feel like celebrating. Oh, he had pretended not to care, but he was very sad. And when he got sad, he got sleepy. Today he was so sleepy that he didn’t even dream. It was in this sad, deep, dreamless sleep that Hook found Peter. As he stood over the bed and looked down, Hook felt slightly sorry for the boy. After all, Peter was only a child, and Hook wasn’t completely evil. But then Peter smiled in his sleep—perhaps he was dreaming something after all—and that smile seemed so arrogant, it made Hook angry all over again. Hook saw a glass of water on Peter’s night table and knew exactly what to do. In case he should ever be captured, Hook always carried a small bottle of poison with him. Taking it out of his pocket now, he added a few drops to Pe- ter’s water. Peter would wake up, take a sip, and fall to the ground dead. With one last satisfied look back, Hook climbed back up Slightly’s tree. Once above ground, Hook tilted his captain’s hat at a fashionable angle, wound his dark cloak dramatically around himself, and stole away through the forest.
text.T1: Wakakkomana kuli ba mweenye, pele basankwa bakasweekede bakali kuyomusiya, walo Peter taakalimvwa kuti inga wasekelela. Oh, wakali kulicengeezya kuti tabikili maano, pesi wakausa mpoona wakaona. Sunu wali aang`onzi cakuti taakalota akulota. Naakali koona kakunyina kulota Hook wakajana Peter. Naakaimvwii munsimunsi aabulo akulanga aansi, Hook wakamvwa luse ku musankwa. Iwakali biyo mwana ngu Peter, mpoona Hook taakali mubi moyo. Pele Peter wakamwetamweta kung`onzi-ndiza wakali kulota cimwi cintu-alimwi kumwetamweta kwakaboneka kwakulimvwa, alimwi kwakapa kuti Hook anyeme alimwi. Hook wakabona tambula lyakajisi meenda atebule lya Peter lya masiku mpoona wakalizyti icakucita. Kufumbwa kuti bamujata, Hook wakalikweenda aa kabboddela kakajisi musamu uujaya. Wakauzwisya kuzwa munkkomo yakwe akubikka tudosi twamusamu mumeenda aa Peter. Peter ulabuka, akunywa, akuwida aansi akufwa. Naakaceba munsi ca mamanino wakakkomana, Hook wakatanta mujulu kucisamu ca Slghtiy. Naakasika mujulu, Hook wakaswenya nzyeete ambali mbuli mu gayi, akunjila musokwe.

text.S1: Chapter 13 - Carried Off
text.T1: Caandaano ikkumi azyotatwe - Ikuzibweza

text.S1: Peter slept for a long time. Finally, he was awakened by a soft rapping on the door of his tree. When he opened his eyes, it was still dark. He felt for his sword. “Who is it?” he asked. There was no answer, only another knock. “I said, who is it?” Still nothing, only silence. Peter was scared, but also excited. He loved adventures, especially ones that placed him in danger. His heart beat very fast. “I won’t open unless you speak,” he said. “Let me in, Peter,” the visitor finally said in a lovely bell-like voice. It was Tinker Bell! Peter quickly unlocked the door and she flew in, her face flushed and her pretty dress stained with mud. Tinker Bell told Peter that Wendy and the boys had been captured and were now prisoners on the pirate ship. “I must save her!” Peter cried, leaping for his weapons.
text.T1: Peter wakaona kwa ciindi ciamfu. Mamanino, wakabuka akukonkkomona amulyango wa cisamu cakwe. Naakajula meso, kwakacili kusiya. Wakabweza iceba lyakwe. “Ndinywe bani?” wakabuzya. Kwakanyina wakavwiila, kwakali biyo kukonkkomona alimwi. “Ndaamba kuti, nguni ooyo?” alimwi kwakanyina wakavwiila. Peter wakayoowa, alimwi wakaikkomene. Wakalikuyanda kweenda, kapati kwakali kumubika mumapenzi. Imoyo wakwe wakasotauka. “Nsekoojula kuti utaambauli,” wakamba. “Kondinjizya, Peter,” imweenzu wakamba aa jwii libotu. Wakali Tinker Bell! Peter wakafwambaana kujula mulyango mpoona wakaulukila mukati, wakatyompwa aisani cakwe cakabaa aa tombe. Tinker Bell wakaambila Peter kuti Wendy abasankwa bakabajata lino bakali muntolongo mubwato bwa ziggwebenga. “Ndeelede kumufutula!” Peter wakalila, akulundukila kubweza zyakulwanya.

text.S1: But first he would have a sip of the water Wendy had left by his bed. His hand reached for the glass. “No!” Tinker Bell cried, for she had heard Hook mutter about his trick as he sped through the forest. “It is poisoned!” “What? How? By whom?” “Hook.” “Don’t be silly. How could Hook have gotten down here?” “I don’t know, but he did.” Peter Pan was stubborn, and thirsty, so he raised his glass anyway. Tinker Bell flew quickly between his lips and the glass and took a sip of the water instead. “Hey, that’s my water,” Peter protested. Tinker Bell did not answer. She was already spinning dizzily in the air, poisoned. “Tink?” Peter asked, suddenly afraid. “You should have listened to me,” Tinker Bell said weakly. “Oh, Tink, why did you risk your life to save me?” Peter asked. Her wings were weak, but she managed to land gracefully on Peter’s shoulder and give his nose one last loving pinch. She whispered in his ear, “Because I love you, you silly donkey.” Then she flew weakly back to her little cave and collapsed on her bed.
text.T1: Pele kutaanguna ulanywa meenda aakasiya Wendy munsimunsi aabulo. Ikwanza kwakwe kwaka jata tambula. “Peepe! Tinker Bell wakalia, nkaambo wakamvide Hook kaamba aa nzyayanda kucita naakalundukila musokwe. “Ali aamusamu!” “Inzi? Mbuti? Nguni waubika?” “Hook” “Utafubaali, ino Hook inga wasika buti ookuno?” “Nsezyi, pesi wasika.” Peter Pan wakali aankazi, alimwi wakali aanyota, mpoona wakanyamuna itambula. Tinker Bell wakauukila akati ka milomo yakwe aa tambula akunywa meenda. “Hey, meenda aangu aayo,” Peter wakakasya. Tinker Bell taakaavwiila. Wakali kale mujulu kazinguluka, wanywa musamu. “Tink?” Peter wakabuzya mpoona mpoona akuyoowa. “Waeleede kundiswilia,” Tinker Bell wakaamba ajwi lityompedwe. “Oh, Tink, ino wanywida nzi meenda kuyanda kundifutula?” Peter wakabuzya, imapepe aakwe akabula nguzu, pele wakacikonzya kulokela aamubili wa Peter akumusyamba aampemo. Wakapetekezya mukutwi kwakwe, “nkaambo ndakuyanda, okafubafuba.” Mpoona wakaulukila ku mpako yakwe akuwida abulo bwakwe.

text.S1: Peter knelt near Tinker Bell’s limp body in distress. His head filled almost the entire space of her room. Tink’s light was growing darker. Peter knew she would die if it went out entirely. “Oh, Tink,” he cried, “what can I do? I need you. Please don’t leave me now.” “I think I could get well again if children believed in fairies,” Tinker Bell gasped. But there were no children left in the cave! Peter stood up straight and screamed out to all of the children in the universe, to all who might be dream- ing about Neverland, boys and girls in their pajamas, safe in their beds— maybe even you. “Do you believe?” he cried, and his question rang throughout the world. Tink sat up weakly in bed and listened, straining to hear her fate. She and Peter thought they heard some voices, but they weren’t sure. “If you believe,” Peter tried next, “clap your hands. Don’t let Tink die!”
text.T1: Peter wakafugama munsi munsi amubili wa Tinker Bell mutwe kauzwide mung`anda. Mumuni wa Tink wakayakisya mpoona Peter wakazyiba kuti ulafwa kuti uzime oonse. “Oh, Tink,” wakalila, "ino ndi“yani? Ndilakuyanda. Ndakomba utandisiyi lino.” “ndiza inga ndapona kuti naa ibana basyoma mumizimo,” Tinker Bell wakayoya cakucalikizya. Pele kwakanyina bana bakaceede mu mpako! Peter wakaimikilaakukwiila ku bana boonse ba munyika, kuli baabo boonse bakali kulota ali Neverland, ibasankwa abasimbi kabasamide zisani zyakoona aanzizyo, kabaonede mubulo-ndiza anduwe. “Sena ulasyoma?” wakalila. Tink wakabukaakuswiilila, akupenga kumvwa mamanino. Walo aa Peter bakamvwa mbuli kuti bamvwa majwi, pele teebakasyomede. “Kuti naa mwazumina,” Peter wakasola, “kokamba maanza. Utaleki Peter tink afwe!”

text.S1: This time they heard their answer: many children clapping. A few naughty, nasty children hissed, but mostly they clapped—until, that is, the clapping suddenly stopped, having been hushed by worried mothers who had rushed into bedrooms to find out what all the commotion was about. Nevertheless, that bit of clapping was enough. Tinker Bell was saved. Back to her old self, she didn’t even think of thanking the children who believed—although she did want revenge on the few who had hissed. “Now we must rescue Wendy!” Peter vowed. Oh, if only some clapping could work that magic as well. “Yes, yes, we must always think of Wendy,” Tinker Bell said glumly. It was a cloudy night, not good weather for flying, so Peter pressed forward on the ground, in Indian fashion. He could not help but notice that the island was strangely quiet, as though it were still in shock from the recent battle. As Peter walked, he looked for things the boys might have dropped. He had trained them, if ever taken, to leave such clues. Slightly, for example, was to cut trees and Curly to drop seeds. Wendy knew to drop her handkerchief. But he saw nothing. He swore a terrible oath: “Hook or me this time!”
text.T1: Eeci ciindi bakabavwiila. Ibana banji bakali kukamba. Bamwi batamvwi, bakali kufubaala,pele banji bakai kukamba-kusikila kukamba nokwakamana, nobakabakasya kuli bamanyina nkaambo bakali kusabila. Tinker Bell wakafutulwa akujokela mbwakabede, takayeeya akulumba bana bakasyoma-nokuba kuti wakalikuyanda kuba panisa baya bakatondezyede buyanga, “Lino tweleede kufutula Wendy!” Peter wakasyomezya. Oh, kuti kukamba kwakonzya kubeleka kabotu. “Inzya, inzya, lyoonse twelede kuyeeya Wendy,” Tink Bell wakaamba wakaamba katakkomene. Akali masiku aatali mabotu kuuluka, cakapa Peter kuti aa kalisye aansi, mbuli ba mweenye. Wakazoobona kuti aa nsumbu aliumwine ciggambya, mbuli kuti iciggambidwe azyakali kucitika munkondo zyainda. Peter naakali kweenda, wakalikulangaula zintu zyakalosya bana basankwa. Wakali baisyide kusiya zyakuzibisya kuti naa baba nbajatwa. Mbuli Slightly wakli kukonzya kugonka zisamu mpoona Curly kulosya nseke. Wendy wakazyi kulosya katambala. Pele kwiina ncaakabna. Wakasyomezya. “Hook naa mebo cino ciindi!”

text.S1: Chapter 14 - The Pirate Ship
text.T1: Caandaano ikkumi aa zyone – Ibwato Bwa Zigwebenga

text.S1: The Jolly Roger lurked low in the water like a waiting crocodile. The pirates sat on deck in the cool fog of the night, playing cards or napping. Hook could not play, or rest. Distracted, he paced the deck. It wasn’t that he was unhappy. After all, Peter had been removed, and the lost boys were soon to walk the plank. And yet, for some reason, his happiness was incomplete. Like Mr. Darling, Hook worried about things like breeding and class—what he liked to call “good form.” He, too, cared very much what people—especially people with good form—thought about him. Whenever he did something, or wanted something, he would ask himself, Is it good form to do or want such a thing? Sometimes he worried that it was not good form to think so much about good form.
text.T1: Ibwato bwiitwa Jolly Roger bwakali mumeenda mbuli ciwena uulindila. Izigwebenga zyakakkala ansi mubwato mumuo uutontola wamasiku, akusobana nsolo naa koona asyoonto. Hook taakali kukonzya kusobana naa kulyokezya. Wakai kuzinguluka ansi ya bwato. Taakanyemede. Pele taakakkomene kumaninina. Mbuli ba Darling, Hook wakali kupenga kuyeeya zinyina mpindu-nzyaakali kwiita “zintu zibotu.” Awalo wakali kubikkila maano kubantu-kapati bantu bali aa zintu zibotu-kuyeeya ali nguwe. Kufumbwa kuti wacita cintu comwe naa kuyeeya comwe, wakali kulibuzya, nsena ncintu cibotu kucita naa kuyanda cintu camusyobo ooyu? Zimwi ziindi wakali kuyeeya kuti tacili cintu cibotu kuyeeya zintu zibotu.

text.S1: But Hook wasn’t just unhappy; he was also lonely. As hard as it was to believe, Hook hurt. He had no children to love him. It was strange that this should bother him, but it was true all the same. In a way, Hook envied Smee. Smee was the least threatening of the pirates, and yet the children loved him. Michael had even tried on his spectacles. Thinking about the children’s preference for Smee made Hook angry, and he decided to finish off the boys once and for all. “Are the children tied up so they can’t fly away?” he yelled. “Ay, ay,” came the reply. “Well, then, hoist them up!” The boys were brought up on deck before him. “Six of you will walk the plank tonight,” Hook announced, “but I have room for two cabin boys. Who will it be? Which of you will come to work for me?” Tootles stepped forward. “I would, sir, but I don’t think my mother would want me to be a pirate. Would yours, Slightly?”
text.T1: Hook taakali kukkala uutakkomene biyo, pele wakali lendeledwe. Nokuba kuti cakali cintu ciyumu kusyoma, Hook wakali kumvwa moyo kucisa. Wakanyina bana bakali kumuyanda. Cakali kugambya kuti eeci cakali kumucisa, pele akali masimpe. Munzila iimwi, Hook wakali kunyomenena Smee. Smee ngowatakali kuyoosya bwini akati ka zigwebenga, pesi bana bakali kumuyanda. Micheal walo wakai kusama amagilazi aakwe. Hook wakali kunyema nakali kuyeya bana mbobakali kuyanda Smee, mpoona wakayeeya kumanizya basankwa boonse. “Sena bana bali angidwe kutegwa tabatiji?” waka kwiila. Ay, ay,” mbwakavwiila. “Lino, kumubakkwezeka mujulu!” Ibasankwa bakabakkwezyeka mujulu akubabika aansi abwato. “nomuli cisambomwe mulaenda azisamu masiku aano,” Hook wakabazyibya,” pesi ndili jisi kwakukkala bobilo basankwa. Nguni? Nguni uuboola kundibelekele?” Tootles wakaswena kumbele. “Ndime, badaala, pele nsezyi na baama balandizumizya. Hena mbombubo, Slightly?”

text.S1: “I don’t think so,” Slightly said. The twins agreed, as did the others. None of their mothers would approve. “Enough!” Hook cried. He pointed to John. “You!” he said. “You look like you have a little pluck in you. Do you want to be a pirate?” Secretly, John had always dreamed of being a pirate. He even had a pirate name picked ou
text.T1: Tabusi mbondiyeeya,” Slightly wakamba. Bana bamaanga bakazumizya, mbuli bamwi. kunyina bamanyina banga bazumizya. “Mbubo!” Hook wakalila. Wakatondeka kuli John. “Yebo!” wakaamba. “Sena ulayanda kuba cigwebenga?” Alike alilwakwe wakali kunyomenenwa kuba cigwebenga. wakali jisi azyina: Red-Handed Jack. Mujwi lya munsi, wakalyambilila eeci kuli Hook. “Ino, Red-Handed Jack ndizyina libotu!” Hook wakaamba. “Ino mebo inga ndaba ni kuti nda musangana?” Micheal wakabuzya. “Blackbeard Joe,” Hook wakaamba. Micheal wakakkomana. “Sena tucinolemekwaku mwami wa ku England?” John wakabuzya. “Peepe!” Hook wakavwiila. “Welede kusyomezya, Down aa mwami!” “Oh,” John wakaamba, akulosya meso. Takonzyi kuzonda England. “Mubwini, mutabikii maano.”

text.S1: “Then you shall walk the plank, too!” Hook roared. The boys went pale as they saw Jukes and Cecco preparing the piece of wood off which they would walk before falling into the water. But they tried to look brave, especially when Wendy was brought up. She was the brave one. She emerged from belowdecks wearing a dark scowl. “Are you ready to watch your boys walk the plank?” Hook asked her sweetly. “Do you have any last words for them?” “I do,” Wendy replied in a loud, clear voice. “I have a message from their real mothers, and it is a hope that their sons will die bravely and with their heads held high, like proper English gentlemen.” The boys all stood up a little higher, trying to be brave, to do this one last thing for their mothers and Wendy. “Tie her up to the mast,” Hook yelled, and Smee obeyed. “I’ll save you if you promise to be my mother,” Smee whispered to Wendy.
text.T1: “Nkkokuti ulaendela acipulanga, ayebo!” Hook wakatongela. Ibasankwa baka tyompwa nobakabona Jukes aa Cecco kababamba izipulanga aakweendela kabatana wida mumeenda. Pele bakasola kuboneka kuyuma, ikapati nobakamuleta Wendy. Ngowakali muyumu. Wakazwida aansi ya bwato kamemenyene. “Sena ulilibambide kubona basankwa kabaenda azipulanga?” Hook wakamubuzya kabotu kabotu. “Sena ulijisi majwi amamanino ku basankwa?” “Inzya,” Wendy wakavwiila, ajwi liyumu. “Ndila makani kuzwa kuli ba manyina, alimwi ndilobozya kuti ibana babo bafwe cabusicamba akunyamuna mitwe yabo mujulu, mbuli basankwa baku England.” Ibasankwa boonse bakanyamuka asyoonto mujulu, kusola busicamba, ikucita cintu eeci camamanino kuli bamanyina aa Wendy. “Amumwangilile ku kasamu kandembela,” Hook wakakwiila, mpoona Smee wakatobela. “Ndilakufutula kuti usyomezye kuti ulaba bamaama,” Smee wakapetekezya kuli Wendy.
