text.S1: “I would rather have no children at all,” she replied scornfully, even though she had to admit that Smee was the nicest pirate of them all. The boys tried to be brave as they were put on the plank. In the end, however, they were only little boys, and they could not stop themselves from shaking and shivering with fear. Wendy turned her head. She couldn’t look.
text.T1: “Ndalombozya kutaba aabana,” wakavwiila cakutalemeka, nokubakuti wakaelede kuzumina kuti Smee ngowakalomene akati ka zigwebenga. Ibasankwa bakasola kulipa busicamba nobakali kuba bika azipulanga. Kumamanino, pele, bakali biyo basankwa bacili bana, bakakakilwa kuleka kubimba akuzungaana akaambo kakuyoowa. Wendy wakalanga kulubazu kumbi.

text.S1: Hook took a step toward her. He wanted her to watch the boys walk, one by one, off the end of the plank. But he never reached her. He never got to hear her beg for the boys’ lives. Instead he heard tick, tick, tick. It was the terrible tick, he realized, of the crocodile. All eyes were suddenly on Hook. It was almost a sad sight to see this brave pirate captain positively freeze in terror as the ticking sound came nearer and nearer. Even his claw hung inactive, as if it, too, were afraid. Hook fell to the deck and crawled as far from the sound as he could go. “Hide me,” he begged, and the pirates gathered grimly around him in the center of the boat. The lost boys glanced over the side of the boat to look for the crocodile, but to their surprise they saw Peter approaching instead! He signaled them not to give any sign, and kept on ticking and climbing.
text.T1: Hook wakbweza ntaamu kuya kumbele.wakali kuyanda kulangilila basankwa kabaenda azipulanga omwe omwe. Pele taakasika kuli nguwe. Takamumvwa kukombelezya abuumi bwa basankwa. Ncaakali kumvwa biyo kwakali kulia kwa nkoloko. Kwakali kulila kuyoosya, wakayeeya kuti, ngu ciwena. Oonse meso mpoona mpoona akali ali Hook. Cakali kuyoosya kubona cigwebenga nciinga sicamba kaciyoowede kulila kwankoloko nokwakaswena munsi munsi. Amala aakweakaboneka kubula nguzu, mbuli kuti aalo akali yowede. Hook wakawida aansi mubwato akukalaba kuzwa ku kusabila kwankoloko. “Amundisise,” waka kombelezya, azigwebenga zyaka muzinguluka akati ka bwato. Ibasankwa bakaswekeede bakalanga kumbali ya bwato kuti babone ciwena, pele bakabona Peter uzaabuboola! Wakatondezya kuti batapi cakutondezya, akutolelela kulila kwa nkoloko akutanta.

text.S1: Chapter 15 - Hook or Me This Time!
text.T1: Caandaano Ikkumi aa zyosano - Hook naa Mebo Cino Ciind

text.S1: Odd things often happen without us even noticing. Such was the case with Pe- ter’s ticking. A few minutes earlier, on his way to the boat, Peter had passed by the crocodile and noticed that he was no longer making noise. After a momen- t’s thought, he realized that the clock must have finally wound down. Peter knew that the beasts on the island feared the crocodile and avoided the ticking sound. Without even thinking about it, he began to imitate the ticking so that he could pass through the forest unbothered. The crocodile heard this, and perhaps because he missed the sound, he began to follow Peter. As Peter swam, newly ticking, to the boat, he had one thought about the upcoming battle: Hook or me this time. Only one of them would walk away alive, he vowed.
text.T1: Izintu zinyongene zivwula kucitika katutakubwene. Eeci ncecakali kucitika kuli Peter naa kali kulila mbuli nkoloko. Kaindi kasyoonto kacitana citika,naakali kuunka ku bwato, Peter wakainda munsi aa ciwena abujana kuti wakaleka kusabila. Nokwakainda kaindi kasyoonto, wakayeeya kuti inkoloko ndiza yakaleka kubeleka. Peter wakalizyi kuti izinyama aa nsumbu zyakali kuyoowa ciwena mpoona zyakali kusola kuzimaanya kulila kwa nkoloko. Kakunyina akuyeeya, wakatalika kutobelezya kulila kwa nkoloko kutegwa acikonzye kwiinda musokwe kakunyina kupenzyegwa. Ciwena wakmvwa eeci, ndiza nkaambo kakuti kunyina kusabila nkwakali kumvwa, wakatalika kutobela Peter. Peter naakali kusamba, iikulila kwa nkoloko kumbi, ku bwato, wakalijisi muzeezo omwe ankondo yakali kuboola: Hook naa mebo sunu. Omwe biyo ngowakali kukonzya kufutuka, wakasyomezya.

text.S1: One of the pirates spotted Peter as he was climbing up the side of the boat. Before he could cry out, John clamped his hands over the pirate’s mouth. The other boys quickly caught him and tossed him overboard with a gentle splash. The pirates were now looking over the other side of the boat, searching for the crocodile. Peter, who had temporarily stopped ticking, tiptoed into a cabin belowdecks. “I think it’s gone, Captain,” Smee said. “Well, then, here’s to Johnny Plank!” Hook cried, in an even worse mood now because the boys had seen him scared. He started to sing: “Yo ho, yo ho, the frisky plank, you walks along it so, till it goes down and you goes down to the dark water below!” Hook paused.
text.T1: Omwe wa ziggebenga wakabona Peter naakali kutanta mujulu ku mbali ya bwato. Katana lila John wakabika kwanza kwakwe amulomo wa ciggwebenga. Ibasankwa bamwi bakamujata akumusowaila. iziggwebenga zyakali kulangaula ku lubazu umwi lwa bwato, kulangaula ciwena. Peter, iwakalekede kumvwika mbuli nkoloko, wakasobelela kunjila mukaanda aansi aa bwato. "Ndayeeya kuti wainka, nobasololeli,” Smee wakamba. Hook wakalila, munzila, iitaluleme, lino, nkaambo kakuti ibasankwa bakamubona mbwakayoowede. Wakatalika kwiimba: “Yo ho, yo ho, izipulanga zyakusobanya, weenda azyalo, kusikila ziunke aansi anduwe uunke aansi mumeenda mukati!” Hook wakaumuna.

text.S1: “Now, tell me,” he said, not unkindly. “Would you like a bit of a snack before you go? There are some sandwiches in the cabin.” “No!” the boys cried, not only because they weren’t hungry, but because Peter was hiding in the cabin. “I can’t very well send you off to the depths below on empty stomachs, can I?” Hook asked. “Jukes, go get the sandwiches.” “Ay, ay,” Jukes said, and went inside. Within seconds there was a dreadful cry from inside the cabin. The cry was followed by a strange crowing sound, which confused the pirates but which the boys understood perfectly. “What is that noise?” Hook asked. “Is that a bird? Someone go check on Bill Jukes.” The Italian Cecco went inside for a peek and then ran out, pale. “Bill Jukes is gone,” he reported.
text.T1: “Lino, kondaambia,” wakaamba, kutali mububi. “Mulayanda kakulya kasyoonto nomutana unka? Kuli tunkwa mukaanda.” “Peepe!” ibasankwa bakalila, kutali biyo kuti nkaambo bakali aazala, pele nkaambo kakuti Peter wakayubide mukaanda. “Nsekonzi kuti ndikutume aansi ameenda kakunyina kulya, te kai?” Hook wakabuzya. “Jukes, koya ukalete tunkwa.” “Ay, ay,” Jukes wakaamba, mpoona wakanjila mukati. Mukaindi kasyoonto kwakali kulila kuyoosyakuzwa mukaanda mukati. Ikulila kwakatobela aa kukwiila, icakanyonganya ziggwebenga pele basankwa balo bakalizyi kabotu. “Ino kusabila ooko?” Hook wakabuzya. “Sena nciyuni? Umwi akaakulange Bill Jukes.” Cecco waku Italy wakanjila mukati akusondela mpoona wakatija, katyompedwe. “Bill Jukes waunka,” wakatola makani.

text.S1: “Gone?” the other pirates asked. “I can’t see what—it’s too dark in there—but there’s something in there, crowing,” Cecco said. “Go and bring it to me,” Hook demanded. “Don’t make me,” Cecco cried, but seeing Hook flex his claw, Cecco obeyed. Within seconds there was another screech and then more crowing. “Who’s going to bring me that rooster?” Hook demanded. “Did you volunteer, Starkey? My hook seems to think you did.” “I’d rather swing,” Starkey said in a low voice, and the rest of the pirates mumbled their agreement. “Is this mutiny?” Hook said. “With Starkey as the ringleader?” He extended his claw. “Perhaps you would like to shake my hand, Starkey,” he said. Starkey looked around for help but found none. Hook advanced with a gleam in his eye. Before Hook could get him, Starkey jumped on the pirates’ cannon, shimmied out to its edge, and threw himself into the sea.
text.T1: “Waunka?” ziggwebenga zimwi zyakabuzya. “Nsekonzi kubona nzi—kulasiya ookuya-pele kuli ciliko okuya, ikulila,” Cecco wakaamba. “Koya ukacilete,” Hook wakamutuma. “Uta ndipangi,” Cecco wakalila, pele kubona Hook wakanjizya mala, Cecco wakamvwiida. Kaindi kasyoonto kwakali ku syamba mpoona ikukwiila alimwi. Nguni utindiletele mukombwe uuya?” Hook wakayanda. “Sena waka lipa, Starkey? Hook wangu waboneka mbuli kuti wakalipa.” “Cabota ndazinguluka,” Starkey wakaamba ajwi libombede, mpoona ziggwebenga zyacaaa zyaka zuminizya. “Sena ooyu ngu Mutiny?” Hook wakaamba. “Aa Starkey kali musololeli wabo?” wakatondezya mala aakwe. “Ndiza uyanda kujuzya maanza angu, Starkey,” wakaamba. Starkey wakalangaula mumbali lyakwe ibakumugwasya pele kwakanyina. Hook wakaswena akumwesya meso. Hook katana mubweza, Starkey wakasotokela ntobolo ya ziggwebenga, akuijata nkili kumbali, akulisowela mumulonga.

text.S1: “Never mind,” Hook muttered. “I’ll go get that rooster myself!” A minute later, Hook came staggering out without his lantern. “Something blew out my light,” he said, shaking. “And Cecco is missing.” Pirates are a superstitious bunch, and this was too much for them.
text.T1: “Utapengi,” Hook wakalabaika. “Ndilaunka ndikamubweze mukombwe ndelike!” Kaindi kasyoonto, Hook wakaboola kadadalika kakunyina mumuni. “Cintu cimwi cazima mumuni wangu,” wakaamba, akubimba. “Mpoona Cecco wasweeka.” Iziggwebenga zilaanguzu zyazyeelo, eeci caindilila kuli nzizyo.

text.S1: “This ship’s cursed,” one of them muttered. “Haunted,” the others agreed. Knowing it was Peter, Michael giggled. Hook noticed this. It gave him an idea. “Open the cabin door and push the lost boys in,” he suggested. “If they kill the bird, so much the better, and if it kills them, we’re none the worse. We’re going to kill them anyway.” The boys pretended to cry and struggle as they were pushed inside. “Now let’s listen,” Hook said, and the pirates all crowded around the door. Meanwhile, Peter had found the key to unlock the boys’ chains. They looked for weapons while Peter snuck out through an opposite porthole and cut Wendy’s bonds. They could have flown away, but Peter had vowed that it was Hook or him this time. He told Wendy to go hide with the boys, wrapped himself in her cloak, and took her place on the mast.
text.T1: “Ibwato bwakasinganisigwa.” Omwe wabo wakalabalika. “bulijisi madaimona,” bacaaa bakazumizya. Micheal wakaseka nkaambo wakalizyi kuti ngu Peter. Hook wakabona eeci. Cakamupa muzeezo. “Kojula mulyango wakaanda mponona utonkele basankwa bakasweekede mukati,” wakapa muzeezo. “Kuti naa bajae ziyuni, inga caba kabotu, lino kuti zyaba jaya, tatubijide kwiinda. Tulabajaya nokuba boobo.” Ibasankwa bakalicengezya kulia akupenga nobakabatonkela mukati. “Lino atuswiilile,” Hook wakaamba, mpoona ziggwebenga zyoonse zyakaboola amuyango. Cimwi ciindi Peter wakajana kabulo kaku kkinuzya nketani. Bakayandaula zyakulwanya Peter naakazwa kwiinda mukapulo akuddunsula zyakangide Wendy. Nobakauluka, pele Peter wakasyomezya kuti ngu Hook naa nguwena cino ciindi. Wakaambila Wendy kuyooyuba abasankwa, akulizambaila mulembo, akubbweza cilao cakwe acisamu casaili cabwato.

text.S1: Then he took a deep breath and crowled. The pirates were terrified. Had the crow killed all the boys? Would it kill them next? “Lads,” Hook suggested, “perhaps our run of bad luck is due to the lady we have on board. Let’s get rid of her and see if our luck changes.” “Throw her overboard,” the pirates cried, and rushed at the figure in the cloak. “There’s no one who can save you now,” the pirates hissed. “There’s one person,” the figure at the mast replied in a strangely low voice. “Peter Pan!” As he spoke, Peter threw off the cloak and revealed his face. Suddenly everyone understood what was happening. “Get him!” Hook cried, but not very convincingly. He sensed that Peter was about to best him once again, and it was too much for him. Hook’s fierce heart broke.
text.T1: Mpoona wakayoya akukalaba. Iziggwebenga zyakanyongana. Sena mukombwe wakbajaya boonse basankwa? Sena cicilila ulajaya mbabo? “Nobenzuma,” Hook wakapa muzeezo, “ndiza twabula coolwe akaambo ka musimbi ngo tujisi okuno. Katumusowa tubone naa coolwe cesu cilacinca.” “Katumusowa,” ziggwebenga zyakalila, akulundukila kucintu cakazambailidwe mumulembo. “Kunyina uukonzya kukufutula lino,” ziggwebenga zyakasyomezya. “Kuli muntu omwe,” Iwakangidw kucisamu wakavwiila ajwi lyakali kugambya. “Peter Pan!” Nakali kwambaula, Peter wakasowa mulembo akulitondezya kumeso. Mpoona boonse bakazyiba cakali kucitika. “Amumubweze!” Hook wakalila, pele icakutasyoma.wakayeeya kuti Peter ulamwiinda maano alimwi, eeci cakamumana nguzu. Imoyo wa Hook wakaanduka.

text.S1: “Fight!” Peter cried. The boys burst out of the cabin, and a fierce battle with the pirates began. The pirates were stronger, but the boys were smarter and fought in pairs. Some of the pirates jumped overboard, while others ran away and hid. Finally only Hook was left. The boys surrounded him. Even alone, he was strong and brave and kept them away using nothing but his hook. He lifted one boy up with it and used him as a shield. Peter jumped into the circle. “Stand back!” he cried. “This man is mine!” For a long time, the enemies just looked at each other. “So,” Hook said. “This is all your doing.” “It is,” Peter crowed. “Cocky, arrogant boy,” Hook said. “Prepare to meet your end.” “And you!” Peter cried.
text.T1: “Kulwana!” Peter wakalila. Ibasankwa bakazwa mukaanda, mpoona nkondo iiyoosya aziggwebenga yakatalika. Iziggwebenga zyakali aanguzu, pesi basankwa balo bakali cenjede akulwana bobilo bobilo. Zimwi ziggwebenga zyakasotoka, mpoona zyacaala zyakatija akuyooyuba. Kumamanino kwakacaala biyo Hook. Ibasankwa bakamuzinguluka. Aciindi nali aike, wakali muyumu akubakonga kubelesya biyo meja. Wakanyamuna musankwa omwe ameja akumubelesya mbuli cakulikwabilila. Peter wakasotokela mukati. “Kamujoka munsi!” wakalila. “Ooyu musankwa nguwangu!” Kwakaindi kasyoonto basinkondonyina bakalangana. “Pele,” Hook wakaamba. “Eeyi micito yako yoonse.” “Inzya,” Peter wakakwiila. “Cocky, kulisumpula,” Hook wakaamba. “Kolibambila kuswangana amamanino aako.” “Anduwe!” Peter wakalila.

text.S1: A dramatic sword fight followed, during which both man and boy fought bravely. Finally, Hook moved to get Peter with his iron hand. Peter ducked and lunged with his sword, piercing Hook in the ribs. Hook stared down at the wound in surprise. As you may recall, the only blood he could not stand to look at was his own. He dropped his sword. “Now,” the boys cried. It was time to finish Hook off! They lunged forward, but Peter put up his hand, stopping them. “Pick up your sword,” he told Hook, who obeyed. “What are you?” Hook asked. “How is it possible that you have beaten me? You cannot be just an ordinary boy.” “I am not an ordinary boy,” Peter said. “I am young. I am joyful. I am a little bird that just escaped its shell. And, above all, I am fair.” Hook narrowed his eyes. “Enough,” he said. “Back to the fight!”
text.T1: Kwakacitika nkondo mpati, yakalwana balombwana abasankwa. Kumamanino, Hook wakaswenena kuli Peter akwanza kwakwe kwa nsimbi. Peter wakayasa Hook mutubambo amapanga. Hook wakalanga aa cilonda akugambwa. Kuti mulayeeya ibulowa mbwatakali kuyanda kubona mbulowa bwakwe. Wakalosya panga lyakwe aansi. “Lino,” basankwa bakalila. Cakali cindi cakumanizya Hook! Bakaswenena kumbele, pele Peter wakanyamuna kwaanza, kubakasya. “Kobweza panga lyako,” wakambila Hook, mpoona wakamvida. ‘Uli nzi?” Hook wakabuzya. “Caubauba buti kuti unduume? Tokonzi kuba musankwa buyo.” “Inzya nseli musankwa buyo,” Peter wakaamba. “Ndili mwana. Ndila kkomana. Ndili kayuni kasyoonto ikazwa biyo mucipapa ca maji. Mpoona atala aazyoonse ndili kabotu.” Hook wakacesya meso. “Zyavula,” wakaingula.” Kujokela kukulwana!”

text.S1: He swung his sword around wildly. Anyone else would have been hit, but Peter ducked as if the wind were working to protect him, blowing him just the right distance this way and that. Desperate, Hook ran off and returned with a grenade. “In two minutes,” he cried when he returned, “this ship will be blown to bits!” But Peter just picked up the grenade and threw it overboard. Hook hated how calmly and bravely Peter was behaving. Peter was showing . . . could it possibly be . . . good form? The thought of this was too much to bear. As the boys drew closer, Hook barely even saw them. His mind was elsewhere—back in his school days when he had first learned of good form.
text.T1: Wakazingulusya panga lyakwe canguzu. Nakali muntu uumbi nakamuyasa, pele peter wakakwabililwa mbuli kuti imuo wakali kubelekela akumukwabilila. Hook wakatija naakajoka wakali jisi ibbomba. “Mumaminiti obilo,” wakalilanaakajoka, “Oobu bwato bula bboloka!” Pele Peter wakalibweza ibbomba akulisowela kule. Hook taakali kuyanda Peter mbwakali kutazungaana alimwi akutayoowa. Peter wakali kutondezya . . . . kuba kabotu? Imuzeezo ooyu wakali kucisa. Ibasankwa nobakasika munsi munsi, Hook taakamubona akumubona. Imizeezo yakwe yakali biyo kumbi – izyakaindi naakacili kucikolo naakatalika kuzyiba zya kuba kabotu!

text.S1: Seeing Peter advancing with his sword, Hook turned and stood at the edge of the boat, looking down at the sea. He saw that the crocodile was there waiting for him. Peter kicked him overboard. As Hook fell, he realized, much to his delight, that this kick was actually very bad form. Feeling superior, Hook went happily to the crocodile. With the fight at last over, Wendy emerged from the cabin below. The boys danced around her, pointing out all of the places where they had fought. “Yes, yes, you are very brave boys,” Wendy said, “but it’s past your bedtime. Let’s get into the pirates’ bunks, messy as they are, and get some rest.” All of the boys went down to sleep except Peter. He fell asleep up on deck, next to the pirates’ cannon. Wendy sat next to him the whole time, softly rubbing his head to protect him from bad dreams.
text.T1: Naakabona Peter uzabuboola aa panga lyakwe, Hook wakajokela akwiimikila kumbali kwabwato, akulanga mumulonga. Wakabona kuti ciwena wakali mumeenda uamulindila. Peter wakamubbakela. Hook naakawa, wakayeeya kuti kubbakela ooku kwakali cintu cibyabi. Kulimvwa kusumpuka, Hook wakainka kakkomene kuli ciwena. Nokwakamana kulwana, Wendy wakazwa mukaanda. ibasankwa bakazyana akumuzinguluka, akutondeke zyoonse zilao mpobakali kulwanina. “Inzya, inzya, mulibayumu nobasankwa,” Wendy wakaamba, “pele ciindi cakoona cainda kaindi. Atuunke ku malo aziggwebenga , nokuba kuti ali addoti, tusole koona.” Boonse basankwa bakainka mukoona kuzwisya buyo Peter. Wakaona ansi mubwato, munsi munsi aa ntobolo ya ziggwebenga. Wendy wakakkaa munsimunsi lyakwe ciindi coonse, akulikwezya kabotu kaboyu mumutwe kutegwa ataloti ziloto zibyabi.

text.S1: Chapter 16 - The Return Home
text.T1: Caandano Ikkumi aa cisambomwe – Ikujoka Ku Nga`nda

text.S1: Everyone woke up early next day. It was a very long journey back home and the sea was quite rough, so the going would be slow. With slight alterations from Wendy, the pirates’ clothes fit the boys just fine—pants cut off at the knees and jaunty hats and eye patches. The scowls they added themselves. Peter, of course, was the captain. Nibs and John were first and second mates. None of the boys had any training in sailing a pirate ship, but they pre- tended they did—which in Neverland is always enough. As they worked, secur- ing jibs and sheets and all sorts of other sailor words, they sang and cheered heartily. Finally, they got the ship out into the open sea, let loose her sails, and started for England. It was time.
text.T1: Boonse baka buka kubuceedo ibuzuba bwaka cilila. Lwakali lweendo lulamfu lubyabi lwakujokela ku maanda, ameenda akali amagunyugunyu, cakapa kuti lweendo lumuke. Wendy wakasola kucesya zisani zyaziggwebenga, mpoona zyakabaelela ibasankwa boonse. Peter, wakali ngomusololeli. Nibs aa John bakali beenzinyina bakutanguna aa bakacilila. Kunyina musankwa naba omwe wakaiide kwenzya bwato, pele bakali kuli cengezya buyo kuti balicizyi – ku Neverland nceciyandika. Nobakali kubeleka bakali buyaa bwimba akukkomana camoyo omwe. Kumamanino, bakagusya bwato akububika mumeenda kutegwa batalike lweendo lwabo kuya ku England. Cakasika ciindi.

text.S1: Peter had decided that they would sail as far as the Azore Islands, and then fly the rest of the way. He stood at the wheel and addressed his pirate crew. “You scum,” he cried. “You mangy dogs! There will be no mutiny on my ship, or else!” The boys knew that Peter was only pretending to be a pirate, but—unlike them—he couldn’t always tell the difference. He was even wearing Hook’s old clothes. And so they laughed, but nervously. Let us leave the boys on the boat and travel back to the Darlings’ home. It seems a shame to have neglected it all this time. But Mrs. Darling wouldn’t have wanted us to focus on her when we could, instead, be keeping an eye on her little ones. It would serve those naughty children right if their beds were not made and their room was all dusty and their parents weren’t even home, having forgotten all about them.
text.T1: Peter wakasyomezya kuti bayoenda kusikila kule mbuli ku Azore Islands, mpoona lwacaala lweendo bakauluke. Wakaimikila kuvwili akupa malailile kui boonse bakali mubwato. “No matombe,” wakalila. Nobabwa baciswa! Kunonyina bazange mubwato bwangu, buyo buyo!” Ibasankwa bakalizyi kuti Peter wakalikulicengezya buyo kuba ciggwebenga, pele-kutali mbuli mbabo-takali kukonzya kutondezya kwiimpana. Wakali kusama azisani zyakaindi zya Hook. Mpoona bakaseka, pesi kabayoowede. “Katubasiya basankwa mpoona tujoke kung`anda ya ba Darling. Cilausisya ikutaibikila maano ciindi coonse eeci. Pele bamuka Darling tabakonzyi kuyanda kuti tubabikile maano, pele inga bayanda kuti tubikile maano kubana basyoonto. Kutegwa baya bana batayandi kuyala bulo kabapaniswa alimwi mobaona mwakali lusuko abazyali babo teebakali kujanika kung`anda, kabali babaluba.

text.S1: Of course, this is not the case, and this is the kind of thing children count on so they can have their adventures. The only difference from when they left is that Nana is no longer chained. Mr. Darling could admit when he was wrong. The second the children had flown, he had invited Nana back into the house, where she had stayed. Then, however, he had done a most unusual thing. He had gone down on all fours and crawled into Nana’s kennel himself! Mrs. Darling had begged him to come out, but he had said, “Not until the children come back.” Every morning, the kennel was carried with Mr. Darling in it to the office, and then back again at night. This is my punishment, and it is proper, he thought. Given how much he cared what other people thought of him, it was a hard punishment indeed. People laughed and pointed, peering inside, and he became known as “Darling in the Kennel.”
text.T1: Inzya, takali kaambo aaka, alimwi nzezintu ibana nzyobabala kutegwa kabajana kuyaabwendeenda. Ikwimpana kuliko kuzwa nobakaunka nkwakuti Nana wakaleka kwaangililwa. Ba Darling bakalikukonzya kuzumina kuti balubizya. Ibana mbobakaunkila, wakaita Nana kujoka kung`anda, nkwakali kukkala. Mpoona, pele, wakacita cintu cita citwi. Wakainka kusobana nsolo akusobelela mu kaanda ka babwa lwakwe mwini! Ba muka Darling baka mukombelezya kuti azwe anzee, pele wakaamba kuti, “cita kuti bana bajoke” Lyoonse mafumofumo kaanda ka babwa kakali kubwezegwa aba Darling kukatola ku ofesi, alimwi akukajosya masiku. Ooku nkokundipanisa camasimpe, wakayeeya. Ibantu bakaseka akutondeka, akusondelamukati, mpoona wakaitwa kuti “Darling Wamu Kaanda Kababwa.”

text.S1: The true beauty of his sacrifice, however, soon shone through. When the public learned why he had confined himself to Nana’s kennel, they began to follow him, not to laugh, but to praise. Girls asked for his autograph. Society types invited him to dinner—in his kennel and black tie, of course. KENNEL—one headline in the papers read—THE NEW GOOD FORM. It was what he had always wanted, and yet Mr. Darling could not enjoy his new status in the community. Mrs. Darling was sad as well. When she managed to fall asleep, usually in her chair by the fire, she would dream of her children. This night was no different. Tonight, however, let us whisper in her ear that the children are on their way home. But perhaps we should not, because she has woken up with a start, calling out their names. There is a chill in the air, but the Darlings would never dare close the win- dow. It must always stay open for the children. Little do they know that, at this moment, there is someone at that window. It is Peter. He has flown ahead, with Tinker Bell.
text.T1: Ibubotu bwa kulipa, pele bwakalibonya. Ibantu boonse nobakazyiba ncaaka syomede mukaanda ka babwa ika Nana, bakatalika kumutobela, kutali kumuseka pele kumu lumbaizya. Ibasimbi bakali kumulomba kuti abalembe naa ku saina mumaanza aabo. Bamwi bantu bakali kumutamba kuyoolya cakulya camasiku-mukaanda kababwa kasamide aa tai iisiya. IKAANDA KA BABWA-imutwe wamakani mbowakabalwa-ICINTU CINYOWANI CIBOTU. Ncaakali kuyanda lyoonse, pele ba Darling tebakakkomana mbwakatalika kwiitwa mumunzi. Bamuka Darling bakali tyompedwe abalo. Nobakacikonzya koona, mucuuno cabo munsimunsi amulilo, bakali kulota ibana babo. Pesi ndiza tutabaambili nkaambo kakuti, nobabuka basaanguna kwiita mazyina aabana babo. Wauluka kusolola, aa Tinker Bell.

text.S1: “Open,” Peter muttered bitterly, upon seeing the window. “I knew it would be.” Peter came up with one final plan. He would fly in quietly—so as not to wake Mr. Darling in his kennel—lock the window, and then sneak out through the front door. That way, when Wendy and the boys arrived, they would think their parents had forgotten about them, and they would have to come back to Neverland. Oh, this is a brilliant idea! he thought. He didn’t care about Wendy’s or her mother’s feelings—only about what he wanted. Children can be selfish that way. On his way back out of the house, however, Peter passed Mrs. Darling, sleeping by the fire. Seeing the dried tears on her puffy face, he felt guilty for the first time. I need her, too! he wanted to shout. We can’t both have her.

text.S1: The next morning, Mrs. Darling walked into her children’s bedroom and there they were, her babies, sound asleep as though they had never left. For a moment she thought she must have imagined them leaving in the first place. If it were not for Mr. Darling asleep in his kennel, she wouldn’t have been sure. Of course, the children were only pretending to sleep. Unable to stand the suspense any longer, they leaped from their beds, screaming, and ran to hug and kiss their mother.

text.S1: The boys went to school. They learned many things but, eventually, they for- got how to fly. They said it was because they were not practicing, but in truth it seemed that they no longer believed. And besides, they no longer had fairy dust to help them. Michael held on to his belief far longer than the others. And Peter did come back, as he’d promised, at the first sign of spring. Wendy had grown up since he’d seen her last, and she was worried he would notice. He didn’t. As usual, he thought and talked mainly about himself. She had been looking forward to reliving old adventures, but Peter had had so many new ones since theirs, he didn’t even remember them. “Who is Captain Hook?” he asked. “You don’t remember killing him and saving all of our lives?” ”I forget them when they are gone,” Peter replied. The next spring, Wendy waited, but Peter never came. “Maybe he’s sick,” Michael said. “Maybe we just imagined him.” Wendy cried at that. Could it be? But the following year, Peter came as planned. He didn’t even seem to realize he had missed a year. And that was the last time a girl named Wendy ever saw a boy named Peter Pan.

text.S1: Years later, when Wendy was married and living in the house she had grown up in, and all of the lost boys were men, she had a little girl named Jane, who loved to ask questions about Peter. Some days, Wendy could barely remember him—she had already forgotten many details—and was glad to tell someone about him before she forgot him entirely. “I know all about him, Mama,” Jane said. Wendy looked up, startled. “You do?” she asked. “I know him, too,” Jane said. Of course she did, Wendy realized, smiling sadly. All children did. One day, Wendy was sitting on Jane’s bed. She had just finished putting Jane to sleep when Peter flew in through the open window and dropped onto the floor. He was the same as ever. “Hello, Wendy,” he said, as though no time had passed. “Where are John and Michael?”

text.S1: Peter started to cry, so Wendy went downstairs to get him some warm milk. While she was gone, his sobs woke Jane. She knew at once who the boy was. By the time Wendy returned, Peter was once again laughing, and Jane was flying around the room with him, giggling. “He needs a mother, Mama,” Jane said. “I know,” Wendy said sadly. Wendy shut her eyes. “All right,” she whispered. And—just as Jane would with her own daughter, and Jane’s daughter would with her own daughter after that—Wendy watched her baby fly into the sky and off to Neverland until she was as small as the smallest star. Then, turning from the window, she whispered, “Good night,” to Peter, and to Jane, and to you.
